Session 4: DataFrames and Loading Data

Answers with reasoning for the 12 self-check items and the predict-then-run boxes, the real output of every lab solution with notes on what to check while you circulate, the answers to the two lesson pages' own Quick Quizzes, and the warm-up and exit-ticket answers.

Session 4 12 self-check items 5 lab pairs Confidential
How this key is organized

Self-check numbering matches the workbook: Q1 to Q6 are on Lesson 2.1, Q7 to Q12 on Lesson 2.2. Each item repeats the four options with the correct one marked and says why each wrong option is wrong. Every 'what does this print' answer and every lab output below was produced by running the code against the course data. The lesson pages' own five-question Quick Quizzes (three options each) are answered at the end of each lesson's part.

2.1 · DataFrames and Series: self-check

Q1
What does this print?
s = pd.Series([5, 6, 7], index=["x", "y", "z"])
t = pd.Series([1, 1], index=["z", "x"])
print((s + t).tolist())
A) [6, 7, 7]
B) [6.0, 7.0, nan]
C) [6.0, nan, 8.0]
D) A ValueError, because the lengths differ
Why: Series arithmetic aligns on labels: x gets 5 + 1, z gets 7 + 1, and y has no partner, so it is NaN. The NaN makes the whole result float.
A is wrong: That adds by position and treats the missing partner as nothing; pandas matches labels.
B is wrong: That adds by position (5 + 1, 6 + 1) and puts the gap last. The gap belongs to the label y, in the middle.
D is wrong: Two NumPy arrays of lengths 3 and 2 would raise an error. Two Series align and fill with NaN.
Q2
What does this print?
df = pd.DataFrame({"n": [10, 20, 30, 40]}, index=["a", "b", "c", "d"])
print(len(df.loc["a":"c"]), len(df.iloc[0:2]), df.iloc[-1, 0])
3 2 40
Why: A .loc slice includes its end label, so a, b, c are three rows. An .iloc slice leaves out the stop, so positions 0 and 1 are two rows. .iloc[-1, 0] is the last row, first column: 40.
Q3
In a table of 242 products, products.info() shows the line rating 234 non-null float64. What does that line tell you?
A) 8 products have no rating
B) There are 234 different ratings
C) The ratings are stored as text
D) 8 products have a rating of 0
Why: Non-Null Count is the number of values that are present. 242 rows minus 234 present leaves 8 missing ratings.
B is wrong: The number of distinct values comes from .nunique(), not from info().
C is wrong: The dtype on that line is float64: numbers. Text would say str.
D is wrong: A rating of 0 is a value and would be counted as non-null. Missing is not zero.
Q4
Which line correctly counts the products that are in the Tents category or cost less than $20?
A) (products["category"] == "Tents" | products["price"] < 20).sum()
B) (products["category"] == "Tents" or products["price"] < 20).sum()
C) products[("category" == "Tents") | ("price" < 20)].sum()
D) ((products["category"] == "Tents") | (products["price"] < 20)).sum()
Why: Each condition sits in its own parentheses, | combines them element by element, and .sum() of the mask counts the True rows.
A is wrong: Without parentheses | is evaluated before == and <, so Python tries "Tents" | products["price"] first and raises an error.
B is wrong: or wants a single True or False on each side; a Series is 242 of them (ValueError: ambiguous truth value).
C is wrong: It compares the text "category" with "Tents", not the column. The column must be written products["category"].
Q5
What does the last line print? (The second line also produces a warning.)
df = pd.DataFrame({"price": [10, 50, 90]})
df[df["price"] > 40]["price"] = 0
print(df["price"].tolist())
[10, 50, 90]
Why: Chained assignment. df[df["price"] > 40] creates a temporary table that behaves as a copy; the 0 is written into that and thrown away. df is unchanged and pandas warns with ChainedAssignmentError. The working form is df.loc[df["price"] > 40, "price"] = 0.
Q6
After top = products.sort_values("price", ascending=False), what is top.index[0]?
A) 0, because sorting renumbers the rows
B) The original row label of the most expensive product
C) The highest price
D) 241, the last position
Why: sort_values reorders the rows and their labels travel with them. The first row of top still carries the label it had in products (19 in the course data).
A is wrong: Rows are renumbered only if you add .reset_index(drop=True).
C is wrong: The index holds labels, not values. The highest price is top["price"].iloc[0].
D is wrong: 241 is the label of the last row of products; it has nothing to do with the sort.

2.1 · Predict, then run

P1
Labels travel with their values.
s = pd.Series([3, 1, 2], index=["c", "a", "b"])
print(s.sort_values().index.tolist(), s.iloc[0], s.loc["a"])
['a', 'b', 'c'] 3 1
Why: Sorting by value puts 1, 2, 3 in order, and their labels a, b, c come along. s itself is unchanged (sort_values returned a new Series), so .iloc[0] is still the first value typed, 3, and .loc["a"] is the value labeled a, 1.
P2
A piece of a table, changed.
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
part = df[df["x"] > 2]
part["x"] = 0
print(df["x"].sum(), part["x"].sum(), part.index.tolist())
10 0 [2, 3]
Why: part is an independent table from the moment it is created (copy-on-write), so setting its column to 0 leaves df at 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. part kept the row labels of the rows it came from: 2 and 3.
P3
Looking for missing values.
r = pd.Series([4.5, np.nan, 3.0])
print((r == np.nan).sum(), r.isna().sum(), r.mean())
0 1 3.75
Why: == np.nan is False everywhere because NaN is not equal to anything, so it counts 0. .isna() finds the one missing value. .mean() skips missing values: (4.5 + 3.0) / 2 = 3.75.

2.1 · Lab reference solutions

labs/module-04/l2_1-dataframes-series/busiest_days_solution.py

Question: Which were the five biggest store-days by revenue, were they promo days, and how often does a store pass $15,000 in a day?

How the solution works: sort_values("revenue", ascending=False) with a list of four column names gives the top-five table (nlargest(5, "revenue") is equally good). Two masks, big and promo, are built once and combined three ways: big.sum(), (big & promo).sum() and (big & ~promo).sum(). idxmax() returns the row label, which goes straight into .loc.

shape: (2903, 8)
date                 str
store                str
visitors           int64
transactions       int64
units              int64
revenue          float64
staff_on_duty      int64
promo_day          int64
columns with missing values: {'revenue': 6}
            date  store   revenue  promo_day
971   2024-08-31  Boise  27677.10          1
1331  2024-11-30  Boise  27199.33          1
2781  2025-11-30  Boise  25457.62          1
2777  2025-11-29  Boise  25419.88          1
1335  2024-12-01  Boise  25160.28          1
days above $15,000: 101
  of those, promo days: 36
  of those, ordinary days: 65
share of all promo days that pass $15,000: 37.5 %
best day    : label 971, 2024-08-31, Boise, $27,677.10
quietest day: label 115, 2024-01-29, Flagstaff, $2,093.79
  • All five biggest days are Boise on sale weekends (Labor Day weekend 2024, then the Black Friday weekends).
  • 101 store-days pass $15,000: 36 promo days and 65 ordinary days. The two parts must add up to the first number; if they do not, a pair of parentheses is missing.
  • Only 37.5% of promo store-days pass $15,000, so 'big day' and 'promo day' are not the same thing. A good discussion point.
  • A count of 0 for 'ordinary days' usually means ~ was applied to the combined mask instead of to promo.
  • The one column with missing values is revenue (6). Learners who skip TODO 1 will not notice that sort_values put those rows last.
labs/module-04/l2_1-dataframes-series/recommend_groups_solution.py

Question: Split the 0-to-10 'would you recommend us?' answers into promoters, passives and detractors, and compare Asheville shoppers with everyone.

How the solution works: The column starts as "no answer" and three .loc lines overwrite it. A comparison with NaN is False, so the 54 blanks are never overwritten. The score is the difference of two mask means among the rows that answered. The solution wraps that in a small function so it can be reused for the Asheville piece; learners may simply repeat the three lines.

(1800, 12)
group
passive      637
promoter     556
detractor    553
no answer     54
score, all shoppers: 0.2
Asheville responses: 202 | answered: 197
score, Asheville   : -14.7
rows of survey that say 'checked': 0
rows of asheville that say 'checked': 202
  • Group counts: passive 637, promoter 556, detractor 553, no answer 54 (total 1,800).
  • Score for all shoppers 0.2; for Asheville -14.7 (202 responses, 197 answered). Asheville is clearly worse: the same store that stands out later in the course for staff satisfaction.
  • The denominator is the people who answered (1,746 overall, 197 in Asheville), not all rows. Dividing by all 202 Asheville rows gives -14.4 instead of -14.7. Ask: 'What is your denominator?'
  • The last two lines must read 0 and 202: changing the Asheville piece never changes survey. No warning appears, because this is not chained assignment.
  • If the counts are wrong, read the three masks aloud: >= 9, .between(7, 8) (both ends included) and <= 6. A common slip is < 6, which leaves the 241 sixes as 'no answer'.
labs/module-04/l2_1-dataframes-series/debug_filters.py
  • Bug 1: products["Price"] raises KeyError: 'Price'. The column is price (names are case-sensitive). Prints 82.95.
  • Bug 2: and between two masks raises the 'truth value of a Series is ambiguous' ValueError. Use & with parentheses. Prints 14.
  • Bug 3: no parentheses around the conditions, so & is evaluated first and raises a TypeError. Wrap each condition. Prints 7.
  • Bug 4 (silent): == np.nan is never True. Use .isna().sum(). Prints 8, not 0.
  • Bug 5 (silent): chained assignment; a ChainedAssignmentError warning and 0 products on sale. Use products.loc[products["stock_status"] == "low_stock", "on_sale"] = True. Prints 29.

2.1 · The lesson page's Quick Quiz

These are the five questions at the end of the lesson page (three options each), with the lesson's own explanation.

2.1 Q1
What does this print?
qa = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=["a", "b", "c"])
qb = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=["b", "c", "d"])
print((qa + qb).tolist())
A) [11, 22, 33]
B) [nan, 21.0, 32.0, nan]
C) [10.0, 21.0, 32.0, 3.0]
Why: Series arithmetic aligns on labels. Only b and c exist in both, giving 21 and 32. Labels a and d exist in one Series only, so the result there is NaN, and the NaNs make the whole result float.
2.1 Q2
Which expression returns a DataFrame rather than a Series?
A) products[["price"]]
B) products["price"]
C) products.iloc[0]
Why: A list of column names inside the brackets always returns a DataFrame, even when the list holds a single name.
2.1 Q3
What does this print?
qdf = pd.DataFrame({"n": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]}, index=[10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print(len(qdf.loc[10:30]), len(qdf.iloc[0:2]))
A) 2 2
B) 3 3
C) 3 2
Why: loc slices by label and includes both ends: labels 10, 20 and 30 make three rows. iloc slices by position and excludes the stop: positions 0 and 1 make two rows.
2.1 Q4
What does this print?
qorig = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3]})
qpart = qorig[qorig["x"] > 1]
qpart["x"] = 0
print(qorig["x"].tolist())
A) [1, 2, 3]
B) [1, 0, 0]
C) [0, 0, 0]
Why: Under copy-on-write qpart behaves as an independent copy from the moment it is created, so writing to it changes qpart only. qorig keeps 1, 2, 3.
2.1 Q5
You want the products that cost more than $100 and are out of stock. Which line is correct?
A) products[products["price"] > 100 and products["stock_status"] == "out_of_stock"]
B) products[products["price"] > 100 & products["stock_status"] == "out_of_stock"]
C) products[(products["price"] > 100) & (products["stock_status"] == "out_of_stock")]
Why: Each condition sits in its own parentheses and they are joined with the element-by-element and operator, so the result is one mask with a True or False per row.

2.2 · Loading Data: self-check

Q7
What does this print?
f = io.StringIO("id,qty\n1,4\n2,\n3,6\n")
print(pd.read_csv(f, dtype={"qty": "Int64"})["qty"].tolist())
A) [4.0, nan, 6.0]
B) [4, <NA>, 6]
C) [4, 0, 6]
D) A ValueError: Integer column has NA values
Why: "Int64" with a capital I is the nullable integer: the whole numbers stay whole and the gap is shown as <NA>.
A is wrong: That is what you get with no dtype: the gap forces the column to float64.
C is wrong: pandas never invents a 0 for a missing value.
D is wrong: That error comes from lowercase "int64", the NumPy type, which cannot hold a missing value.
Q8
A text export starts with two lines of notes, then the header store;week;revenue, then rows such as Boise;2024-W01;55.400,22. Which call loads revenue as a number?
A) pd.read_csv(f, sep=";", skiprows=2, decimal=",", thousands=".")
B) pd.read_csv(f, sep=";", header=None)
C) pd.read_csv(f, skiprows=2, decimal=",")
D) pd.read_csv(f, sep=";", skiprows=3, decimal=",", thousands=".")
Why: Four facts in the text, four options: semicolons, two note lines above the header, a decimal comma and a dot for thousands.
B is wrong: header=None says the file has no header at all, so the notes and the header row land in the data and every column is text.
C is wrong: Without sep=";" pandas splits on commas, so each line is cut at the decimal comma.
D is wrong: skiprows=3 skips the header line too, so the first data row becomes the column names.
Q9
What does this print?
recs = [{"id": 1, "tags": [{"t": "a"}, {"t": "b"}]},
        {"id": 2, "tags": [{"t": "c"}]}]
print(pd.json_normalize(recs, record_path="tags", meta=["id"]).shape)
(3, 2)
Why: record_path="tags" makes one row per item of each inner list: 2 + 1 = 3 rows. The columns are t (from the items) and id (copied from the parent by meta).
Q10
You load orders.csv with no options. orders["order_date"].dt.month raises AttributeError: Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values. What is the right fix?
A) Add index_col="order_date" to the load
B) Convert the column with .astype("int64")
C) Add encoding="latin-1" to the load
D) Load with parse_dates=["order_date"], or convert with pd.to_datetime()
Why: The column is str: pandas does not guess dates. parse_dates converts it while loading; pd.to_datetime converts it afterward. Then .dt works.
A is wrong: That moves the column into the index but leaves it as text.
B is wrong: A date such as 2024-01-01 is not a whole number; the conversion fails.
C is wrong: The encoding is about characters, not types. The file already reads correctly.
Q11
What does this print?
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
df.to_csv("q11.csv")
print(pd.read_csv("q11.csv").columns.tolist())
['Unnamed: 0', 'a']
Why: Without index=False, to_csv writes the index as an extra first column with no name. Read back, it becomes a column called Unnamed: 0.
Q12
A CSV file is larger than your computer's memory. You need the sum of one of its columns. Which approach is the right one?
A) Load the whole file, then delete the columns you do not need
B) Read the first 1,000 rows with nrows and multiply up
C) Read it with usecols and chunksize, keeping a running total
D) Open it in a spreadsheet program and save it as Excel first
Why: usecols loads only the column you need and chunksize hands you one piece at a time, so only one chunk is ever in memory. Sums add up across chunks exactly.
A is wrong: The load itself is what fails: the file does not fit.
B is wrong: That is an estimate from the first rows, not the sum, and the first rows are rarely typical.
D is wrong: A spreadsheet program holds the file in memory too, and has a row limit.

2.2 · Predict, then run

P1
A code that looks like a number.
text = "sku,zip\nA1,02134\nB2,97701\n"
a = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text))
b = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text), dtype={"zip": "str"})
print(a["zip"].tolist(), b["zip"].tolist())
[2134, 97701] ['02134', '97701']
Why: Read as a number, 02134 loses its leading zero for good. dtype={"zip": "str"} keeps it as text. The test from the lesson: would it make sense to add two of them? If not, it is text.
P2
A key that is not there.
recs = [{"id": 1, "geo": {"city": "Bend"}}, {"id": 2}]
flat = pd.json_normalize(recs)
print(flat.columns.tolist(), flat["geo.city"].isna().sum())
['id', 'geo.city'] 1
Why: The inner dictionary becomes a dotted column, geo.city. The second record has no geo key, so its cell is NaN: one missing value. Nothing fails and no record is dropped.
P3
A title above the header.
text = "Sales report,draft\nday,sales\nMon,10\nTue,12\n"
a = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text))
b = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text), skiprows=1)
print(a.columns.tolist(), a.shape, b.columns.tolist(), b["sales"].sum())
['Sales report', 'draft'] (3, 2) ['day', 'sales'] 22
Why: Without skiprows, pandas takes the first line as the header, so the columns are called Sales report and draft, the real header day,sales lands in the data as a row (three rows instead of two), and no error is raised. Skipping the one title line puts day,sales in the header position, and sales is a number column that adds up to 22.

2.2 · Lab reference solutions

labs/module-04/l2_2-loading-data/till_export_solution.py

Question: Load the till system's one-week export (till_export_week08.txt) so every column has the right dtype, then prove the load is right against daily_sales.csv.

How the solution works: Each option answers one thing visible in the first six lines of the file: semicolons (sep=";"), three lines of notes (skiprows=3), amounts such as 3.536,91 (decimal=",", thousands="."), the word n/a (na_values), and dates such as 17.02.2025 (parse_dates with date_format="%d.%m.%Y"). The proof is a comparison with the same week of the clean file: revenue with np.isclose, visitors with ==.

Exported by the till system; n/a = register total not received

  • Correct dtypes: date datetime64[us], store str, three int64 columns, revenue float64. Shape (28, 6).
  • One missing revenue: Bend on 2025-02-19 (a genuine gap in the course data).

labs/module-04/l2_2-loading-data/product_pages_solution.py

Question: In November 2025, which product pages were viewed most, and do visitors stay longer on product pages than on other pages?

How the solution works: record_path="pages" makes one row per page view (9,348) and meta copies session_id and converted onto each. Two types need repair: at is text, and converted arrives through meta as dtype object, so it is cast with .astype(bool). Product pages are the paths that start with /product/; removing that prefix leaves the SKU. The result is written to OUTPUT as Parquet and CSV and read back.

['site', 'period', 'note', 'sessions'] 2400
page views: (9348, 5)
path             str
seconds        int64
at               str
session_id       str
converted     object
after the fix: datetime64[us] bool
product-page views: 2793 in 1610 sessions
sku
SNW-1016    22
PCK-1026    21
CLM-1019    20
ACC-1010    19
KIT-1025    19
mean seconds, product pages: 46.2
mean seconds, all pages    : 48.1
Parquet: datetime64[us] | equal to the original: True
CSV    : str | equal to the original: False
  • 9,348 page views; 2,793 of them are product pages, in 1,610 sessions.
  • Most viewed: SNW-1016 (22), PCK-1026 (21), CLM-1019 (20), then ACC-1010 and KIT-1025 (19 each). The counts are close together: there is no runaway favorite, and that is the honest answer.
  • Mean time: 46.2 seconds on product pages against 48.1 on all pages. Visitors do not stay longer on product pages.
  • Parquet reads back with datetime64[us] and equals is True; the CSV reads back with str and equals is False.
  • The converted column as object is a real surprise: meta columns are not type-inferred. It is the lab's 'check the translation' moment.
  • Learners who pass record_path="cart.items" get a KeyError: a nested path is a list, ["cart", "items"] (that is the lesson's bonus challenge).
labs/module-04/l2_2-loading-data/targets_vs_actuals_solution.py

Question: Which of the four stores beat its 2025 revenue target, and by how much?

How the solution works: The Monthly Sales sheet has its header on the row at position 3, so header=3 (the same as skiprows=3); the Targets sheet is tidy. A four-turn loop over the store names sums one column of monthly and one filtered column of targets, collecting a dictionary per store. pd.DataFrame(rows) turns the list into a table, a new column gives the percentage, and to_excel with index=False writes it.

2.2 · The lesson page's Quick Quiz

These are the five questions at the end of the lesson page (three options each), with the lesson's own explanation.

2.2 Q1
The second row of this small file has an empty amount. What does the code print?
qtext = io.StringIO("id,amount\n1,10\n2,\n3,30\n")
qdf = pd.read_csv(qtext)
print(qdf["amount"].dtype)
A) int64
B) float64
C) str
Why: The empty cell becomes NaN, and NumPy int64 cannot hold NaN, so pandas reads the column as float64. Asking for the nullable Int64 dtype keeps it as whole numbers.
2.2 Q2
A worksheet has a title in row 1, a note in row 2, a blank row 3, and the column names in row 4. Which call reads it correctly?
A) pd.read_excel(path, nrows=4)
B) pd.read_excel(path, header=4)
C) pd.read_excel(path, skiprows=3)
Why: Skipping the first three rows makes row 4 the first row pandas sees, and it uses that row as the header. header=3 would do the same.
2.2 Q3
In a list of JSON records, some records have a utm dictionary and others have no utm key at all. What does pd.json_normalize(records) do with the records that lack it?
A) Keeps them, with NaN in the utm.* columns
B) Drops those records from the result
C) Raises a KeyError for the first record without the key
Why: json_normalize builds the columns from every key it finds in any record and fills NaN where a record does not have that key. In this lesson 916 sessions had NaN in the utm columns.
2.2 Q4
You save a table with df.to_csv("out.csv"). A colleague reads it and finds an extra first column named Unnamed: 0. What happened?
A) The file's header row was written twice
B) The index was written as a column; index=False prevents it
C) The file was saved in the wrong encoding
Why: to_csv writes the index as the first column unless told not to, and the default index has no name. Reading the file back turns it into a column called Unnamed: 0. Write with index=False.
2.2 Q5
A table with a datetime column and a category column is written to CSV and to Parquet. Read back with no options, only the Parquet version still has those dtypes. Why?
A) Parquet compresses the data, and CSV does not
B) read_parquet is better at guessing types from the values
C) A Parquet file stores each column's type with the data; a CSV is only text
Why: A Parquet file stores a schema, the type of every column, alongside the values, so nothing has to be guessed. A CSV file is plain text and every type must be inferred or supplied again on each load.

Warm-up Answers

  1. You write rng = np.random.default_rng(42). What is rng, and what does the 42 do? Answer: A random number generator. The seed fixes where its sequence starts, so the same code run from the top gives the same numbers.
  2. Can rng.integers(1, 7, size=5) ever return a 7? Answer: No. The upper end is left out, so the values are 1 to 6 (a die).
  3. What does replace=False guarantee in rng.choice(skus, size=10, replace=False)? Answer: Ten distinct items: nothing is picked twice.
  4. For two 1-D arrays of length 3, what is the difference between a * b and a @ b? Answer: a * b is position by position and gives three numbers; a @ b is the dot product, one number: a weighted sum.
  5. A matrix of shape (726, 3) is multiplied with @ by a vector of shape (3,). What shape is the result, and what must match? Answer: (726,). The inner numbers must match (3 and 3): one dot product per row.

Exit Ticket Answers

  1. You run df[df["price"] > 100]["price"] = 0. What happens to df, and what should you write instead? Answer: Nothing happens to df (pandas warns with ChainedAssignmentError): the first brackets made a temporary copy. Write df.loc[df["price"] > 100, "price"] = 0.
  2. On a table with the default index, how many rows do df.loc[0:3] and df.iloc[0:3] return, and why are they different? Answer: 4 and 3. .loc slices by label and includes the end; .iloc slices by position and leaves out the stop.
  3. You save a table that has a date column to out.csv and to out.parquet. Read back with no options, which file gives the date back as a date, and why? Answer: The Parquet file. It stores each column's dtype with the data; a CSV is only text, so the date comes back as str unless you pass parse_dates again.

Common Wrong Answers and What They Reveal

  • Q2 answered 2 2 40 or 3 3 40. The learner has one slicing rule, not two. Send them back to the one-line experiment: .loc includes the end label, .iloc leaves out the stop position.
  • Q5 answered [10, 0, 0]. They believe a filtered piece is a window onto the table (the NumPy view model from Lesson 1.1). Re-run the tents demonstration and have them say the copy-on-write rule in their own words.
  • Q4 answered A (no parentheses). They know to use | but not that it binds tighter than == and <. Have them add the parentheses and explain what Python tried to compute first.
  • Exit ticket 1 answered 'it sets them to 0'. The warning was not noticed. Show the cell again in a notebook and ask them to find the word ChainedAssignmentError.
  • Q7 answered A ([4.0, nan, 6.0]). They have learned 'gaps make floats' but not that Int64 is the cure. That is half right; point at the capital I.
  • Q9 answered (2, 2). They expect one row per record. Draw the tree: record_path makes one row per item of the inner list, so 2 + 1 = 3 rows.
  • Q11 answered ['a']. They do not yet see the index as something that gets written. Have them open the CSV in a text editor and look at the first column.
  • Lab till_export: 29 rows and a text revenue. The header was skipped or counted as a note. Ask which line holds the column names, then recount skiprows.
  • Lab recommend_groups: a different score for Asheville. Usually the denominator: all 202 responses instead of the 197 who answered. Ask what notna() is for.

Session 5: Cleaning and Grouping

Answers with reasoning for the 12 self-check items and the predict-then-run boxes, the real output of every lab solution with what to check while circulating, the fixes for the 'find the bug' handout, the two lesson pages' own Quick Quiz answers, and the warm-up and exit-ticket answers.

Session 5 12 self-check items 4 lab pairs Confidential
How this key is organized

Self-check numbering matches the workbook: Q1 to Q6 are on Lesson 2.3, Q7 to Q12 on Lesson 2.4. Each item repeats the four options with the correct one marked and says why each wrong option is wrong. Every printed output below comes from running the code against the course data. The lesson pages' own five-question Quick Quizzes (three options each) are answered at the end of each lesson's part.

2.3 · Cleaning Data: self-check

Q1
An audit shows that the Store column has 31 distinct values. Pinecrest has four stores and an online shop. What is the right first move?
A) Delete the rows whose store name is unusual
B) Print value_counts() to see the variants, then strip, fix the case, and map what is left
C) Convert the column to the category dtype
D) Fill the unusual names with the most common store
Why: Look before you fix. value_counts() shows which variants exist; whitespace and case are mechanical, and the remaining misspellings need a mapping dictionary that you write from what you see.
A is wrong: Those rows are real orders with a badly typed store name. Deleting them deletes revenue.
C is wrong: A category column with 31 categories is still 31 stores. The dtype does not merge spellings.
D is wrong: That would move orders from Boise, Bend and the rest to Online: an invented value, not a repair.
Q2
What does this print?
d = pd.Series(["2024-03-05", "03/05/2024", "March 5, 2024", "2024-02-30"])
iso = pd.to_datetime(d, format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
us = pd.to_datetime(d, format="%m/%d/%Y", errors="coerce")
print(iso.notna().sum(), iso.fillna(us).notna().sum())
1 2
Why: The ISO pass understands only the first value: the next two are in other formats and February 30th does not exist, so all three become NaT. Filling from the month/day/year pass recovers the second value. The written-out date needs a third pass, and the impossible date stays missing.
Q3
What does this print?
s = pd.Series(["none", "TRAIL15", "-", "trail15"])
p = s.str.upper()
print(p.where(~p.isin(["NONE", "-"])).tolist())
A) ['NONE', 'TRAIL15', '-', 'TRAIL15']
B) ['TRAIL15', 'TRAIL15']
C) [nan, 'TRAIL15', nan, 'TRAIL15']
D) [nan, 'TRAIL15', nan, 'trail15']
Why: .str.upper() standardizes the case, and .where(condition) keeps a value where the condition is true and puts a missing value where it is false. The two placeholders become real missing values; the length stays 4.
A is wrong: That is p before .where(): the placeholders are still there, counted as promo codes.
B is wrong: .where() never removes rows; it replaces values. The result has four items.
D is wrong: The last code was uppercased before the test, so it is TRAIL15.
Q4
In orders_messy.csv one order total is $4,990.00, while the largest genuine order is $4,893.00. What justified dividing the $4,990.00 by 100?
A) It is above the 99th percentile of order totals
B) It is an online order, and online totals are less reliable
C) It is a round number, which suggests a typing error
D) Its item lines add up to $34.95, so the recorded total is over 100 times what was bought
Why: An outlier is a question, not a verdict. The independent evidence is in order_items.csv: the order's items total $34.95, and the recorded total is about 143 times that. The genuine $4,893 order matches its items.
A is wrong: So is the genuine $4,893 bulk order. Being extreme is not evidence of an error.
B is wrong: Nothing in the data says online totals are less reliable; the twelve largest genuine orders are all online.
C is wrong: Plenty of real totals are round numbers. That is a hunch, not evidence.
Q5
What does this print?
df = pd.DataFrame({"total": [10.0, None, 50.0]})
print(df["total"].mean(), df["total"].fillna(0).mean())
30.0 20.0
Why: .mean() skips the missing value: (10 + 50) / 2 = 30. Filling the gap with 0 claims that the customer paid nothing and divides by three: 60 / 3 = 20. A fill is a claim about the data.
Q6
trial has 406 missing payment methods. What happens when you run trial["payment_method"].fillna("unknown", inplace=True)?
A) trial is unchanged, and pandas warns with ChainedAssignmentError
B) The 406 gaps in trial are filled with unknown
C) A TypeError, because text cannot be used to fill a column
D) The gaps are filled, but only in the first 406 rows
Why: trial["payment_method"] is a new, derived object. Under copy-on-write, filling it 'in place' changes that temporary object and never reaches trial. Assign the result back: trial["payment_method"] = trial["payment_method"].fillna("unknown").
B is wrong: That is what older pandas did, and what old tutorials promise. Under copy-on-write it no longer happens.
C is wrong: Filling a text column with text is fine; the problem is where the result goes.
D is wrong: fillna fills by position of the gaps, not the first rows; and here nothing in trial is filled at all.

2.3 · Predict, then run

P1
Case without whitespace.
s = pd.Series([" Bend", "bend ", "BEND", "Bend OR"])
print(s.str.title().nunique(), s.str.strip().str.title().nunique())
4 2
Why: Title case alone leaves four different values, because two of them still carry a space and Bend OR becomes Bend Or. Stripping first merges the three spellings of Bend. Two remain: Bend and Bend Or, and the second needs a mapping, which is a decision, not a mechanical step.
P2
A detector for values that are not numbers.
s = pd.Series(["$1,200.50", "80", "free", None])
n = pd.to_numeric(s.str.replace("$", "").str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")
print(n.tolist(), n.isna().sum())
[1200.5, 80.0, nan, nan] 2
Why: After the symbols are removed, two values convert. free cannot, so coerce makes it NaN; the empty value was already missing. Two NaNs, for two different reasons: one was a word that needs a decision (free means 0), the other was never there.
P3
Three ways to lose rows.
df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 2, 3], "promo": [None, "A", "A", None],
                   "amt": [5.0, 7.0, 7.0, None]})
print(len(df.drop_duplicates()), len(df.dropna()), len(df.dropna(subset=["amt"])))
3 2 3
Why: One exact duplicate goes, leaving 3. dropna() with no arguments drops every row with a gap in any column: only the two rows with a promo code survive. Naming the column that matters keeps the 3 rows that have an amount.

2.3 · Lab reference solutions

labs/module-05/l2_3-cleaning-data/register_log_solution.py

Question: Clean the Asheville manager's hand-typed log of May 2025 (asheville_may_log.csv) and score it against the same 31 days of daily_sales.csv.

How the solution works: Structure first: strip and lowercase the headers, rename three of them, save the TOTAL row's number, drop that row and the 3 exact duplicates (31 rows). Text: strip and title-case the store name, map the one misspelling; reduce yes/Yes/Y/YES and no/No/N to their first letter and map to 1/0. Numbers: remove $ and ,, coerce (the word pending becomes NaN); revenue per transaction exposes one day that is 100 times too large (9,551 per sale against a median of 90), fixed with one .loc assignment; the count columns become Int64. Dates: three formats, one pass each, combined with fillna. Two values stay blank. The stretch step repairs one of them with a firm rule: the TOTAL row minus the sum of the known days.

Revenue ($)       str        0        32

Promo?            str        1         7
rows: 35 | exact duplicate rows: 3
after structure: (31, 8) | stated total: 201379.71

{'no': 21, 'No': 4, 'N': 2, 'yes': 1, 'Yes': 1, 'Y': 1, 'YES': 1}
['Asheville'] {0: 27, 1: 4}
not a number: [['05/09/2025', 'pending']]
{'min': 73.24, '50%': 90.06, 'max': 9551.47}
lost decimal point: [['2025-05-17', 93.0, 888287.0]]
dates per format: 17 10 4
                        dtype  missing  distinct

store                     str        0         1

the pending day, recovered from the TOTAL row: ['2025-05-09'] 3668.5
cells compared: 217 | still blank: 1 | wrong: 0
  • Audit before: 35 rows, 3 exact duplicates, Store with 5 distinct spellings, Promo? with 7, Revenue ($) as text, four count columns as float (the TOTAL row's empty cells did that).
  • After structure: (31, 8) and a stated total of 201,379.71.
  • Not a number: pending on 05/09/2025. Lost decimal point: 2025-05-17, 888,287.00 for 93 transactions. The genuine promo-day figure of $16,558.00 (May 24) must NOT be touched: 96.83 per sale is ordinary.
  • Dates per format: 17 ISO, 10 month/day/year, 4 written out. No date is missing.
  • Scorecard: cells compared: 217 | still blank: 2 | wrong: 0. The two blanks are the pending revenue and one n/a visitor count, which read_csv turned into NaN by itself.
  • Stretch: 201,379.71 minus the known revenue is 3,668.50, the true figure for May 9. Scorecard then says 1 blank. The visitor count cannot be recovered from this file: it stays blank.
  • wrong: 1 nearly always means the lost decimal was not repaired, or a threshold on revenue alone caught May 24 as well. wrong: 31 in one column means promo_day is still text.
labs/module-05/l2_3-cleaning-data/total_row_check_solution.py

Question: If someone simply added up Order Total in orders_messy.csv, how far off would they be, and which flaw moves the sum the most?

How the solution works: The TOTAL row's 3,950,701.45 is the sum of all true order totals (it equals the sum of order_total in orders.csv). The lab converts the column, takes the careless sum, then applies three repairs in turn and records the sum after each: dropping the 212 duplicates, making the 15 negative totals positive, and dividing the 8 lost-decimal totals by 100 (found with the item-subtotal ratio from the lesson). What is left is explained to the cent by the 40 blank totals.

                      step        sum     change  off_by_pct
              careless sum 4126451.89        NaN        4.45
       drop 212 duplicates 4083821.73  -42630.16        3.37
15 negatives made positive 4090475.89    6654.16        3.54
     8 lost decimal points 3943079.74 -147396.15       -0.19
stated total (TOTAL row): 3,950,701.45
gap after all repairs   : 7,621.71
blank totals: 40 | their true sum in orders.csv: 7,621.71
the gap is exactly the blank totals: True
  • Careless sum 4,126,451.89: 4.45% too high.
  • Dropping duplicates: -42,630.16. Negatives made positive: +6,654.16. Lost decimals: -147,396.15, the largest effect by far, from only 8 rows.
  • After all repairs 3,943,079.74, which is 7,621.71 below the stated total. The 40 orders with a blank total add up to exactly 7,621.71 in orders.csv.
  • Discussion: eight rows did three times the damage of 212 duplicates. Counting how many rows a flaw touches says little about how much it matters.
  • If after_decimals is unchanged, the ratio was computed before order_id was converted to int64, so .map() found no matches.

2.3 · The lesson page's Quick Quiz

These are the five questions at the end of the lesson page (three options each), with the lesson's own explanation.

2.3 Q1
What does this print?
qs = pd.Series(["12", "7", "n/a", "3.5"])
print(pd.to_numeric(qs, errors="coerce").tolist())
A) [12.0, 7.0, nan, 3.5]
B) Nothing: it raises a ValueError at 'n/a'
C) [12.0, 7.0, 0.0, 3.5]
Why: errors='coerce' converts every value that can be a number and turns the rest into NaN instead of raising an error. The NaN makes the result float.
2.3 Q2
A column holds " boise", "BOISE " and "Boise". After .str.title() alone, how many distinct values does it have?
A) 1
B) 2
C) 3
Why: Title case does not remove whitespace, so a leading space, a trailing space and no space are still three different texts. Strip first, then fix the case.
2.3 Q3
Forty of 20,302 orders have no recorded total, and nothing in the file lets you work it out. You need the average order value. What is the most defensible approach?
A) Fill the 40 gaps with 0 so that every row has a number
B) Leave them missing, compute the mean of the known totals, and report that 40 were excluded
C) Call dropna() on the table first, then take the mean
Why: mean() skips missing values, so the average is computed from the 20,262 known totals, and stating that 40 were excluded lets a reader judge the result. No value is invented.
2.3 Q4
What does this print?
qd = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3], "v": ["a", "a", "b", "c", "c", "d"]})
print(len(qd.drop_duplicates()), len(qd.drop_duplicates(subset=["id"])))
A) 3 3
B) 4 4
C) 4 3
Why: Comparing whole rows leaves four distinct rows: 1 a, 2 b, 3 c and 3 d. Comparing only id keeps the first row of each id, which leaves three, and silently discards the 3 d row.
2.3 Q5
One order total is $55,690, far above the rest. What should you do first?
A) Look for independent evidence about that order, such as its item lines
B) Delete every order above a chosen threshold
C) Replace it with the median order total
Why: An extreme value is a question. Independent evidence, here the item lines for that order, tells you whether it is a real bulk order or an entry error, and what the right value is.

2.4 · GroupBy Operations: self-check

Q7
What does this print?
df = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["a", "a", "b"], "amt": [10, 30, 5]})
r = df.groupby("store")["amt"].agg(["count", "mean"])
print(r.shape, r.loc["a", "mean"])
A) (3, 2) 20.0
B) (2, 2) 40.0
C) (2,) 20.0
D) (2, 2) 20.0
Why: Two groups give two rows, and two function names give two columns. The index is the store, so r.loc["a", "mean"] is the mean of 10 and 30.
A is wrong: Aggregation returns one row per group, not one per original row.
B is wrong: 40 is the sum for store a; the column asked for is the mean.
C is wrong: A list of two functions makes a DataFrame with two columns, not a Series.
Q8
What does this print?
df = pd.DataFrame({"k": ["x", "x", "y"], "v": [1, 3, 10]})
df["share"] = df["v"] / df.groupby("k")["v"].transform("sum")
print(df["share"].tolist())
[0.25, 0.75, 1.0]
Why: transform("sum") returns one value per original row: 4, 4, 10 (each row's group total). Dividing each value by its own group's total gives each row's share of its group.
Q9
orders has a True/False column returned. Which expression gives the fraction of each channel's orders that were returned?
A) orders.groupby("channel")["returned"].mean()
B) orders.groupby("channel")["returned"].count()
C) orders.groupby("channel")["returned"].size()
D) orders.groupby("channel")["returned"].nunique()
Why: True counts as 1 and False as 0, so the mean of a boolean column within each group is the rate.
B is wrong: count is the number of non-missing values: every order, returned or not.
C is wrong: size is the number of rows in each group.
D is wrong: nunique is the number of distinct values: 2 for each channel (True and False).
Q10
orders.groupby("promo_code").size().sum() gives 2,148, but orders has 20,302 rows. Why?
A) size() skips rows whose order total is missing
B) groupby removes duplicate rows before it counts
C) Rows whose key is missing are dropped by default; dropna=False keeps them as a group
D) promo_code is text and must be a category before grouping
Why: 18,154 orders have no promo code. By default groupby silently leaves out every row whose key is missing. dropna=False adds a group for them, and the sizes then add up to 20,302.
A is wrong: size() counts rows whatever they contain; it does not look at order_total.
B is wrong: groupby never removes duplicates.
D is wrong: Text keys group perfectly well. The dtype is not the issue.
Q11
What does this print?
df = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a", "b"], "x": [1.0, None, 3.0]})
print(df.groupby("g")["x"].size().tolist(), df.groupby("g")["x"].count().tolist())
[2, 1] [1, 1]
Why: size counts rows: two in group a, one in group b. count counts non-missing values of x: group a has one missing, so 1 and 1.
Q12
You want the original order rows of every customer who placed 25 or more orders. Which call returns them?
A) orders.groupby("customer_id")["order_id"].count() >= 25
B) orders.groupby("customer_id").filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 25)
C) orders.groupby("customer_id").agg(n=("order_id", "count"))
D) orders.groupby("customer_id")["order_id"].transform("count")
Why: filter hands each group to the function and keeps all rows of the groups for which it returns True: fewer of the same rows.
A is wrong: That is a True/False Series with one value per customer, not order rows.
C is wrong: That is a summary with one row per customer.
D is wrong: That is one count per order row: the first half of the transform-then-mask pattern. You would still need orders[... >= 25].

2.4 · Predict, then run

P1
An average of averages.
df = pd.DataFrame({"team": ["a", "b", "a", "b", "a"], "pts": [2, 10, 4, 20, 6]})
means = df.groupby("team")["pts"].mean()
print(means.tolist(), means.mean(), df["pts"].mean())
[4.0, 15.0] 9.5 8.4
Why: Team a averages 4 over three rows and team b averages 15 over two rows. The mean of those two means, 9.5, weights the teams equally; the mean of all five rows, 8.4, weights every row equally. They differ because the groups are different sizes.
P2
A key with gaps.
df = pd.DataFrame({"code": ["X", None, "X", None], "amt": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
print(len(df.groupby("code")), len(df.groupby("code", dropna=False)),
      df.groupby("code")["amt"].sum().sum())
1 2 4
Why: By default the two rows with no code are dropped, so there is one group (X) and the sums add up to 1 + 3 = 4, not 10. With dropna=False the missing key becomes a second group.
P3
Three shapes.
df = pd.DataFrame({"k": ["a", "a", "b"], "v": [1, 2, 3]})
a = df.groupby("k")["v"].sum()
t = df.groupby("k")["v"].transform("sum")
f = df.groupby("k").filter(lambda g: len(g) > 1)
print(len(a), len(t), len(f))
2 3 2
Why: agg (here sum) returns one row per group: 2. transform returns one value per original row: 3. filter returns the original rows of the groups that pass the test: only group a has more than one row, so 2 rows.

2.4 · Lab reference solutions

labs/module-05/l2_4-groupby-operations/store_days_solution.py

Question: For each store: days, revenue and conversion; how much a promo day brings in; whether the lesson's growth claim (+19.7% Flagstaff, -5.0% Asheville) holds; and how many days were at least twice the store's own average.

How the solution works: One named aggregation gives the store table; conversion is the sum of transactions divided by the sum of visitors, computed after the aggregation. Two keys (store, promo_day) and unstack give ordinary and promo-day means side by side, and a ratio column gives the lift. A computed year key reproduces the growth figures the lesson quotes. transform("mean") puts each store's average on every row so that each day can be compared with its own store.

  • Promo days bring in 1.88 to 1.98 times an ordinary day's revenue in every store.
  • The trap: ordinary days average 7,211.74 and promo days 13,950.46; the average of those two is 10,581.10, but the true average store-day is 7,435.04, because only 96 of 2,903 store-days are promo days.
  • Growth, 2024 to 2025: Flagstaff +19.7%, Boise +9.3%, Bend +3.8%, Asheville -5.0%. The lesson's claim holds.
  • Standout days (at least twice the store's own average): Flagstaff 21, Bend 15, Boise 15, Asheville 12; 63 in all, and 61.9% of them were promo days. The biggest relative day is Bend on 2024-08-31, 2.99 times its average.
  • A learner whose conversion column is a mean of daily ratios gets nearly the same numbers here; ask them which one answers 'what share of all visitors bought?' (the ratio of sums).
labs/module-05/l2_4-groupby-operations/basket_sizes_solution.py

Question: How big is a typical basket, are the best sellers by units the best sellers by revenue, what share of its order is each line, and which orders have six or more lines?

How the solution works: Grouping by order_id gives one row per order (20,302) with lines, units and subtotal; grouping by sku gives one row per product (240) with units, revenue and distinct orders. transform("sum") puts each order's subtotal on every one of its lines so a share can be computed. filter with len(g) >= 6 and the transform-then-mask version return the same 1,106 lines.

labs/module-05/l2_4-groupby-operations/debug_groupby.py

2.4 · The lesson page's Quick Quiz

These are the five questions at the end of the lesson page (three options each), with the lesson's own explanation.

2.4 Q1
What does this print?
qdf = pd.DataFrame({"team": ["a", "a", "b", "b", "b"], "pts": [1, 3, 2, 4, 6]})
qres = qdf.groupby("team")["pts"].transform("mean")
print(len(qres), qres.tolist())
A) 2 [2.0, 4.0]
B) 5 [2.0, 2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0]
C) 5 [1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0]
Why: transform returns one value for every original row: each row gets the mean of its own group. Team a averages 2 and team b averages 4, repeated for their two and three rows.
2.4 Q2
You want one row per store, with a column orders (the number of orders) and a column revenue (the sum of order_total). Which call produces it?
A) orders.groupby("store").agg({"order_total": {"revenue": "sum"}})
B) orders.groupby("store")["order_total"].transform("sum")
C) orders.groupby("store").agg(orders=("order_id", "count"), revenue=("order_total", "sum"))
Why: Named aggregation: each keyword is the new column name, and its tuple gives the source column and the function. The result has one row per store and exactly these two columns.
2.4 Q3
Two of the five rows have no code. What does this print?
qd2 = pd.DataFrame({"code": ["X", None, "X", None, "Y"], "amt": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]})
print(qd2.groupby("code")["amt"].sum().sum())
A) 9
B) 15
C) nan
Why: By default groupby drops rows whose key is missing. Only X (1 + 3) and Y (5) form groups, so the group sums total 9, not 15. dropna=False would keep the missing key as a group.
2.4 Q4
The five stores' average order totals are $174.90, $172.91, $177.22, $183.61 and $204.65. Their mean is $182.66, but the average over all orders is $194.60. Why do the two differ?
A) Rounding errors build up when averages are averaged
B) Missing order totals were skipped in one calculation and not in the other
C) The groups are very different sizes, and a mean of means weights each group equally
Why: Averaging the five store averages gives each store equal weight, but the online shop has 12,854 orders and Asheville 1,413. The true overall average weights every order equally, so the large online group pulls it up.
2.4 Q5
Which statement about orders.groupby("payment_method")["promo_code"] is true?
A) .size() counts all orders in each group; .count() counts only those with a promo code
B) .size() and .count() always return the same numbers
C) .count() returns the number of distinct promo codes in each group
Why: size counts the rows in each group whatever they contain. count counts only the non-missing values of the selected column, so it reports how many orders in each group used a promo code.

Warm-up Answers

  1. What three things make up a Series? Answer: An array of values, an index of labels, and an optional name.
  2. On a table with the default index, how many rows do df.loc[0:3] and df.iloc[0:3] return? Answer: 4 and 3: a label slice includes its end, a position slice leaves out the stop.
  3. df[df["price"] > 100]["price"] = 0 changes nothing. What do you write instead? Answer: df.loc[df["price"] > 100, "price"] = 0: one .loc on the table you want to change.
  4. A column of birth years loads as float64 and prints 1989.0. Why, and what is the fix? Answer: Some years are missing and NumPy's int64 cannot hold a missing value. Load it as "Int64" (capital I).
  5. After pd.read_excel(...) the columns are called Unnamed: 1, Unnamed: 2. What happened, and what do you check after every load? Answer: The header is not on the row pandas read as the header (skiprows / header). After every load: shape, dtypes, head().

Exit Ticket Answers

  1. In what order do you repair a damaged table, and why does structure come first? Answer: Structure (headers, rows that are not data, duplicates), then text, numbers, dates, missing values. Fixing the shape first makes later steps simpler and counts honest (for example astype fails while a TOTAL row is present).
  2. Forty of 20,302 order totals are blank and nothing in the file gives their value. You need the average order value. What do you do, and what do you say? Answer: Leave them missing, take the mean of the known totals, and report that 40 orders were excluded. Filling with 0 or with the median would invent data.
  3. One row per group; one value per original row; fewer of the same rows. Name the groupby tool for each. Answer: agg (or a built-in such as sum); transform; filter (or a transform and a mask).

Common Wrong Answers and What They Reveal

  • Q2 answered 2 2 or 1 3. They expect one format string to understand another format, or they expect the impossible date to be parsed. Have them print iso and us side by side: each pass understands its own format only, and February 30th stays NaT.
  • Q5 answered 30.0 30.0. They think fillna(0) is neutral. Ask what three customers paid in the second calculation: 10, 0 and 50.
  • Q6 answered B ('the gaps are filled'). The copy-on-write rule from Session 4 has not transferred to inplace=True. Show the cell and the warning; the fix is to assign the result back.
  • Q4 answered A ('above the 99th percentile'). They treat 'extreme' as 'wrong'. Remind them that the $4,893 bulk order is extreme and true.
  • Q8 answered [4, 4, 10] or a two-item list. They are thinking of agg. Draw the two shapes: transform returns one value per original row.
  • Q11 answered [2, 1] [2, 1]. size and count are the same to them. Ask what count does with the missing value in group a.
  • Exit ticket 2 answered 'fill with the mean'. It leaves the mean unchanged, which feels safe, but it invents 40 perfectly average orders and shrinks the spread. With 40 gaps in 20,302 rows, leaving them missing costs nothing.
  • Lab register_log: wrong: 1. The lost decimal was missed, or a threshold on revenue caught the genuine promo day. Ask for the evidence in the row (revenue per transaction).
  • Lab store_days: 726 days for Asheville. count on revenue was used for the number of days. Ask what happens to a day with no revenue figure.

Session 6 12 self-check items 5 lab pairs Confidential
How this key is organized

Self-check numbering matches the workbook: Q1 to Q6 are on Lesson 2.5, Q7 to Q12 on Lesson 2.6. Each item repeats the four options with the correct one marked and says why each wrong option is wrong. Every printed output below comes from running the code against the course data. The lesson pages' own five-question Quick Quizzes (three options each) are answered at the end of each lesson's part.

2.5 · Merging and Joining: self-check

Q1
What does this print (the lengths of an inner, a left and an outer merge)?
a = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2, 3], "x": ["p", "q", "r"]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"k": [2, 3, 3, 4], "y": [10, 20, 30, 40]})
print(len(a.merge(b, on="k")), len(a.merge(b, on="k", how="left")),
      len(a.merge(b, on="k", how="outer")))
A) 2 3 4
B) 3 3 5
C) 3 4 5
D) 3 4 4
Why: Key 2 matches once and key 3 matches twice: 3 rows in the inner join. The left join also keeps key 1 with no partner: 4 rows. The outer join adds key 4 from the right: 5 rows.
A is wrong: That counts matching keys, not rows. Key 3 appears twice on the right, so it produces two rows.
B is wrong: A left join keeps the unmatched left row (key 1), so it has one more row than the inner join.
D is wrong: The outer join also keeps key 4, which exists only in the right table.
Q2
You want to add each customer's loyalty tier to orders without losing any order, and you want the merge to fail loudly if customers ever contains a duplicated id. Which call does both?
A) orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id")
B) orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
C) orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="inner", validate="one_to_one")
D) pd.concat([orders, customers])
Why: how="left" keeps every order, and validate="many_to_one" checks that customer_id is unique in the right-hand table, raising MergeError if it is not.
A is wrong: The default is an inner join: 739 orders with no customer record disappear, and nothing checks for duplicate ids.
C is wrong: An inner join loses the unmatched orders, and one_to_one fails at once because a customer has many orders.
D is wrong: concat stacks the two tables on top of each other; it does not match rows by key.
Q3
What does this print?
o = pd.DataFrame({"order": [1, 2], "total": [100, 50]})
i = pd.DataFrame({"order": [1, 1, 1, 2], "sku": ["a", "b", "c", "d"]})
m = o.merge(i, on="order")
print(m["total"].sum(), m.drop_duplicates("order")["total"].sum())
350 150
Why: The merged table has one row per line, so order 1's total of 100 appears three times: 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 = 350. Going back to one row per order before summing gives the true 150.
Q4
orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="outer", indicator=True) shows 739 rows marked left_only. What are they?
A) Orders whose customer_id has no row in customers
B) Customers who have never placed an order
C) Orders that matched more than one customer
D) Duplicate orders that the merge removed
Why: left_only means the key was found only in the left table, the one before .merge: orders with no customer record (the closed accounts).
B is wrong: Those are the right_only rows: keys found only in customers (1,058 of them).
C is wrong: Rows that match are marked both, however many partners they have.
D is wrong: A merge never removes duplicates, and the indicator does not report them.
Q5
What does this print?
a = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["Boise"], "rev": [100]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["Bend"], "rev": [80], "visitors": [300]})
c = pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True)
print(c.shape, c["visitors"].isna().sum())
(2, 3) 1
Why: concat stacks the rows and matches columns by name. The first table has no visitors column, so its row gets NaN there: 2 rows, 3 columns, 1 missing value.
Q6
daily has the columns date and store; weather has date and city (the same four place names). Each has one row per place per day. Which call attaches the weather to every sales row?
A) daily.merge(weather, on=["date", "store"])
B) daily.merge(weather, on="date", how="left")
C) pd.concat([daily, weather], ignore_index=True)
D) daily.merge(weather, left_on=["date", "store"], right_on=["date", "city"], how="left", validate="one_to_one")
Why: The key is the pair (date, place), and the place column has a different name in each table, so the key columns are named for each side with left_on and right_on.
A is wrong: on= needs the same names in both tables; weather has no store column, so this raises KeyError: 'store'.
B is wrong: Matching on the date alone pairs every store's sales with all four cities' weather: four times the rows.
C is wrong: concat stacks the tables into one long table with half-empty columns; it does not match rows.

2.5 · Predict, then run

P1
An outer join with an indicator.
left = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2, 2], "a": ["x", "y", "z"]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"k": [2, 2, 3], "b": [10, 20, 30]})
m = left.merge(right, on="k", how="outer", indicator=True)
print(len(m), (m["_merge"] == "both").sum(), (m["_merge"] == "left_only").sum())
6 4 1
Why: Key 2 appears twice on each side, so it makes 2 × 2 = 4 rows marked both: a many-to-many match. Key 1 exists only on the left (1 row) and key 3 only on the right (1 row). 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.
P2
Missing keys.
a = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1.0, np.nan], "a": ["x", "y"]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"k": [np.nan, np.nan], "b": ["p", "q"]})
print(len(a.merge(b, on="k")), len(a.merge(b, on="k", how="left")))
2 3
Why: In a pandas merge a missing key matches every other missing key (unlike SQL). The one left row with NaN matches both right rows: 2 rows in the inner join. The left join adds the unmatched key 1: 3 rows. Remove or fill missing keys before merging on a column that has them.
P3
An average after a merge.
o = pd.DataFrame({"order": [1, 2], "total": [300, 100]})
i = pd.DataFrame({"order": [1, 1, 1, 2], "qty": [1, 1, 1, 1]})
print(o["total"].mean(), o.merge(i, on="order")["total"].mean())
200.0 250.0
Why: The two orders average 200. After the merge order 1 appears three times (once per line), so the mean becomes (300 + 300 + 300 + 100) / 4 = 250. Orders with more lines are counted more often. Compute order-level statistics on the orders table.

labs/module-06/l2_5-merging-joining/customer_profiles_solution.py

Question: Who are the five biggest spenders by name, how many account holders never ordered (and in which tier), and which orders belong to nobody in customers.csv?

How the solution works: Orders are first reduced to one row per customer id (3,942 rows), so both keys are unique and the merge onto customers is one-to-one: 4,850 rows in, 4,850 out. indicator=True marks the 1,058 accounts with no orders as left_only; their order count and spend are filled with 0, which is the honest value for a count and a sum. A second, outer merge of the two key columns audits the other side: 150 ids have orders but no account.

  • Summary: 3,942 rows, key unique on both sides. Profiles: 4850 -> 4850, with 3,792 both and 1,058 left_only.
  • Top five spenders: Rosa Blackwood (GA, 39 orders, $8,305.39), Zoe Diaz (WA, 41, $7,729.68), Rosa Ibarra (AZ, 36, $6,868.83), Joanna Amato (ID, 14, $6,792.90), Liam Paredes (OR, 29, $6,630.48). All Gold.
  • By tier: 37.5% of the 2,822 Basic accounts never ordered; Gold and Silver have 0%, as they must (a tier above Basic is earned by spending). Average spend per account: Basic $203, Silver $1,064, Gold $2,515.
  • Audit: 150 ids with orders but no account, 739 orders, $154,273.80: the closed accounts from the lesson. So only $3,796,427.65 of the $3,950,701.45 of order value can be attached to a named customer.
  • 4,850 becoming 3,792 means the default inner join was used. More than 4,850 means the orders were merged without aggregating first (one row per order).
  • Average spend here counts every order status. If someone's figures differ slightly, ask whether they filtered to completed orders: a fair choice, as long as they say so.

labs/module-06/l2_5-merging-joining/debug_merges.py
  • Bug 1: ValueError: You are trying to merge on str and int64 columns for key 'order_id'. Do not convert the key to text (or convert it back with .astype("int64")). Prints 45490.

2.5 · The lesson page's Quick Quiz

These are the five questions at the end of the lesson page (three options each), with the lesson's own explanation.

2.5 Q1
What does this print (the lengths of an inner, a left and an outer merge)?
ql = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2, 2, 3], "a": ["w", "x", "y", "z"]})
qr = pd.DataFrame({"k": [2, 2, 4], "b": ["p", "q", "r"]})
print(len(ql.merge(qr, on="k")), len(ql.merge(qr, on="k", how="left")), len(ql.merge(qr, on="k", how="outer")))
A) 2 4 5
B) 4 4 5
C) 4 6 7
Why: Key 2 is repeated on both sides, so it makes 2 x 2 = 4 rows: that is the inner join. A left join adds the unmatched left keys 1 and 3 for 6. An outer join also adds right key 4 for 7.
2.5 Q2
You merge orders (20,302 rows) with customers using the default settings and get 19,563 rows. What happened?
A) The default inner join dropped 739 orders whose customer has no row in customers
B) pandas removed 739 duplicate orders during the merge
C) 739 customers had no orders, so they were left out
Why: The default is an inner join, which keeps only keys present in both tables. 739 orders have a customer_id with no row in customers, so they were dropped without any message.
2.5 Q3
After orders.merge(items, on="order_id"), the sum of order_total is $11.0 million, though the orders table sums to $4.0 million. Why?
A) Some orders had no matching item lines
B) Each order's total is repeated on every one of its item lines, so it is counted several times
C) The item lines include revenue that the orders table left out
Why: The merge is one-to-many: each order row is repeated once per item line, and its order_total with it. Summing the repeated column counts an order with three lines three times.
2.5 Q4
What does validate="many_to_one" check in orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", validate="many_to_one")?
A) That every order finds a matching customer
B) That customer_id is unique in orders
C) That customer_id is unique in customers
Why: many_to_one allows repeated keys on the left and requires each key to appear at most once on the right. If customers had a duplicated id the merge would raise a MergeError instead of silently duplicating orders.
2.5 Q5
You have twelve monthly files with identical columns and want one table of all their rows. Which tool fits?
A) pd.concat(list_of_tables, ignore_index=True)
B) Eleven calls to merge on the date column
C) pd.merge_asof on the date column
Why: concat stacks tables on top of each other, matching columns by name. Collect the twelve DataFrames in a list and call it once, with ignore_index=True to renumber the rows.

2.6 · Pivot Tables and Reshaping: self-check

Q7
What does this print?
t = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["a", "a", "b"], "year": [2024, 2024, 2025], "amt": [10, 30, 5]})
p = t.pivot_table(index="store", columns="year", values="amt")
print(p.loc["a", 2024], p.shape)
A) 20.0 (2, 2)
B) 40 (2, 2)
C) 20.0 (3, 2)
D) A ValueError: Index contains duplicate entries
Why: No aggfunc was given, so the cells hold the mean: store a in 2024 is the mean of 10 and 30. Two stores by two years makes a 2 by 2 grid (two of its cells are empty).
B is wrong: 40 is the sum. The default aggregation of pivot_table is the mean.
C is wrong: The grid has one row per distinct store (2), not one per source row.
D is wrong: That error comes from pivot(), which cannot combine rows. pivot_table() combines them.
Q8
What does this print?
w = pd.DataFrame({"month": ["Jan", "Feb"], "Boise": [5, 6], "Bend": [3, 4], "Online": [1, 2]})
tidy = w.melt(id_vars="month", var_name="store", value_name="rev")
print(tidy.shape, tidy["rev"].sum())
(6, 3) 21
Why: Two rows times three store columns gives six rows. The tidy table has three columns: month, store and rev. Melting moves values without changing them, so they still add up to 21.
Q9
In pd.crosstab(orders["channel"], orders["status"], normalize="index"), the cell in row online, column returned is 0.069. What does it mean?
A) Of all returned orders, 6.9% were online
B) 6.9% of all orders are online orders that were returned
C) Online orders are 6.9% more likely to be returned than store orders
D) Of online orders, 6.9% were returned
Why: normalize="index" divides each cell by its row total, so every row adds up to 1: the cell is a share of the online orders.
A is wrong: That is the column percentage, normalize="columns" (77.9% on the course data).
B is wrong: That is normalize="all": a share of the grand total.
C is wrong: The cell is a share, not a comparison. The comparison is 6.9% against 3.4% for stores.
Q10
A pivot that counts order lines by category and month, with margins=True, shows a grand total of 44,881. The source table has 45,490 rows. What is the most likely explanation?
A) fill_value=0 removed the lines in empty cells
B) margins=True leaves the largest category out of the total
C) 609 lines have a missing category (or month), and rows with a missing key are dropped silently
D) pivot_table removes duplicate rows before counting
Why: A pivot, like a groupby, leaves out rows whose row or column key is missing. On the course data 609 lines use discontinued SKUs that have no category after a left merge. Label them and pivot again.
A is wrong: fill_value only changes how empty cells are displayed; it removes nothing.
B is wrong: Margins are computed from all the rows that reached the pivot.
D is wrong: pivot_table never removes duplicates; it aggregates them.
Q11
What does this print?
idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["a", "b"], [2024, 2025]])
s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4], index=idx)
u = s.unstack()
print(u.shape, u.loc["b", 2024])
(2, 2) 3
Why: unstack() takes the innermost index level (the year) and swings it up into the columns: two rows (a, b) by two columns (2024, 2025). The value for b in 2024 was the third one, 3.
Q12
orders.pivot(index="store", columns="status", values="order_total") raises ValueError: Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape. What is the right response?
A) Call orders.drop_duplicates() first, then pivot() again
B) Decide how to combine the rows and use pivot_table(..., aggfunc="sum")
C) Sort the table by store and status, then pivot() again
D) Convert store and status to the category dtype
Why: Thousands of orders share each store and status, and pivot() only rearranges: it cannot put several rows in one cell. pivot_table() with an explicit aggfunc says how to combine them.
A is wrong: The orders are not duplicate rows (each has its own id). And dropping on store and status would throw away almost all of them.
C is wrong: Sorting does not change how many rows land in each cell.
D is wrong: The dtype of the keys is not the problem; the number of rows per cell is.

2.6 · Predict, then run

P1
An empty cell.
t = pd.DataFrame({"pay": ["card", "cash", "card"], "ch": ["web", "shop", "shop"],
                  "n": [1, 1, 1]})
p = t.pivot_table(index="pay", columns="ch", values="n", aggfunc="count")
print(p.shape, p.isna().sum().sum(), p.loc["card", "web"])
(2, 2) 1 1.0
Why: Two payment methods by two channels is a 2 by 2 grid. Nobody paid cash on the web, so that one cell is NaN, and the NaN turns the whole web column into floats: the count for card on the web prints as 1.0. fill_value=0 would make it an honest 0 and keep the counts whole.
P2
Labels after a pivot.
t = pd.DataFrame({"month": ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"], "store": ["a"] * 4,
                  "rev": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
print(t.pivot(index="month", columns="store", values="rev").index.tolist())
['Apr', 'Feb', 'Jan', 'Mar']
Why: Pivot methods sort their row and column labels, and text sorts alphabetically: Apr, Feb, Jan, Mar. No error is raised. Pivot on the month number, or reindex with the labels in calendar order.
P3
A margin of means.
t = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["a", "a", "a", "b"], "amt": [10, 10, 10, 50]})
p = t.pivot_table(index="store", values="amt", aggfunc="mean", margins=True)
print(p["amt"].tolist(), t.groupby("store")["amt"].mean().mean())
[10.0, 50.0, 20.0] 30.0
Why: The store means are 10 and 50. The margin All is the mean of all four rows, (10 + 10 + 10 + 50) / 4 = 20, not the mean of the two store means, 30. Store a has three times as many rows, so it counts three times as much.

labs/module-06/l2_6-pivot-tables/survey_by_age_solution.py

Question: Which survey question does each age group score lowest, and how many answers are behind each average?

How the solution works: melt turns the five satisfaction columns into two (item, score): 1,800 responses times 5 questions is 9,000 rows. Because each (age group, question) pair now has hundreds of rows, pivot() would raise the duplicate-entries error; pivot_table combines them, once with mean and once with count. idxmin(axis=1) reads across each row. stack() pushes the question labels back into the index, and rename plus reset_index makes a tidy table of 30 rows.

How the solution works: store_weather.csv has exactly one row per (date, city), so plain pivot() rearranges it into 731 rows by 4 columns with no empty cell. idxmax(axis=1) names the warmest column on each date. For the monthly grid several days land in each cell, so pivot_table with aggfunc="mean" is needed. Pivoting on %b month names shows the alphabetical sort; reindex with the twelve names restores calendar order. melt returns to 2,924 rows.

2.6 · The lesson page's Quick Quiz

These are the five questions at the end of the lesson page (three options each), with the lesson's own explanation.

2.6 Q1
A colleague writes orders.pivot_table(index="store", columns="channel", values="order_total") and titles the result "Revenue by store and channel". What is wrong?
A) The call fails, because index and columns must be lists
B) The cells are average order values, because the default aggfunc is the mean
C) The cells are counts of orders, because nothing was summed
Why: With no aggfunc, pivot_table uses the mean. The cells are average order values, so calling the table revenue is wrong. Writing aggfunc='sum' gives revenue.
2.6 Q2
What is in the Bend row, 2024 column of the table this code prints?
toy = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["Boise", "Boise", "Bend"],
                    "year": [2024, 2025, 2025],
                    "sales": [10, 20, 30]})
print(toy.pivot_table(index="store", columns="year", values="sales", aggfunc="sum"))
A) NaN, because no row has that store and year
B) 0, because the sum of no rows is zero
C) Nothing: the code raises an error because the grid is incomplete
Why: No row has store Bend and year 2024, so there is nothing to sum and the cell is NaN. Adding fill_value=0 would show 0 instead.
2.6 Q3
df.pivot(index="date", columns="store", values="revenue") raises ValueError: Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape. What does that tell you?
A) Some revenue values are missing
B) The date column is text and must be converted first
C) At least one date and store pair appears on more than one row
Why: pivot only rearranges, so each date and store pair may appear once. Duplicates mean either the data has repeated rows to investigate, or you need pivot_table with an aggfunc to combine them.
2.6 Q4
A wide table has 12 rows and the columns Month, Boise, Bend, Flagstaff, Asheville, Online. How many rows does table.melt(id_vars="Month") have?
A) 60
B) 72
C) 12
Why: Month is kept as the identifier and the other 5 columns are stacked, so each of the 12 months appears once per store: 12 x 5 = 60 rows, with columns Month, variable and value.
2.6 Q5
A pivot of average order value by store with margins=True shows store means of 175.10, 172.47, 177.21, 182.39 and 203.20, and an All value of 193.17. The plain average of the five store means is 182.07. Why is All different?
A) It is a rounding error that grows with the number of rows
B) The margin leaves out the rows with missing values, so it uses fewer orders
C) All is the mean of every order, so the store with the most orders counts the most
Why: Margins apply the aggfunc to all the underlying rows. The store with the 203.20 mean has far more orders than the others, so it pulls the overall mean toward itself.

Warm-up Answers

  1. In what order do you repair a damaged table? Answer: Structure (headers, stray rows, duplicates), then text, numbers, dates, and last the missing values.
  2. What does pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce") do with the value free, and why is that useful? Answer: It turns it into NaN instead of raising an error, so it works as a detector: values that became NaN but were not empty are the ones to look at.
  3. orders.dropna() kept 2,085 of 20,302 rows. Why, and what should you write? Answer: It drops every row with a gap in any column, and most orders have no promo code. Name the columns that matter: dropna(subset=[...]).
  4. You need each order's total next to its store's average order. Which groupby tool gives one value per original row? Answer: transform (for example orders.groupby("store")["order_total"].transform("mean")).
  5. Grouped by promo_code, the group sizes add up to 2,148, but there are 20,302 orders. What happened? Answer: Rows whose key is missing are dropped by default. dropna=False keeps them as a group.

Exit Ticket Answers

  1. You merge orders (20,302 rows) with customers using the default settings and get 19,563 rows. What happened, and what would you write instead? Answer: The default inner join dropped the 739 orders whose customer_id has no row in customers. Write orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one") and count the rows.
  2. After orders.merge(items, on="order_id"), the sum of order_total is $11.0 million instead of $4.0 million. Why? Answer: The result has one row per order line, so each order's total is repeated on every one of its lines and counted several times. Sum order-level columns on the orders table (or after drop_duplicates("order_id")).
  3. A count pivot with margins=True has a grand total of 44,881, but the source table has 45,490 rows. What does that tell you, and what do you do? Answer: 609 rows have a missing value in the row or column key and were dropped silently. Find them, give them an honest label (for example fillna("Discontinued")), and pivot again until the corner matches the source.

Common Wrong Answers and What They Reveal

  • Q1 answered 2 3 4. They count keys, not rows: key 3 appears twice on the right, so it makes two rows. Have them write out the rows of the inner join by hand.
  • Q3 answered 150 150. They do not yet see that the merged table repeats order-level values. Ask what one row of m is, then have them print m.
  • Q4 answered B ('customers who have never placed an order'). Left and right are swapped in their head. left_only means the key exists only in the table before .merge: here, orders.
  • Q2 answered A (the default merge). They have the mechanics but not the habit. Ask how many rows that call returns on the course data (19,563) and where the other 739 went.
  • Q7 answered B (40 (2, 2)). The spreadsheet habit: a pivot sums. In pandas the default is the mean.
  • Q8 answered (2, 4) 21 or (6, 2) 21. melt is still fuzzy: each store column becomes rows, and the result has the id column plus two new ones. Melt a three-row table by hand.
  • Q9 answered A ('of all returned orders, 6.9% were online'). Row and column percentages are confused. Ask which total the cell was divided by: with normalize="index", its row.
  • Exit ticket 3 answered 'the margins are wrong'. They trust the source less than the grid. The margin is computed correctly from the rows that reached the pivot; the question is which rows did not.
  • Lab customer_profiles: 3,792 rows after the merge. The default inner join. Ask what the row count should have been, and what how= says.
  • Lab payment_returns: 0.0 in the cash/Online rate cell. fill_value=0 was copied from the count pivot. Ask: zero percent of what?
