2.7 · Time Series: self-check

Q1
After raw = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv"), the line raw["date"].dt.month raises AttributeError: Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values. What is the cause?
A) Some dates are missing from the file
B) The column was loaded as text; pass parse_dates=["date"] or convert with pd.to_datetime
C) .dt only works on the index, not on a column
D) month is a method and needs parentheses
Why: With no instructions read_csv keeps dates as text, and text has no .dt accessor. Parse at load time, then check df.dtypes.
A is wrong: Missing days do not change the dtype of the days that are present.
C is wrong: .dt is for columns (Series). A DatetimeIndex has the same properties directly, without .dt.
D is wrong: .dt.month is a property. The error is raised at .dt, before month is even looked up.
Q2
What does this print?
s = pd.Series(range(10),
              index=pd.date_range("2025-01-28", periods=10, freq="D"))
print(len(s.loc["2025-01"]), len(s.loc["2025-01-30":"2025-02-02"]))
4 4
Why: "2025-01" selects every row in January: the 28th, 29th, 30th and 31st. The string range includes both ends: January 30 and 31, February 1 and 2.
Q3
wide has one row per date and 727 rows between 2024-01-01 and 2025-12-31, a span of 731 days. What does wide.asfreq("D") return?
A) 727 rows; the four gaps are interpolated
B) 731 rows; the four new rows are filled with 0
C) An error, because the index has missing dates
D) 731 rows; the four new rows hold NaN
Why: asfreq("D") gives the table one row for every calendar day. Rows that did not exist appear as NaN: pandas shows you the gap and leaves the decision to you.
A is wrong: pandas never estimates values unless you call interpolate() or ffill() yourself.
B is wrong: Zero is a claim (the store sold nothing). pandas does not make it for you; you fill closed days with 0 on purpose.
C is wrong: Missing dates are exactly what asfreq is for. It needs a DatetimeIndex, not a complete one.
Q4
What does this print?
s = pd.Series([10.0, np.nan, 30.0],
              index=pd.to_datetime(["2025-05-01", "2025-05-02", "2025-05-03"]))
print(s.resample("ME").agg(["sum", "count"]).values.tolist())
A) [[40.0, 2.0]]
B) [[nan, 3.0]]
C) [[40.0, 3.0]]
D) [[nan, 2.0]]
Why: sum skips the missing value and adds 10 + 30. count counts only real values, so it says 2, which is how you find out that the total of 40 is built from two days and not three.
B is wrong: pandas aggregations skip NaN by default, and count never counts a missing value.
C is wrong: count is the number of non-missing values, not the number of rows in the bucket.
D is wrong: The count is right, but the sum is not NaN: sum skips missing values (that is the danger).
Q5
Bend has no rows at all for three days in August 2024. On that rows-only Series, what does bend_rows.diff(7) compare the first Saturday after the gap with?
A) The previous Saturday, seven days earlier
B) Nothing: the result is NaN because the window crosses a gap
C) The value seven rows earlier, which is ten days back and not a Saturday
D) Nothing: pandas raises an error on an irregular index
Why: shift and diff count rows, not days. With three rows missing, seven rows back is ten days back. No error and no warning: complete the calendar with asfreq("D") first.
A is wrong: That is what you want, and what you get only on a complete calendar.
B is wrong: NaN is what the completed calendar gives for the days after a gap, because a week earlier is unknown there. Rows-only data has no NaN to pass on.
D is wrong: pandas is happy to shift any index. The mistake is silent.
Q6
What does this print?
m = pd.Series([200, 220, 264],
              index=pd.date_range("2025-01-31", periods=3, freq="ME"))
print((m.pct_change() * 100).round(1).tolist())
[nan, 10.0, 20.0]
Why: pct_change() is the change from the previous row divided by the previous row: 20/200 = 10% and 44/220 = 20%. January has no previous row, so it is NaN.

2.7 · Predict, then run: answers

Predict 2.7.1
How many rows does each selection return? (Two numbers.)
days = pd.Series(1, index=pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="D"))
print(len(days.loc["2024-02"]), len(days.loc["2024-12-30":"2024-12-31"]))
29 2
Why: 2024 is a leap year, so February has 29 days. The string range includes both ends: December 30 and December 31.
Predict 2.7.2
One Sunday is missing from this small table. What are the two weekly sums, and the two counts?
s = pd.Series([5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9],
              index=pd.date_range("2025-03-03", periods=14, freq="D").delete(6))
print(s.resample("W").agg(["sum", "count"]).values.tolist())
[[30, 6], [63, 7]]
Why: March 3, 2025 is a Monday, and the first Sunday (March 9) was deleted. The first week has six rows of 5 (sum 30, count 6); the second has seven rows of 9 (sum 63, count 7). The sum alone would suggest the second week was twice as good; per recorded day it went from 5 to 9.
Predict 2.7.3
What does diff() print for the last row, and why is that surprising?
s = pd.Series([100, 104, 120],
              index=pd.to_datetime(["2025-06-01", "2025-06-02", "2025-06-06"]))
print(s.diff().tolist())
print(s.asfreq("D").diff().tolist())
[nan, 4.0, 16.0]
[nan, 4.0, nan, nan, nan, nan]
Why: On the rows-only Series, diff() subtracts the previous row: 120 - 104 = 16, although that row is four days earlier. After asfreq("D") the three missing days exist as NaN, and every difference that touches one of them is NaN: the honest answer to "how much did it change since yesterday?"

2.7 · Lab reference solutions

Lab 2.7-A · An honest weekly calendar: labs/module-07/l2_7-time-series/units_calendar_solution.py

What it practices: the order of operations on a new column (units) and a new bucket (weeks). units has no blank values, so after zeroing the four closed days the only unknowns are the five failed-export days (Bend 3, Flagstaff 2).

Step 1. The calendar has 731 days and the wide table 727 rows. calendar.difference(units.index) is the four dates on which no store has a row. The reverse, units.index.difference(calendar), is empty and is the usual slip.

Step 4. Two weeks have fewer than 7 days, for two different reasons. The week ending 2024-08-18 has 4 days because the export failed on August 12 to 14. The week ending 2026-01-04 has 3 days because the data stops on Wednesday, December 31: a "W" bucket runs Monday to Sunday and is labeled with its Sunday, even when that Sunday is past the end of the data.

Step 5. Take the maximum only over complete weeks. Here the best week overall is also complete (ends 2025-08-31, 1,767 units: Labor Day weekend), so a learner who skips the filter gets the same answer by luck. Ask what the code would have done if the best week had been a partial one.

Step 6. -96 and +80 are real. -542 is the 4-day week compared with a 7-day week, and +443 is the next full week compared with the 4-day week. One incomplete bucket spoils two changes. An honest table shows NaN or a footnote for both.

Lab 2.7-B · Is the online return rate getting worse?: labs/module-07/l2_7-time-series/returns_trend_solution.py

What it practices: resample(..., on=) on a table whose dates are a column; the mean of a True/False column as a rate; diff(12) for year over year in percentage points; and reading a noisy series without inventing a story.

The answer is "no trend". The yearly rate went from 7.11% to 6.76%. Seven months of 2025 were worse than a year earlier and five were better, with changes between -2.80 and +2.84 points. A month has only 24 to 51 returns, so a handful of orders moves the monthly rate by a point or more.

Accept any conclusion that reports the yearly rates and says the monthly differences are noise. Push back on "April 2025 was much worse" (+2.84 points, on 46 returns) or "returns improved in May and June" presented as findings: ask how many returns that difference is.

Gaps: orders.csv has orders on every one of the 731 days, so every monthly count is a full month. The count column here is the number of orders, which is the denominator of the rate.

2.8 · Window Functions: self-check

Q7
What does this print?
s = pd.Series([4, 8, 6, 10])
print(s.rolling(3, min_periods=2).mean().tolist())
A) [nan, nan, 6.0, 8.0]
B) [4.0, 6.0, 6.0, 8.0]
C) [nan, 6.0, 6.0, 8.0]
D) [6.0, 6.0, 8.0, nan]
Why: The window is this row and the two before it, and it answers as soon as 2 values are present. Row 1 has only one value (NaN); row 2 is the mean of 4 and 8; then the full windows give 6 and 8.
A is wrong: That is the strict default, where all 3 values must be present.
B is wrong: That is min_periods=1, where one value is enough.
D is wrong: A trailing window looks backward, so the gap is at the start, not the end.
Q8
What does this print?
s = pd.Series([5, 3, 9, 4, 9])
print((s == s.cummax()).tolist())
[True, False, True, False, True]
Why: cummax() is the best value so far: 5, 5, 9, 9, 9. A row equals it when it sets or ties the record. The last 9 ties the record, so it is True as well.
Q9
A long table has columns store, date, revenue, sorted by date and then store. Which code adds each store's own 7-day average, lined up with the right rows?
A) df["avg"] = df["revenue"].rolling(7).mean()
B) df["avg"] = df.groupby("store")["revenue"].rolling(7).mean()
C) df["avg"] = df.groupby("date")["revenue"].transform(lambda s: s.rolling(7).mean())
D) Sort by store and date, then df["avg"] = df.groupby("store")["revenue"].transform(lambda s: s.rolling(7).mean())
Why: Sort, group, window. transform returns one value per row with the original index, so the new column lines up.
A is wrong: Seven consecutive rows are different stores on neighboring days: a number with no meaning.
B is wrong: The result has a two-level index (store, row label), and assigning it back raises TypeError: incompatible index of inserted column with frame index.
C is wrong: Grouping by date puts four stores of one day in each group: every result is NaN, and it is the wrong grouping anyway.
Q10
What does this print?
s = pd.Series([30, 10, 30, 20])
print(s.rank(ascending=False, method="dense").tolist())
A) [1.0, 3.0, 1.0, 2.0]
B) [1.5, 4.0, 1.5, 3.0]
C) [1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 3.0]
D) [3.0, 1.0, 3.0, 2.0]
Why: With ascending=False the largest value gets rank 1. The two 30s tie for first. "dense" leaves no gap after a tie, so 20 is rank 2 and 10 is rank 3.
B is wrong: That is the default method="average": the tied values share positions 1 and 2.
C is wrong: That is method="min" (sports ranking): after two firsts the next rank is 3.
D is wrong: That is a dense rank with the default ascending=True, where the smallest value is rank 1.
Q11
To flag unusual days, an analyst computes lift = rev / rev.rolling(28).mean() and flags days where lift >= 1.5. What is wrong with the baseline?
A) A 28-day window is too long to react to a sale
B) Each day is inside its own baseline, so every spike is understated; use rev.shift(1).rolling(28).mean()
C) A rolling mean cannot be used as a divisor
D) The first 27 rows are NaN, so the division fails
Why: The window ends on the day being judged, so part of the spike is already in the average it is compared with. Shift first, then roll: the baseline then holds only what was known that morning.
A is wrong: Window length is a judgment call, not an error. The leak is the problem at any length.
C is wrong: Dividing two aligned Series is ordinary pandas.
D is wrong: NaN rows give NaN lifts and are simply not flagged; nothing fails.
Q12
What does this print?
s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
print(s.shift(1).rolling(2).sum().tolist())
[nan, nan, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0]
Why: shift(1) gives NaN, 1, 2, 3, 4. A 2-row sum needs two real values: the first two rows have none or one, then 1+2, 2+3, 3+4. Each result uses only the rows before its own.

2.8 · Predict, then run: answers

Predict 2.8.1
How many NaN values, and what is the last number?
s = pd.Series([2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12])
r = s.rolling(4).mean()
print(int(r.isna().sum()), r.iloc[-1])
3 9.0
Why: A window of 4 is full for the first time on the 4th row, so the first 3 results are NaN. The last window holds 6, 8, 10 and 12: mean 9.0.
Predict 2.8.2
Two groups stacked in one column. What does each line print?
t = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b"],
                  "v": [1, 2, 3, 10, 20, 30]})
print(t["v"].cumsum().tolist())
print(t.groupby("g")["v"].cumsum().tolist())
[1, 3, 6, 16, 36, 66]
[1, 3, 6, 10, 30, 60]
Why: The plain cumsum runs straight through both groups: 6 + 10 = 16 carries group a's total into group b. The grouped version restarts at the first row of each group. This is the long-table trap in its smallest form, and it is how year to date works.
Predict 2.8.3
Which of the three columns could you have computed on the morning of each row? Predict the last row of each.
s = pd.Series([10, 10, 10, 40, 10])
print(s.rolling(3).mean().round(1).tolist())
print(s.rolling(3, center=True).mean().round(1).tolist())
print(s.shift(1).rolling(3).mean().round(1).tolist())
[nan, nan, 10.0, 20.0, 20.0]
[nan, 10.0, 20.0, 20.0, nan]
[nan, nan, nan, 10.0, 20.0]
Why: Only the third. The trailing mean already contains the 40 on the day of the spike (20.0). The centered mean sees the spike one row early (20.0 on the third row) and has no value on the last row. The shifted version is still 10.0 on the day of the spike and only reacts the day after.

2.8 · Lab reference solutions

Lab 2.8-A · Foot traffic: when did Flagstaff pass Bend?: labs/module-07/l2_8-window-functions/foot_traffic_solution.py

What it practices: rolling().mean() and its NaN edge, min_periods, comparing two smoothed series, cummax() for records, and rolling().sum() with idxmax() for a best stretch. Everything is on the wide calendar, so no grouping is needed.

Step 2. With min_periods=21 the first 28-day value appears on row 21 (2024-01-21), and the five unknown visitor days (Bend 3, Flagstaff 2) cost nothing: each affected window still has 25 or 26 known days.

Step 3 has two defensible answers and one better one. Flagstaff's 28-day average is first above Bend's on 2024-12-25, but the lead changed hands several times after that. Bend was last ahead on 2025-06-03, so the answer to "since when has Flagstaff been ahead?" is 2025-06-04. Flagstaff led on 324 days in all. The known mask in the solution keeps rows where both averages exist; without it, the NaN rows at the start count as "not ahead", which happens to give the same date here.

Step 4. 18 record days. A tie with the previous record would also be True (see self-check Q8); there are none in this column.

Step 5. The label that idxmax() returns is the last day of the 7; subtract 6 days for the start. Three of the four stores peak around Labor Day or Memorial Day sale weekends; Flagstaff peaks in the week before Christmas 2025, which fits its growth.

Lab 2.8-B · The online shop: milestones, ranks and a fair baseline: labs/module-07/l2_8-window-functions/online_milestones_solution.py

What it practices: a running total that restarts per group, ranking within groups, cummax(), and the leakage idea from the project on a new series.

Step 1. 2024 passed $1,000,000 on December 11; 2025 on October 16, about eight weeks earlier in the year. Full-year totals: 1,077,800.75 and 1,280,183.70 (+18.8%).

Step 2. December is rank 1 and February rank 12 in both years. In between, the order changes: May was 2nd in 2024 and 5th in 2025. rank returns floats; the solution converts to int only because there are no ties.

Step 4. The record day, 2025-06-24, is a Tuesday with $8,960.15. Against the mean of the four Tuesdays before it (4,066.72) it is 2.20 times normal. With the day inside its own 4-Tuesday window the "baseline" rises to 5,583.56 and the ratio falls to 1.60. Across two years, 25 days reach 2 times an honest baseline and only 2 reach 2 times a leaky one: the leak hides exactly the days the baseline exists to find.

A question worth asking: why was that Tuesday so large? done[done["order_date"] == "2025-06-24"] shows one order of $4,184.90, one of the twelve bulk outfitter orders described in data/README.md. A real order, not an error.

2.8 · The lesson page's own Quick Quiz

These five questions are on the lesson page (three options each). Letters and reasons are read from the lesson.

#Question (short form)AnswerReason
Q1NaN count in s.rolling(7).mean() for 100 complete daily valuesBThe trailing window is full for the first time on row 7, so 6 NaN, all at the start.
Q2pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4]).rolling(2).sum().tolist()C[nan, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0]: each value is the row plus the one before; the first row has none.
Q3df["revenue"].rolling(7).mean() on a table sorted by date, then storeASeven consecutive rows mix different stores. Sort by store and date, then groupby with transform.
Q4A feature for predicting today's revenue, safe from leakageCrev.shift(1).rolling(7).mean(): the window covers yesterday and the six days before.
Q5pd.Series([50, 80, 80, 95]).rank(ascending=False, method="min")A[4.0, 2.0, 2.0, 1.0]: 95 is first, the two 80s both get 2, the next rank is 4.

Warm-up Answers

  1. What is the default how= of merge, and what happens to a row whose key has no match? Answer: inner. The row is dropped with no warning. In Lesson 2.5 that lost 739 orders whose customer has no row in customers.csv. Use how="left" when you are adding columns to a main table.
  2. After a merge the result has more rows than the left table. What does that tell you? Answer: The key repeats on the other side (one-to-many or many-to-many), so left rows were duplicated. Count rows before and after, and state the relationship with validate=.
  3. What does pivot_table compute in each cell if you leave out aggfunc? Answer: The mean. A table titled "revenue" built that way shows average order values. Always write aggfunc.
  4. df.pivot(index="date", columns="store", values="revenue") raises ValueError: Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape. What does the error tell you about the data? Answer: At least one date and store pair appears on more than one row. pivot only rearranges; choose how to combine the repeats and use pivot_table(..., aggfunc=...).
  5. A sheet has one row per month and one column per store. Which method turns it into tidy rows of month, store, revenue? Answer: melt(id_vars="Month", var_name="store", value_name="revenue"). Twelve rows and five store columns become 60 rows.

Exit Ticket Answers

  1. You resample daily revenue to monthly totals with .sum(). What do you print beside every total, and why? Answer: The count of days with a value (for example .agg(["sum", "count"])). Sums skip NaN silently, so a month with missing days looks like a weak month.
  2. Write an expression for a 7-day average of the Series rev that is safe to use for judging or predicting today. Answer: rev.shift(1).rolling(7).mean() (or rev.rolling(7, closed="left").mean()). Shift first, so today is not inside its own baseline.
  3. List the order of operations for a time series, and name the step people skip most often. Answer: Parse the dates; put them in the index; complete the calendar with asfreq; decide what each gap means; only then resample, shift or compare. The skipped step is completing the calendar.

Reading the tickets: a ticket that says "mean" or "nothing" for question 1 needs the Bend August example again. For question 2, rev.rolling(7).mean().shift(1) is also correct (the same numbers); rev.rolling(7).mean() and anything with center=True are the leak, and those learners get a two-minute recap at the start of Session 8, where leakage returns as the cutoff rule. For question 3, accept any wording that puts the calendar before the arithmetic.

2.9 · Feature Engineering Basics: self-check

Q1
Marketing asks which customers will order again, so one row of the feature table is a customer. Which of these is not a valid column for that table as it stands?
A) Days from the customer's signup to the cutoff date
B) The order_total of each of the customer's orders
C) The number of orders the customer placed before the cutoff
D) The share of the customer's orders that were placed online
Why: A customer has many orders, so "the order total" is many values, not one fact about the customer. Aggregate it first (a sum, a mean, a maximum) and it becomes a customer feature.
A is wrong: One number per customer: a fine feature (tenure).
C is wrong: One number per customer, and it respects the cutoff.
D is wrong: The mean of a True/False column per customer: one number each.
Q2
What does this print?
ages = pd.Series([18, 24, 25, 40])
bands = pd.cut(ages, bins=[17, 24, 34, 120], labels=["18-24", "25-34", "35+"])
print(bands.tolist())
['18-24', '18-24', '25-34', '35+']
Why: By default each bin includes its right edge and excludes its left: (17, 24], (24, 34], (34, 120]. So 24 is still in the first band and 25 starts the second. That is why the first edge is 17, not 18.
Q3
What does this print?
x = pd.Series([0, 10, 20, 30])
print(pd.cut(x, bins=[0, 10, 20]).isna().sum())
A) 0
B) 1
C) 2
D) 4
Why: The bins are (0, 10] and (10, 20]. The value 0 is not in (0, 10] because the left edge is excluded, and 30 is beyond the last edge. Both become NaN, with no warning.
A is wrong: Two values fall outside the bins; cut does not stretch the edges to fit.
B is wrong: 30 is outside, and so is 0: the left edge of the first bin is excluded unless you pass include_lowest=True.
D is wrong: 10 and 20 sit exactly on right edges, which are included.
Q4
customers has 4,850 rows. per_customer, built with orders.groupby("customer_id").agg(...), has 3,942 rows. What does customers.merge(per_customer, on="customer_id") return with the default settings?
A) 4,850 rows, with NaN for customers who never ordered
B) 3,942 rows, one for every customer id in the orders
C) 8,792 rows, every row of both tables
D) 3,792 rows: every customer who never ordered is gone
Why: The default is an inner join, which keeps only ids found in both tables. The 1,058 customers with no orders vanish (and so do the 150 order ids with no account). For a feature table, use how="left" from the table that defines the unit, and check that the row count did not change.
A is wrong: That is what how="left" gives, and it is what you want.
B is wrong: 150 of those ids belong to closed accounts with no row in customers, so they cannot match either.
C is wrong: A merge matches rows; it does not stack the two tables.
Q5
A method needs numbers. You have loyalty_tier (Basic, Silver, Gold) and acquisition_channel (five values with no order). Which encoding is appropriate?
A) Ordered integer codes for the tier; one yes/no column per channel with pd.get_dummies
B) Integer codes 0 to 4 for the channel, in alphabetical order; one yes/no column per tier
C) Integer codes for both, because they take the least space
D) Standardize both columns to mean 0 and standard deviation 1
Why: The tier is ordinal: 0, 1, 2 says Gold is above Silver is above Basic, which is true. The channel is nominal: numbering it would tell a model that one channel is "twice" another, so each channel gets its own yes/no column.
B is wrong: This has it backwards: it invents an order for the channels and throws away the real order of the tiers.
C is wrong: Small is not the goal. Codes on a nominal column state an order that does not exist.
D is wrong: Scaling works on numbers. Text has to be encoded first, and scaling does not fix a made-up order.
Q6
You build features as of the cutoff 2025-07-01 to predict who orders in the following six months. A colleague's n_orders counts all of each customer's orders in the file. What happens?
A) An error: pandas refuses to aggregate rows dated after the cutoff
B) Nothing important: more data makes a better feature
C) The feature looks more predictive than it is, because orders after the cutoff are in both the feature and the target
D) The feature becomes useless, because the extra rows add noise
Why: This is the "rows from the future" leak. Anyone who ordered after the cutoff has a higher count because of it, so the count partly contains the answer. It will look excellent in testing and fail on a real today. Filter to order_date < cutoff before aggregating.
A is wrong: Leaks never raise an error. That is what makes them dangerous.
B is wrong: On a real cutoff date those rows do not exist yet, so the feature cannot be computed as tested.
D is wrong: The opposite: it becomes suspiciously good. "Too good" is the warning sign.

2.9 · Predict, then run: answers

Predict 2.9.1
The same three values, binned twice. What does each line print?
v = pd.Series([10, 20, 30])
edges, names = [0, 10, 20, 30], ["a", "b", "c"]
print(pd.cut(v, bins=edges, labels=names).tolist())
print(pd.cut(v, bins=edges, labels=names, right=False).tolist())
['a', 'b', 'c']
['b', 'c', nan]
Why: By default each bin includes its right edge: 10 is in (0, 10], 20 in (10, 20], 30 in (20, 30]. With right=False each bin includes its left edge instead, so 10 moves to [10, 20), 20 to [20, 30), and 30 is no longer inside any bin: it becomes NaN with no warning.
Predict 2.9.2
Three customers, one of whom never ordered. What are the two lists?
people = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3]})
bought = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 3], "total": [10.0, 20.0, 7.0]})
per = bought.groupby("id").agg(n=("total", "count"), avg=("total", "mean"))
t = people.merge(per, on="id", how="left")
t["n"] = t["n"].fillna(0).astype(int)
print(t["n"].tolist(), t["avg"].tolist())
[2, 0, 1] [15.0, nan, 7.0]
Why: The left merge keeps customer 2 with NaN in both new columns. The count is filled with 0, which is a fact. The average is left missing: there is no average of zero orders.
Predict 2.9.3
What are the column names, and what does each column add up to?
d = pd.get_dummies(pd.Series(["web", "store", "web"]), dtype=int)
print(d.columns.tolist(), d.sum().tolist(), d.sum(axis=1).tolist())
['store', 'web'] [1, 2] [1, 1, 1]
Why: One column per category, in alphabetical order: store, then web. Column sums count the rows in each category (1 and 2). Every row has exactly one 1, so each row sums to 1.

2.9 · Lab reference solutions

Lab 2.9-A · Which orders come back?: labs/module-08/l2_9-feature-engineering/order_features_solution.py

What it practices: choosing a unit of analysis (an order), flags, a per-entity aggregate joined back with a left merge, qcut and cut, checking each feature against the target with rate and size, and an interaction feature.

Step 2. The category of a line is read from the SKU prefix (FTW), not by merging with products.csv. That is deliberate: 609 order lines use six discontinued SKUs that are not in the catalog, and a merge would give them no category (Lesson 2.5). ("is_footwear", "any") is True when at least one line of the order is footwear.

Step 3. 20,302 rows before and after, and no order without lines. validate="one_to_one" would raise if per_order had two rows for one order.

Step 5. What separates: channel (online 6.9%, store 3.4%), footwear (10.7% against 4.2%), order value (top half about 6.5% to 6.8%, bottom half 4.4% to 4.9%) and number of lines (4.3% for one line, rising to 7.4% for five or more). What does not: a promo code (5.4% against 5.7%) and the weekend (5.4% against 5.7%).

Step 6 is the finding. Online orders containing footwear: 14.4% returned (2,854 orders). The other three combinations: 3.3%, 3.8% and 4.8%. In a store, people try shoes on; online they cannot. Neither is_online nor has_footwear shows this alone. Features can be combined, and the combination came from thinking about how the business works.

Step 7. status is what returned was computed from. Kept as a feature it predicts the target perfectly and means nothing. More generally: nothing recorded after the order shipped may be a feature for "will it be returned".

Lab 2.9-B · How busy will the store be tomorrow?: labs/module-08/l2_9-feature-engineering/store_day_features_solution.py

What it practices: a ratio within a group (transform), bins with open outer edges, a window feature built on the completed calendar (Lesson 2.7 meets 2.8), and a leak audit where the cutoff is a time of day.

Step 4. Relative traffic: cold days 0.82 of normal, hot days 1.15; rainy 0.82 against 1.03; promotion days 1.70; weekends 1.35 against 0.86.

Step 5. On 104 rows, seven rows back is not seven days back, because 21 store-days have no row. The first examples are the days after Thanksgiving 2024, where the rows-only lag is off by one day and compares a Friday with a Thursday. No error. The calendar version (asfreq("D"), then shift(7)) is correct, and it is NaN where last week is unknown.

Step 6. transactions, units and revenue correlate with visitors at 0.94 to 0.96 because they are counted during the day being predicted: leaks. The calendar lag (0.86) is honest. promo_day is planned in advance. high_f is the measured high: on the evening before, only a forecast exists. staff_on_duty (0.93) is the interesting one: it is fixed in advance, so it passes the cutoff rule, but it encodes a manager's own forecast of demand. Whether to use it depends on what the prediction is for.

3.1 · Line, Scatter and Bar Charts: self-check

Q7
Question: "Do products with more reviews tend to have higher ratings?" Which chart answers it?
A) A line chart of rating against review count
B) A scatter plot: one dot per product, review count against rating
C) A bar chart with one bar per product
D) A histogram of the ratings
Why: Two numeric columns, and the question is whether they move together: one dot per row, nothing joined, because the products have no order.
A is wrong: A line joins points in order and suggests one product leads to the next.
C is wrong: 242 bars compare products one by one; they do not show a relationship between two measures.
D is wrong: A histogram shows one column's distribution. The review counts are not in it.
Q8
What does this print?
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
bars = ax.bar(["a", "b", "a", "b", "a"], [1, 5, 3, 2, 2])
print(len(bars), len(fig.axes))
plt.close(fig)
5 1
Why: ax.bar draws one bar per value it is given and never aggregates: five bars, piled up at two x positions. The figure still has one Axes.
Q9
A tutorial writes plt.title("Revenue"). You are holding the chart in a variable ax. What do you write?
A) ax.set_title("Revenue")
B) ax.title("Revenue")
C) fig.set_title("Revenue")
D) ax.title = "Revenue"
Why: On an Axes the labeling methods start with set_: set_title, set_xlabel, set_ylabel, set_xlim.
B is wrong: ax.title is the title object itself; calling it raises TypeError: 'Text' object is not callable.
C is wrong: A Figure has no set_title; the title of one chart belongs to its Axes.
D is wrong: This replaces the title object with a string and draws nothing.
Q10
A histogram of 20,302 order totals with bins=40 shows almost everything in three bars, on an axis that runs to $5,000. What is the best fix?
A) bins=400, so that the bars are narrower
B) Delete the large orders from the DataFrame before plotting
C) range=(0, 1000), and say in the title how many orders are not shown
D) Switch to a bar chart with one bar per order
Why: A few very large orders stretch the range. range= puts the 40 bins where the orders are, and the title tells the reader what was left out.
A is wrong: The axis still runs to $5,000, with most of it empty.
B is wrong: The bulk orders are real. Removing rows changes the data; choosing a range only changes the view.
D is wrong: 20,302 bars is not a distribution, and ax.bar does not count anything.
Q11
What does this print?
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
counts, edges, patches = ax.hist([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 9], bins=4, range=(0, 8))
print(counts.tolist(), len(edges))
plt.close(fig)
[1.0, 5.0, 0.0, 0.0] 5
Why: Four bins over 0 to 8 are each 2 wide: 0 to 2, 2 to 4, 4 to 6, 6 to 8. The value 1 is in the first; 2, 2, 3, 3, 3 are in the second. The 9 is outside the range and is silently left out. Four bins have five edges.
Q12
A scatter plot of 2,903 store-days shows a solid blob in the lower left: you cannot tell 5 overlapping dots from 500. Which change fixes it?
A) A larger figsize
B) linewidth=0.8 and linestyle="--"
C) bins=40 and range=(0, 1000)
D) A smaller s and an alpha below 1
Why: This is overplotting. Smaller dots overlap less, and see-through dots make dense regions darker, so density becomes visible.
A is wrong: A bigger figure spreads the same solid dots; the dense region is still a blob.
B is wrong: Those style a line. A scatter has none.
C is wrong: Those belong to ax.hist.

3.1 · Predict, then run: answers

Predict 3.1.1
One figure, a loop that plots three columns. What are the two numbers?
t = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [2, 1], "c": [3, 3]})
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for col in t.columns:
    ax.plot(t.index, t[col], label=col)
print(len(fig.axes), len(ax.lines))
plt.close(fig)
1 3
Why: plt.subplots() made one Axes, and every ax.plot call adds a line to that same Axes: one chart, three lines.
Predict 3.1.2
No error. How many bars, and how tall is the tallest thing you can see?
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
bars = ax.bar(["x", "y", "x"], [5, 2, 9])
print(len(bars), max(bar.get_height() for bar in bars))
plt.close(fig)
3 9
Why: Three bars, one per value, with two of them piled at "x". You would see a bar of height 9 at "x": the larger of 5 and 9, not their sum of 14.
Predict 3.1.3
Three dates given as text, out of order. Where does Matplotlib put them on the x axis?
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(["2025-01-03", "2025-01-01", "2025-01-02"], [3, 1, 2])
print(list(ax.get_xticks()))
plt.close(fig)
[0, 1, 2]
Why: Text values are categories. Matplotlib places them at positions 0, 1, 2 in the order they arrive, so January 3 comes first on the axis. It does not know they are dates, so it cannot sort or space them. Parse dates before plotting.

3.1 · Lab reference solutions

Lab 3.1-A · Four questions, four charts: labs/module-08/l3_1-line-scatter-bar/four_questions_solution.py

What it practices: choosing the chart from the question; the five-line pattern four times; aggregating before a line and a bar and not before a scatter or a histogram; bar_label, alpha, axvline; saving with fig.savefig.

Question 1: a line. Seven yearly counts, 614 to 838, best year 2024. The reference solution sets ax.set_ylim(bottom=0) so the rise in 2024 is not exaggerated. Bars are acceptable for seven years; ask what the learner would do with 84 months.

Question 2: horizontal bars. value_counts().sort_values() is smallest first, and barh draws the first row at the bottom, so the longest bar (organic, 1,517) ends up on top.

Question 3: a scatter. 228 dots, not 242: weight_kg is missing for 14 products and Matplotlib leaves those rows out silently. The reference title says so. Correlation 0.69: heavier products do cost more, with a wide spread. Accept "tend to"; push back on "because".

Question 4: a histogram. 30 bins, each $20.28 wide; median $82.95; 21 products above $300 form a long right tail. No range= is needed here: the tail is part of the answer and 242 rows leave no bar empty of meaning. A learner who did a groupby first has confused the histogram with a bar chart.

Lab 3.1-B · Chart repair: labs/module-08/l3_1-line-scatter-bar/chart_repair_solution.py

What it practices: recognizing the three silent chart mistakes from the lesson on new data, and fixing the cause in pandas, not the symptom in Matplotlib.

Chart 1. ax.bar drew one bar per order. The visible heights were each method's largest single order (card $3,779.45, gift card $840.60, cash $702.25, digital wallet $640.80), which even ranks the methods wrongly. After groupby(...).sum(): card $132,538, digital wallet $46,513, gift card $16,563, cash $12,888.

Chart 2. Flagstaff's export failed on January 21 and 22, 2025, so those days have no rows and the line ran straight across them. set_index("date")["visitors"].asfreq("D") puts the days back as NaN, and a line breaks at NaN. The reader can now see that data is missing.

Chart 3. The file was read without parse_dates, so the dates are text and Matplotlib treats each as a category: 731 ticks printed on top of each other. The fix is at read_csv, not in tick settings. With real dates there are 9 ticks.

3.1 · The lesson page's own Quick Quiz

These five questions are on the lesson page (three options each). Letters and reasons are read from the lesson.

#Question (short form)AnswerReason
Q1Typical order total and how much the totals varyBA histogram: it bins one numeric column and counts the rows in each bin.
Q2print(len(fig_q.axes), len(ax_q.lines)) after two plot callsC1 2: one Axes; each ax.plot call adds a line to it.
Q3Visible height of ax.bar(daily["store"], daily["revenue"])AEach store's single highest daily revenue: 2,903 bars pile up and only the tallest shows.
Q4Figure and AxesCA Figure is the whole canvas; an Axes is one chart on it, with its own x and y axis.
Q5A line plotted over three days with no rowsAA straight segment across the gap. Restore the calendar with asfreq so the days hold NaN and the line breaks.

Warm-up Answers

  1. You resample daily revenue to monthly totals. What do you print beside every total? Answer: The count of days with a value. Sums skip NaN silently, so a month with missing days looks like a weak month.
  2. What does wide.asfreq("D") do to a table with dates in the index? Answer: It gives every calendar day a row. Days that had no row appear, filled with NaN, and you then decide what each gap means.
  3. On a gap-free daily Series, how many NaN values does s.rolling(7).mean() have, and where? Answer: Six, at the start. A 7-row window is full for the first time on row 7.
  4. Write a 7-day average of rev that is safe for judging today. Answer: rev.shift(1).rolling(7).mean(). Shift first, so today is not inside its own baseline.
  5. A long table holds four stores stacked in one column. What three things do you do, in order, to get each store's own 7-day average? Answer: Sort (by store, then date), group (by store), window (inside transform). The first rows of each group should come out NaN.

Exit Ticket Answers

  1. Before you build any feature, what is the first thing you decide? Answer: The unit of analysis: what one row of the table represents (a customer, an order, a store-day). Every feature must be one fact about that unit.
  2. State the cutoff rule in one sentence. Answer: For every feature: could I have computed this value on the cutoff date, using only what existed then? If not, it leaks.
  3. Name the chart for each question: (a) how did it change over time, (b) do two numbers move together, (c) which group is bigger, (d) what values are typical and how spread out are they? Answer: (a) line, ax.plot; (b) scatter, ax.scatter; (c) bar, ax.bar or ax.barh, after aggregating; (d) histogram, ax.hist, on the raw rows.

Reading the tickets: for question 1, "load the data" or "choose the features" means the unit of analysis has not landed; start Session 9 by asking what one row is in the nine-panel project. For question 2, accept any wording with "on that date" and "only what existed then". For question 3, the common slip is (c) and (d) swapped: bar and histogram look alike and answer different questions. Those learners should redo self-check Q8 and Q11.

Wrong answer or symptomWhat it revealsWhat to do
Q2 answered ['18-24', '25-34', '25-34', '35+']Believes bins include their left edge, as Python ranges do.Read (17, 24] aloud as "above 17, up to and including 24". Predict 2.9.1 shows both conventions.
Q3 answered B (one NaN)Sees the value beyond the last edge but not the excluded left edge.pd.cut(pd.Series([0]), bins=[0, 10]) on the projector; then include_lowest=True.
Q4 answered AAssumes a merge keeps the left table.The default is inner. Count rows before and after every merge; this is Session 6's first lesson again.
Q5 answered B or COrdinal and nominal are not yet separate ideas.Ask: "Is Gold more than Silver? Is referral more than social?" The first has an answer.
Q6 answered B, or exit ticket question 2 left vagueThe cutoff rule is not yet operational.Demo step 12 again: 698 customers with zero orders in the whole file, target rate 0.0. "How did the column know?"

Q11 answered with a count for the 9Does not know that range= drops values outside it.That is why the lesson's title says how many orders are not shown.
Lab 2.9-A: 45,490 rows after the mergeMerged the order lines, not the per-order summary: the unit of analysis changed from order to line."What is one row now?" Aggregate first, then merge, with validate="one_to_one".

3.2 · Subplots and Composition: self-check

Q1
What does this print?
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 3)
print(axs.shape, len(fig.axes), type(axs[1, 2]).__name__)
plt.close(fig)
(2, 3) 6 Axes
Why: Rows first, then columns: a 2 by 3 NumPy array holding six Axes. axs[1, 2] is row 1, column 2, the bottom-right panel, and it is one Axes.
Q2
After fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 4), the line axs[0, 2].set_title("Boise") fails. Why?
A) A grid must have at least two rows before panels can be titled
B) A one-row grid comes back as a 1-D array, so it takes one index: axs[2]
C) set_title only works on the figure: fig.set_title
D) The panels are numbered from 1, so the third panel is axs[1, 3]
Why: plt.subplots squeezes away dimensions of length one. One row of four is an array of shape (4,), and two indexes raise IndexError: too many indices for array. Use squeeze=False when you want two indexes every time.
A is wrong: Any grid can be titled; the problem is the index, not the shape.
C is wrong: A Figure has suptitle; each panel's title is still ax.set_title.
D is wrong: Python indexes from 0; the third panel is position 2.
Q3
Four panels show monthly revenue for four stores. When should you pass sharey=True?
A) Always: panels without a shared scale are wrong
B) Never: sharing squashes the smaller stores
C) When the reader should compare sizes across panels; separate scales show each shape but hide the differences in size
D) Only when the panels are in one row
Why: Sharing is a decision about the question. A shared y axis answers "which is bigger?"; separate axes answer "what shape does each have?". When panels do not share a scale, say so in the title or caption.
A is wrong: Separate scales are right when shape is the point, as long as the reader is told.
B is wrong: Squashing is a cost worth paying when size is the point.
D is wrong: Sharing works for any grid shape, and sharey="row" shares by row.
Q4
What does this print?
fig, axd = plt.subplot_mosaic("AAB;CCB")
print(sorted(axd), len(fig.axes))
plt.close(fig)
['A', 'B', 'C'] 3
Why: The string is a picture: one letter per cell, ; between rows. A spans two cells of the top row, C two cells of the bottom row, and B the right column of both rows. Three names, three panels, returned as a dictionary.
Q5
Which chart is an honest use of a second y axis?
A) Revenue on the left and visitors on the right, made with twinx()
B) Revenue on the left and staff on duty on the right
C) Boise's revenue on the left and Asheville's revenue on a separate right-hand scale
D) Temperature in °F on the left and the same values in °C on the right, with secondary_yaxis
Why: When both sides measure the same quantity, a formula ties the two scales together and nobody gets to choose where the lines sit. With two different measures, the scales are arbitrary and the picture can be made to say anything.
A is wrong: Two measures, two arbitrary scales: their crossings and overlaps mean nothing. Stack the panels or plot a ratio.
B is wrong: The same problem, with a causal story ready to be read into it (Lesson 4.4 takes this pair apart).
C is wrong: Two scales for the same unit hide the fact that one store is nearly twice the other.
Q6
Seven categories are drawn on a 3 by 3 grid with for ax, name in zip(axs.flat, categories):. What does the reader see in the last two cells?
A) Two empty frames with ticks from 0 to 1, until you remove them with ax.remove()
B) Nothing: zip deletes the unused panels
C) Copies of the last category
D) An IndexError, because the grid has more panels than names
Why: zip stops at the shorter input and quietly leaves the extra Axes untouched. They look like charts that failed to load. Remove them: for ax in axs.flat[len(categories):]: ax.remove().
B is wrong: zip only stops looping; it does not touch the figure.
C is wrong: Nothing is drawn on the leftover panels at all.
D is wrong: zip never raises for unequal lengths.

3.2 · Predict, then run: answers

Predict 3.2.1
Three grids. What type or shape does each give back?
a = plt.subplots(1, 1)[1]
b = plt.subplots(2, 1)[1]
c = plt.subplots(2, 1, squeeze=False)[1]
print(type(a).__name__, b.shape, c.shape)
plt.close("all")
Axes (2,) (2, 1)
Why: A 1 by 1 grid is squeezed to a single Axes. One column of two is squeezed to a 1-D array of shape (2,). squeeze=False keeps the full 2-D shape (2, 1).
Predict 3.2.2
Two panels with very different data and sharey=True. Same y range or not?
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharey=True)
axs[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 10])
axs[1].plot([0, 1], [0, 2])
print(axs[0].get_ylim() == axs[1].get_ylim())
plt.close(fig)
True
Why: With a shared y axis both panels use one range that fits all the data, here the range of the first panel. The second line now sits low in its panel, which is the honest picture: it is the smaller one.
Predict 3.2.3
A period in the layout picture. How many panels, with which names?
fig, axd = plt.subplot_mosaic([["main", "side"],
                               ["main", "."]])
print(list(axd), len(fig.axes))
plt.close(fig)
['main', 'side'] 2
Why: "main" covers both rows of the left column, so it is one tall panel. "." leaves its cell empty: no panel is made for it. Two names, two Axes.

3.2 · Lab reference solutions

Lab 3.2-A · Foot traffic on one page: labs/module-09/l3_2-subplots-composition/traffic_panels_solution.py

What it practices: a grid and its array, zip(axs.flat, ...), separate against shared scales, suptitle and supylabel, a panel-drawing function for small multiples, and subplot_mosaic with named panels.

The question's answer: comparing mean daily visitors in 2025 with 2024, Flagstaff +21.0%, Boise +9.2%, Bend +2.5%, Asheville -7.5%. The small multiples show it best: Flagstaff's colored line climbs through the gray ones.

Step 1 against Step 2. Own scales: y ranges of roughly (203, 341), (238, 418), (303, 629) and (191, 446), so every line fills its panel and the stores look alike. Shared: one range, and Boise sits well above the rest. A learner who leaves the Step 1 title without saying "each panel has its own scale" has missed the point of the step.

Step 3. Draw the gray lines first and the colored line last; otherwise the gray paints over it. Each panel holds 4 lines.

Step 4. 725 Flagstaff rows (two failed export days). The busiest weekday is Saturday with about 482 visitors; the quietest weekday averages about 252. The histogram needs no dropna() here because visitors have no blank values, unlike revenue in the lesson's Boise version.

Lab 3.2-B · Two measures, honestly: labs/module-09/l3_2-subplots-composition/honest_axes_solution.py

What it practices: twinx() and why it misleads, stacked panels with sharex=True, computing the relationship instead of drawing two lines, and secondary_yaxis with a pair of conversion functions.

Step 1. Same data, right axis 0 to 20 in one panel and 0 to 60 in the other: in the first the rainy-day line swings across the visitors line, in the second it lies flat along the bottom. The figure has 4 Axes (each panel plus its twin).

Step 3 is the discussion. Month by month the correlation of rainy days and mean visitors is only 0.28: the season dominates (summer brings both more rain and more visitors in Asheville). Day by day the effect is clear: 286.8 visitors on dry days against 236.4 on rainy days, -17.6%, the same number as the Lesson 3.1 project. The level of aggregation changes the answer; a twin-axis chart of monthly totals would have hidden the real effect.

Step 4. The warmest month is August 2025 at 86.6 °F (30.3 °C). Nobody chose the right-hand scale: a formula did. That is the test for an honest second axis.

Step 3: monthly correlation of rainy days and visitors: 0.28
        mean visitors on dry days: 286.8 | on rainy days: 236.4 (-17.6%)

3.3 · Customizing Plots: self-check

Q7
A chart shows the monthly online return rate for 2024 and 2025; both lines wobble between about 5.7% and 9.1%. Which title serves a reader best?
A) Online return rate by month
B) Online returns are rising
C) The online return rate held near 7% in both years
D) Why customers send things back
Why: It states what the chart shows, in words a reader can check against the lines. What is plotted (monthly rate, online orders, 2024 to 2025) goes in the subtitle.
A is wrong: A description, not a finding: it spends the most-read text on the chart without saying anything.
B is wrong: A claim the data does not support (the yearly rate went from 7.11% to 6.76%). A finding title can be wrong; check it with a number.
D is wrong: The chart shows how often, not why. Causes stay out of a title unless they have been tested.
Q8
What does this print?
x = 1234567
print(f"${x / 1000:,.0f}K", "{x:.1%}".format(x=0.0712))
$1,235K 7.1%
Why: The first divides by 1,000, rounds to no decimals and adds thousands separators: the FuncFormatter recipe for thousands of dollars. The second multiplies by 100 and adds the percent sign. Matplotlib fills the field named x with each tick value.
Q9
A heatmap shows each store's revenue change against the same month last year, from -12.6% to +29.0%. Which color choice fits?
A) A qualitative palette such as Okabe-Ito, one color per cell
B) A sequential map such as viridis, from the lowest change to the highest
C) A diverging map such as RdBu, with the limits set symmetric around zero
D) A rainbow map such as jet, to show as many levels as possible
Why: Zero is a meaningful midpoint: shrinking and growing are different stories. A diverging map gives the two sides different hues and puts the neutral color at zero, which needs vmin=-limit, vmax=limit.
A is wrong: Qualitative colors are for unordered groups; these numbers have an order.
B is wrong: Viridis would color the small positive changes much like the negative ones, so the reader cannot see where zero is.
D is wrong: Jet's brightness rises and falls, inventing boundaries that are not in the data, and it fails color-blind readers.
Q10
A line chart has four series whose ends are well apart. Why replace the legend with direct labels?
A) The reader no longer has to look a color up in a box, and the chart works even when colors are hard to tell apart
B) Matplotlib raises a warning when a legend has more than three entries
C) Direct labels make the figure render faster
D) Legends cannot be used with gray lines
Why: A legend is a lookup table: find a line, note its color, find it in the box, read the name, come back. A label at the end of each line removes the trip, and it does not depend on color at all.
B is wrong: There is no such warning. Legends are fine when lines cannot be labeled at their ends.
C is wrong: Speed has nothing to do with it; this is about the reader.
D is wrong: A legend works with any colors; with several gray lines it just becomes useless, which is the reason to label directly.
Q11
What does this print?
before = plt.rcParams["axes.spines.top"]
with plt.rc_context({"axes.spines.top": False}):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
inside = ax.spines["top"].get_visible()
plt.close(fig)
print(before, inside, plt.rcParams["axes.spines.top"])
True False True
Why: The figure was created inside the with block, so it was built with the style: no top spine. When the block ends the setting goes back to the default, True, for everything drawn afterward.
Q12
Which edit makes a bar chart of 2025 store revenue misleading?
A) Removing the top and right spines
B) Starting the y axis at $1.5 million to "show the differences better"
C) Adding a faint horizontal grid behind the bars
D) Writing each bar's value on it with bar_label
Why: A bar's length is its value. With the axis cut at $1.5 million, Boise's bar is drawn about four and a half times as tall as Asheville's, although Boise sells less than twice as much. Bars start at zero.
A is wrong: Removing ink that carries no information is clean-up, not distortion.
C is wrong: A faint grid helps the reader estimate values and stays out of the way.
D is wrong: Direct value labels add information and remove a trip to the axis.

3.3 · Predict, then run: answers

Predict 3.3.1
Two format strings. What does each produce?
print("{x:,.0f}".format(x=1234.6), "${x:,.2f}".format(x=7))
1,235 $7.00
Why: , adds thousands separators and .0f rounds to no decimals: 1,235. .2f always shows two decimals, so 7 becomes $7.00. Matplotlib does exactly this with each tick value.
Predict 3.3.2
Which sides of the frame are still visible?
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
print([side for side in ax.spines if ax.spines[side].get_visible()])
plt.close(fig)
['left', 'bottom']
Why: An Axes has four spines: left, right, bottom, top. Hiding two leaves the left and bottom ones, the usual clean frame.
Predict 3.3.3
Three positions and three labels. What do the tick labels say?
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1])
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.5, 1], labels=["start", "middle", "end"])
print([t.get_text() for t in ax.get_xticklabels()])
plt.close(fig)
['start', 'middle', 'end']
Why: set_xticks with labels= fixes the positions and the text together, one label per position. With only two labels for three positions it would raise a ValueError instead.

Lab 3.3-A · From first draft to finished chart: labs/module-09/l3_3-customizing-plots/finish_chart_solution.py

What it practices: checking a finding with numbers, a headline with a subtitle, FuncFormatter, set_xticks with labels, gray plus one, direct labels, an annotation with an arrow, and clean-up, all as small functions that take an ax.

Step 1 decides the headline. 2025 beat 2024 in all 12 months; the largest gap is August (+$33,144), the smallest December (+$4,803); the year went from $1,077,801 to $1,280,184 (+18.8%, the Online growth figure from Lesson 2.4). "Online revenue beat 2024 in every month of 2025" is supported; "online revenue soared" is an adjective, not a finding.

Step 3. The x values are month numbers, so this is not a date axis: ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13), labels=MONTHS) sets positions and labels together. A learner who reaches for mdates here will get odd results; ask what type the x values are.

Steps 4 and 5. Expected checks: y labels $0K, $20K, $40K, $60K; visible spines ['left', 'bottom']; ax.get_legend() returns None. The annotation position takes a few tries; that is normal.

What it practices: choosing a palette type from the data (sequential against diverging), ax.imshow with aspect="auto", a colorbar as the legend of a colormap, tick labels for a grid, and centering a diverging map.

Step 1. Cells run from 214 to 588 mean visitors per day; Boise's row is brightest in every month, and summer and December are bright for every store.

Step 2. Changes run from -12.6% to +29.0%. With symmetric limits (-29.0 to 29.0) white means "no change". With the data's own limits the neutral middle of the map would sit at about +8%, so small gains would look like losses. That is the one line of the lab that matters.

Warm-up Answers

  1. Before you build a feature table, what is the first thing you decide? Answer: The unit of analysis: what one row represents. Every feature must be one fact about that unit.
  2. After a left merge of per-customer summaries, which NaN values become 0 and which stay missing? Answer: Counts and sums become 0 (true statements). Averages, shares and recency stay missing; add a flag such as has_ordered.
  3. State the cutoff rule. Answer: For every feature: could I have computed this value on the cutoff date, using only what existed then? If not, it leaks.
  4. What is the difference between a Figure and an Axes? Answer: The Figure is the whole canvas, the thing that gets saved. An Axes is one chart on it, with its own x and y axis.
  5. ax.bar(daily["store"], daily["revenue"]) draws four bars and no error. What are their heights? Answer: Each store's single highest day: 2,903 bars pile up at four positions and the tallest shows. ax.bar never aggregates; group first.

Exit Ticket Answers

  1. What does plt.subplots(2, 2) give you in axs, and what is the safest way to loop over the panels? Answer: A 2-D NumPy array of four Axes. Loop with for ax, item in zip(axs.flat, items):, which works for every grid shape.
  2. Why is a twin-axis chart of two different measures risky, and what do you draw instead? Answer: The two scales are arbitrary, so where the lines sit, cross or overlap can be changed without changing the data. Stack two panels with sharex=True, or plot the ratio itself.
  3. Rewrite the title "Monthly online revenue, 2024 and 2025" as a finding, and say what you checked first. Answer: For example "Online revenue beat 2024 in every month of 2025", after checking that the 2025 value is higher in all 12 months (it is; the smallest gap is December, $4,803).

Reading the tickets: question 1 answered with "a list" or with for ax in axs (which loops over rows of a 2-D array) needs the shape table again at the start of Session 10. For question 2 accept "the scales can be chosen" in any words; "it looks cluttered" misses the point. For question 3 the check matters more than the wording: a ticket with a headline and no check is the learner to talk to first next time.

How this key is organized

3.4 · Saving Figures: self-check

Q1
A figure is created with figsize=(9, 5) and saved with fig.savefig("sales.png", dpi=120). How many pixels is the image?
A) 900 wide by 500 high
B) 1,080 wide by 600 high
C) 600 wide by 1,080 high
D) 129 wide by 125 high
Why: pixels = inches x dpi, one dimension at a time: 9 x 120 = 1,080 wide and 5 x 120 = 600 high.
A is wrong: That is the size at the default 100 dpi; the call asks for 120.
C is wrong: figsize is (width, height), so the 9 belongs to the width.
D is wrong: dpi multiplies the inches. It is not added to them.
Q2
What does this print?
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
fig.savefig("q2.png", dpi=50)
print(plt.imread("q2.png").shape[:2])
(150, 200)
Why: plt.imread returns an array shaped (rows, columns, channels), so the height comes first: 3 x 50 = 150 rows and 4 x 50 = 200 columns. A common wrong answer is (200, 150): width first, the way figsize is written.
Q3
Two PNG files are both 1,600 by 800 pixels. File A came from figsize=(16, 8) at dpi=100, file B from figsize=(8, 4) at dpi=200. Which statement is true?
A) The two images are identical, because the pixel counts are identical
B) B is blurrier, because its sheet was smaller
C) A holds more detail, because its figure was larger
D) In B the text, lines and markers are twice as large relative to the chart
Why: Text and line widths are measured in points (1/72 inch), so they take up twice the share of an 8-inch sheet that they take of a 16-inch sheet. The dpi then scales the whole sheet to the same 1,600 pixels.
A is wrong: Same pixel count, different drawing: the sheet size decided how big the text is on the sheet.
B is wrong: Both files have exactly 1,600 by 800 pixels; neither is blurrier.
C is wrong: Detail in a PNG is its pixel count, and the counts are equal.
Q4
A scatter plot of 200,000 points must go into a printed report as a PDF. The file is huge and slow to open. What is the best fix?
A) Pass rasterized=True to the scatter layer and keep saving as PDF
B) Save as JPEG instead, because JPEG files are small
C) Lower the dpi of the PDF to 50
D) Add bbox_inches="tight" to the save call
Why: A vector file stores one drawing instruction per dot. Rasterizing only the heavy layer turns the dots into an embedded image, while the axes, title and labels stay sharp vector text.
B is wrong: JPEG smears sharp edges and text; the lesson says never to use it for charts.
C is wrong: Vector marks have no dpi, so the 200,000 instructions are all still there.
D is wrong: That changes the saved area, not the number of marks in the file.
Q5
A chart is saved with transparent=True and pasted onto a dark slide. The title and tick labels cannot be seen. Why?
A) Transparent PNG files cannot contain text
B) The slide program removed the labels when it resized the image
C) Only the background became transparent; the text is still black, on a dark slide
D) The dpi was too low for the labels to be drawn
Why: transparent=True removes the figure's background and nothing else. Black labels on a dark page disappear. Draw the chart in a dark style, or save with a solid facecolor="white".
A is wrong: The text is in the file; it is simply the same color as what is behind it.
B is wrong: Resizing does not delete parts of an image.
D is wrong: A low dpi gives fewer pixels, not missing labels.
Q6
What does this print?
plt.close("all")
first, ax = plt.subplots()
second, ax = plt.subplots()
first.savefig("q6.png")
plt.close(first)
print(len(plt.get_fignums()))
1
Why: Saving a figure does not close it. Two figures were created and one was closed, so pyplot is still holding second. In a loop that makes hundreds of charts this is how memory fills up: create, draw, save, close.

4.1 · Descriptive Statistics I: Center and Spread: self-check

Q7
What does this print?
print(pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40, 400]).median())
A) 100.0
B) 30.0
C) 25.0
D) 400
Why: The median is the middle value of the sorted list. With five values that is the third one, 30. The 400 could be 4,000,000 and the answer would not change.
A is wrong: That is the mean (500 / 5): the balance point, dragged up by the 400.
C is wrong: That is the mean of the two values next to the middle of the first four; there are five values, so there is a single middle.
D is wrong: That is the maximum.
Q8
orders["payment_method"] holds the words card, digital_wallet, cash and gift_card. Which summary of its center makes sense?
A) The mean
B) The median
C) The mode
D) The standard deviation
Why: Categories cannot be added or put in order, so the only center is the most common value: .mode() (card, with 12,392 of the 20,302 orders).
A is wrong: .mean() on text raises TypeError: Cannot perform reduction 'mean' with string dtype.
B is wrong: A median needs an order from smallest to largest; payment methods have none.
D is wrong: That is a measure of spread, and it needs numbers.
Q9
What does this print?
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
print(np.var(x), pd.Series(x).var())
2.0 2.5
Why: The squared deviations from the mean (3) are 4, 1, 0, 1, 4: a sum of 10. NumPy divides by n (10 / 5 = 2.0, ddof=0); pandas divides by n - 1 (10 / 4 = 2.5, ddof=1).
Q10
Pinecrest's order totals have a mean of $194.60, a median of $146.85 and a mode of $53.90. Finance wants a revenue forecast for 1,000 orders next month. Which number do you multiply by 1,000?
A) The mean, $194.60
B) The median, $146.85
C) The mode, $53.90
D) The midpoint of the mean and the median
Why: Only the mean multiplies back to a total: mean x count = sum. The median describes a typical order, and it would understate revenue by about a quarter here.
B is wrong: 20,302 orders x $146.85 is about $2.98 million; the real total is $3.95 million.
C is wrong: The mode of a measured quantity is mostly an accident: $53.90 is 114 of 20,302 orders.
D is wrong: An invented number that is neither the typical order nor the total divided by the count.
Q11
One order in a column of 20,000 order totals was typed as $1,000,000 by mistake. Which pair of summaries barely changes?
A) Mean and standard deviation
B) Range and standard deviation
C) Mean and range
D) Median and interquartile range
Why: The median and the IQR depend only on the order of the values near the middle. One extreme row is just "one more value above the middle". They are robust.
A is wrong: Both are built from every value's distance, so one huge value has huge leverage: in the lesson the SD went from $178.76 to $7,019.02.
B is wrong: The range IS the two extremes, and the SD squares the distance to the bad row.
C is wrong: The mean rose by $49 in the lesson's stress test, and the range became $999,993.62.
Q12
What does this print?
revenue = pd.Series([100.0, np.nan, 300.0])
print(revenue.mean(), np.mean(revenue.to_numpy()), revenue.count())
A) 200.0 nan 2
B) 133.33 nan 3
C) 200.0 200.0 3
D) nan nan 2
Why: pandas skips missing values (skipna=True), so its mean is (100 + 300) / 2. NumPy's np.mean does not skip: one nan makes the answer nan, with no error. .count() counts the values that are present.
B is wrong: pandas does not treat the missing value as 0, and .count() leaves it out.
C is wrong: np.mean returns nan; np.nanmean is the NumPy function that skips.
D is wrong: The pandas method skips the missing value instead of spreading it.

Predict, Then Run: answers

Predict 3.4-1
What does this print? (Careful: which number comes first?)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 2))
fig.savefig("charts/p1.png", dpi=300)
plt.close(fig)
print(plt.imread("charts/p1.png").shape[:2])
(600, 1500)
Why: shape is (rows, columns): the height comes first. 2 inches x 300 dpi = 600 rows, and 5 x 300 = 1,500 columns.
Predict 3.4-2
What two numbers does this print?
for i in range(3):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    fig.savefig(f"charts/p2_{i}.png")
print(len(plt.get_fignums()))
plt.close("all")
print(len(plt.get_fignums()))
3
0
Why: Saving does not close a figure, so after the loop pyplot is still holding all three. plt.close("all") releases them. In your own loops, close each figure right after saving it.
Predict 4.1-1
Three numbers: the mean, the median and the mode. Predict all three.
s = pd.Series([3, 5, 5, 8, 50])
print(s.mean(), s.median(), s.mode()[0])
14.2 5.0 5
Why: The sum is 71, so the mean is 14.2: larger than four of the five values, because the 50 has leverage. The middle value of the sorted list is 5, and 5 is also the only value that appears twice.
Predict 4.1-2
Same three numbers, two libraries. What does each print?
x = np.array([2, 4, 9])
print(np.var(x), pd.Series(x).var())
8.666666666666666 13.0
Why: The mean is 5 and the squared deviations are 9, 1 and 16: a sum of 26. NumPy divides by n = 3 (8.67); pandas divides by n - 1 = 2 (13.0). With only three values the two differ by a third.

The Lesson Pages' Own Quick Quizzes

Each lesson page ends with a five-question Quick Quiz (three options each). Learners do them at home; these are the correct options and the lesson's own reasons.

Lesson 3.4: Q1 C, Q2 B, Q3 A, Q4 B, Q5 A

Lesson 3.4 · Quiz 1
A figure is created with figsize=(8, 4) and saved with fig.savefig("chart.png", dpi=150). How large is the image?
C) 1,200 by 600 pixels
Why: Pixels are inches times dpi: 8 times 150 is 1200 wide and 4 times 150 is 600 high.
Lesson 3.4 · Quiz 2
What does this print?
quiz_fig, _ = revenue_chart("Bend", figsize=(6, 3))
quiz_fig.savefig(out / "quiz.png", dpi=200)
plt.close(quiz_fig)
print(plt.imread(out / "quiz.png").shape)
B) (600, 1200, 4)
Why: The array shape is rows, columns, channels. The image is 3 inches high at 200 dpi, so 600 rows, and 6 inches wide, so 1200 columns, with 4 channels: red, green, blue and alpha.
Lesson 3.4 · Quiz 3
A line chart is going into a printed annual report, and the designer may need to resize it during layout. Which format is the best choice?
A) PDF or SVG, because vector files stay sharp at any size
Why: A vector file stores drawing instructions instead of pixels, so it stays sharp at any size the designer chooses, and its text remains real text.
Lesson 3.4 · Quiz 4
A chart saved from figsize=(16, 9) at dpi=120 fills a slide exactly (1,920 by 1,080), but nobody can read the labels. What is the best fix?
B) Use figsize=(8, 4.5) at dpi=240
Why: Text is sized in points, a fixed fraction of an inch, so on a smaller sheet it takes up more of the chart. Halving the figure size and doubling the dpi keeps 1920 by 1080 pixels and makes the text twice as large.
Lesson 3.4 · Quiz 5
A script saves 300 charts in a loop and gets slower and slower until it runs out of memory. What is missing?
A) plt.close(fig) after each savefig
Why: pyplot keeps every figure it creates until it is closed. Closing each figure after saving it releases its memory, so the loop uses the same small amount for every chart.

Lesson 4.1: Q1 B, Q2 A, Q3 C, Q4 A, Q5 C

Lesson 4.1 · Quiz 1
Pinecrest's order totals have a mean of $194.60 and a median of $146.85. What is the best explanation?
B) A long tail of large orders pulls the mean up, while the median stays with the bulk of the orders
Why: The distribution is right-skewed. Large orders have leverage on the mean, the balance point, but each of them counts as just one value above the middle for the median.
Lesson 4.1 · Quiz 2
What does this print?
ratings = np.array([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])
print(np.std(ratings))
A) 2.0, because NumPy divides the sum of squared deviations by n
Why: The mean is 5 and the squared deviations add up to 32. NumPy divides by n, which is 8, giving a variance of 4 and a standard deviation of 2.0. pandas would divide by 7 and print about 2.14.
Lesson 4.1 · Quiz 3
A column of delivery times is strongly right-skewed and may contain a few data-entry errors. Which pair of summaries describes it most faithfully?
C) Median and interquartile range
Why: The median and the IQR depend only on the order of the values near the middle, so a long tail or a few bad rows barely move them.
Lesson 4.1 · Quiz 4
What does this print?
pay = pd.Series(["card", "cash", "card", "gift_card", "cash"])
print(pay.mode().tolist())
A) ['card', 'cash']
Why: card and cash both appear twice, so there is a tie, and mode() returns a Series containing every winner, sorted.
Lesson 4.1 · Quiz 5
Store A took 10 orders with a mean of $100. Store B took 90 orders with a mean of $200. What is the mean of all 100 orders?
C) $190
Why: Total dollars are 10 x 100 + 90 x 200 = 19,000 over 100 orders, so the mean is 190. Group means must be weighted by group size, never averaged directly.

Warm-up and Exit Ticket Answers

Warm-up
  1. fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2): what kind of object is axs, and what loop visits every panel whatever the grid shape? Answer: A 2-D NumPy array of Axes. for ax, group in zip(axs.flat, groups): works for every grid shape.
  2. What does sharey=True buy you in a grid of panels, and what does it cost? Answer: Heights become comparable across panels. The cost: small series are flattened, so shape is harder to see. Choose on purpose and tell the reader.
  3. Why is a twin-axis chart with two different measures risky, and what should you draw instead? Answer: The two scales are arbitrary, so the chart can be made to say almost anything. Use stacked panels with a shared x axis, or plot a ratio.
  4. What should a finished chart's title say? And the subtitle? Answer: The title states the finding. The subtitle says what is plotted, the units and the period.
  5. You have a dictionary of style settings. How do you apply it to one block of plotting code without changing the rest of the session? Answer: with plt.rc_context(style_dict): around the block.
Exit ticket
  1. A figure has figsize=(6, 4) and is saved with dpi=150. How many pixels wide and high is the PNG? Answer: 900 wide by 600 high (6 x 150 and 4 x 150).
  2. A column of order totals is strongly right-skewed. Which measure of center and which measure of spread do you report for a typical order? Answer: The median and the IQR. (The mean is for totals.)
  3. np.std(x) and pd.Series(x).std() give different answers for the same small list. Why? Answer: NumPy divides by n (ddof=0); pandas divides by n - 1 (ddof=1).

Common Wrong Answers and What They Reveal

What you see or hearWhat it revealsWhat to do
"I raised the dpi and the text is still tiny."They think of dpi as zoom on the text. They have one knob in their head, not two.Back to the sheet and the scanner. Halve the figsize, double the dpi, compare the two files and their imread shapes.
Self-check Q2 answered (200, 150).They read shape as (width, height), the order used by figsize."Rows first, like a DataFrame." Have them print image.shape for a tall, narrow figure.
A blank PNG and no error.plt.savefig() saved pyplot's current figure, not theirs; or they saved after plt.show() in a script.Ask them to point at the figure's name in the save line. Rewrite it as fig.savefig(...).
Q3 answered "identical, the pixel counts are the same".They equate an image with its pixel dimensions and have not connected points to inches.Open the lesson's side-by-side figure or the lab's two newsletter files. Ask what an 11-point label means on each sheet.
"The median is $147, so 20,302 orders bring in about $2.98 million."They treat every center as interchangeable; they have not met the idea that only the mean multiplies back to a total.Compute totals.sum() and both products. The mean is for totals, the median for typical.
"The mean is wrong because of outliers; delete the bulk orders."They believe skew is caused by a handful of errors.Rerun the demo's bulk check: removing the twelve moves the mean by $2. The whole tail does it, and the bulk orders are real.
Q9 answered 2.5 2.5 or 2.0 2.0.They do not know the two libraries have different defaults.Have them run np.std(x), pd.Series(x).std() and np.std(x, ddof=1) on five numbers and say which two match.
Q12 answered nan nan 2.They expect pandas to behave like NumPy with missing values (or the reverse).Print revenue.count() next to len(revenue), then revenue.mean() and np.mean(revenue.to_numpy()).

Session 11 12 self-check items Lessons 4.2–4.3 Confidential
How this key is organized

Each item shows all four options with the correct one marked, then why it is right and why each other option is wrong.
