5.2 · Complex Queries: self-check

Q7
orders has 20,302 rows; 739 of them have a customer_id that is not in customers; 1,058 customers have never ordered. How many rows does orders JOIN customers ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id return?
A) 20,302
B) 19,563
C) 21,360
D) 19,244
Why: A plain JOIN is an inner join: only orders that found a customer survive. 20,302 - 739 = 19,563. The 739 rows vanish with no error.
A is wrong: That is the LEFT JOIN count: every order kept, 739 of them with an empty customer side.
C is wrong: That is the FULL OUTER JOIN: 19,563 + 739 + 1,058.
D is wrong: Customers without orders have no order row to lose, so 1,058 is not subtracted.
Q8
What does this print?
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.executescript("""
    CREATE TABLE o (id INTEGER, total REAL);
    CREATE TABLE i (order_id INTEGER, sku TEXT);
    INSERT INTO o VALUES (1, 100), (2, 50);
    INSERT INTO i VALUES (1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (1, 'c'), (2, 'd');
""")
sql = "SELECT SUM(o.total) FROM o JOIN i ON i.order_id = o.id"
print(conn.execute(sql).fetchone()[0])
350.0
Why: Order 1 has three lines, so its total of 100 appears three times after the join; order 2 appears once. 300 + 50 = 350, not the true 150. This is the fan-out trap: sum a column at the level where it lives.
Q9
Which query lists the customers who have never placed an order?
A) SELECT c.* FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
B) SELECT c.* FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
C) SELECT c.* FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id = NULL
D) SELECT c.* FROM orders AS o LEFT JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL
Why: The anti-join: keep every customer with LEFT JOIN, then keep the rows where the order side is empty. It returns the 1,058 customers with no orders.
B is wrong: An inner join has already thrown away customers with no order, so nothing is left to find.
C is wrong: = NULL is never true. Test for NULL with IS NULL.
D is wrong: That starts from orders: it finds the 739 orders with no customer, the opposite question.
Q10
359 of the 20,302 orders used the code TRAIL15. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE promo_code <> 'TRAIL15' returns 1,789, not 19,943. Why?
A) <> is not a valid operator in SQLite
B) The query needs DISTINCT
C) Text comparison ignores case, so some codes were double counted
D) For the 18,154 orders with no code the comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true
Why: NULL means unknown, so NULL <> 'TRAIL15' is unknown and the row is skipped. To mean "every order that did not use TRAIL15", add OR promo_code IS NULL or compare COALESCE(promo_code, 'none').
A is wrong: <> is the standard not-equal operator (!= works too).
B is wrong: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from a result; it does not bring back skipped rows.
C is wrong: Case has nothing to do with it: 359 + 1,789 + 18,154 = 20,302 accounts for every order.
Q11
What does this print?
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
print(conn.execute("SELECT 7 / 2, 7 / 2.0, 100 * 1 / 4").fetchone())
(3, 3.5, 25)
Why: Dividing one integer by another gives an integer in SQLite (and PostgreSQL): 7 / 2 is 3. One real number makes the arithmetic real: 3.5. 100 * 1 / 4 is all integers: 25. A percentage column that is all zeros is integer division: multiply by 100.0.
Q12
A recursive CTE walks the employee tree from the CEO down. What makes the recursion stop?
A) The LIMIT that every recursive CTE must have
B) It reaches the row whose manager_id is NULL
C) A round of the recursive part finds no new rows
D) It has run once for every row in the table
Why: Each round joins the table to the rows found in the round before. When a round adds nobody (the newest employees manage no one), the loop ends and everything found so far is returned.
A is wrong: A LIMIT is a useful guard while developing, but it is not required and is not what ends a healthy recursion.
B is wrong: The row with a NULL manager is the anchor, the START of the walk.
D is wrong: The number of rounds is the depth of the tree (six levels here), not the number of rows.

5.2 · Predict, then run

P1
Output and reasoning
sql = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees AS e JOIN employees AS m"
print(conn.execute(sql).fetchone()[0])
Answer: 3025. 55 × 55. SQLite treats a JOIN with no ON as a cross join. No error; PostgreSQL would reject it. On orders and order_items the same slip would produce over 900 million rows.
P2
Output and reasoning
print(conn.execute("SELECT NULL = NULL, NULL IS NULL, COUNT(NULL)").fetchone())
Answer: (None, 1, 0). NULL = NULL is unknown (shown as None), not true. NULL IS NULL is 1 (true). COUNT(NULL) is 0, because COUNT of a value skips NULL.
P3
Output and reasoning
q = "SELECT channel FROM orders"
for op in ["UNION", "UNION ALL"]:
    print(op, conn.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ({q} {op} {q})").fetchone()[0])
Answer: UNION 2 / UNION ALL 40604. UNION removes duplicates, so two copies of a column with two distinct values give 2 rows. UNION ALL stacks everything: 20,302 + 20,302.

Worked example (return rate by tier). Output as printed in the workbook: the groups add up to 20,302 orders; the inner join would have kept 19,563. A learner who writes "Gold customers are more careful buyers" has skipped Lesson 4.4's question about how the data was generated.

Why those factors: every SKU has exactly five inventory rows, so each order line is repeated five times (30,894 × 5 = 154,470). Each inventory row is repeated once per 2025 order line of its SKU, about 162 times on average. The fix aggregates each side to one row per SKU before joining; per_sku then has 242 rows and both totals are right. The join to sold is a LEFT JOIN so that a product with no 2025 sales stays, with 0. Common wrong answers: COUNT(DISTINCT ...) tricks to "undo" the fan-out (they cannot fix a sum); 52 * on_hand / sold with integers (38 instead of 38.4 overall); no guard against dividing by zero (NULLIF(sold, 0)).

5.2 · The lesson page's own quiz

  1. Question 1: A. 20,302: a LEFT JOIN keeps every order; the 739 unmatched ones have NULL on the customer side.
  2. Question 2: C. 0: the list contains a NULL, and NOT IN against a list with a NULL is never true.
  3. Question 3: B. Each order's total is repeated once for every line on the order, then summed: the fan-out trap.
  4. Question 4: A. 7: UNION removes duplicates. Four cities are shared; add Online, HQ and Warehouse.
  5. Question 5: C. In the ON clause. In WHERE the condition would discard the NULL rows and undo the left join.

Warm-up and Exit Ticket

Warm-up: retrieval from Session 13
  1. Name three of the six lines of an experiment plan. Answer: Any three of: unit, primary metric, guardrail metric, hypotheses (two-sided, alpha), sample size and duration, decision rule.
  2. Conversion went from 8.86% to 10.03%. Say the lift two ways. Answer: +1.17 percentage points (absolute) and +13% (relative). Both are correct; always say which.
  3. Why is "stop the test the first time p is below 0.05" a problem? Answer: Each look is another chance to cross the line by luck. With weekly looks the false-alarm rate was about 12% instead of 5%; with daily looks about 27%.
  4. What does "grain" mean, and what is the grain of order_items? Answer: What one row represents. One product line on an order (45,490 rows for 20,302 orders). Today's joins live or die on this.
  5. Merging 1,800 survey rows with orders on customer_id gave 9,230 rows. What happened, and what guards against it? Answer: Each response was repeated once per order of that customer. Guard: summarize to one row per customer first, and state the relationship with validate=. In SQL the same trap is called fan-out, and you will see it turn $3.7 million into $10.3 million after the break.
Exit ticket
  1. In one sentence each: what does WHERE filter, and what does HAVING filter? Answer: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped (so it cannot mention an aggregate). HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY (so it can).
  2. Why do values go into SQL through placeholders and never through an f-string? Answer: With a placeholder the SQL text and the value travel separately, so a value can never be read as part of the command. An f-string pastes the value into the command: a quote in the input can change the query (SQL injection), and an honest name like O'Brien breaks it.
  3. orders has 20,302 rows and 739 have no matching customer. How many rows from orders JOIN customers, and how many from orders LEFT JOIN customers? Answer: 19,563 and 20,302. The inner join drops the unmatched rows silently; the left join keeps them with NULL on the customer side.
Common wrong answers and what they reveal
  • "WHERE and HAVING are the same thing" (Q4, exit 1). The learner has not connected the clauses to the order they run in. Have them point at the board: where do the groups come into existence?
  • "The f-string is fine if I trust the input" (Q5, exit 2). They see injection only as an attack. Give the honest failure: a customer called O'Brien.
  • Predicting 20,302 for the inner join (Q7, exit 3). They treat a join as a lookup that cannot fail. Ask what happened to the order whose customer card is missing.
  • 150 for the fan-out item (Q8). The right total, which means the learner did not picture the joined rows. Have them write the four rows of the join by hand.
  • "NULL is like zero" (Q10, lab C). Then <> should have matched. Insist on the word "unknown".
  • "The recursion stops at the CEO" (Q12). The learner reads the tree bottom-up. Trace two rounds from the anchor on the board.

How to Use This Key

5.3 · SQL Window Functions: self-check

Q1
Which pandas line gives the same column as SUM(order_total) OVER (PARTITION BY store), one value on every order row?
A) orders.groupby("store")["order_total"].sum()
B) orders.groupby("store")["order_total"].transform("sum")
C) orders["order_total"].cumsum()
D) orders["order_total"].rolling(5).sum()
Why: transform returns one value per original row, aligned with the rows, exactly like a window function. A window keeps every row; GROUP BY (and .sum() after groupby) collapses them.
A is wrong: That returns five numbers, one per store: the GROUP BY version.
C is wrong: That is a running total over all rows, SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...), with no partition.
D is wrong: That is a moving sum of five rows, unrelated to the store.
Q2
What does this print?
rows = conn.execute("""
    SELECT v, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY v DESC, id),
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY v DESC), DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY v DESC)
    FROM (SELECT 1 AS id, 50 AS v UNION ALL SELECT 2, 70
          UNION ALL SELECT 3, 50 UNION ALL SELECT 4, 40)
    ORDER BY v DESC, id
""").fetchall()
print(rows[-1])
(40, 4, 4, 3)
Why: Order: 70, 50, 50, 40. ROW_NUMBER never repeats: 4. RANK gives both 50s the rank 2 and skips 3, so 40 is 4. DENSE_RANK does not skip: 70 is 1, the 50s are 2, 40 is 3.
Q3
SELECT ... ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rn FROM ... WHERE rn <= 2 fails. Why, and what is the fix?
A) WHERE runs before window functions are computed; compute rn in a CTE and filter it in the outer query
B) ROW_NUMBER needs a ROWS BETWEEN frame; add one
C) rn is a reserved word; rename it
D) PARTITION BY cannot be combined with ORDER BY; remove the partition
Why: Window functions are computed in the SELECT step, after WHERE. The fix is the recipe: number in a CTE, then filter outside it.
B is wrong: Ranking functions ignore the frame entirely.
C is wrong: rn is an ordinary name; the error says "misuse of aliased window function rn".
D is wrong: PARTITION BY with ORDER BY is exactly how you number rows within groups.
Q4
Which frame averages the three months before the current one, without the current month (no leakage)?
A) ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
B) ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING
C) ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
D) ROWS BETWEEN 1 FOLLOWING AND 3 FOLLOWING
Why: The frame ends one row before the current row, so the current month never sees itself. It is the SQL form of shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean().
A is wrong: Three months including the current one: a moving average, not a prior average.
C is wrong: Four rows, including the current one.
D is wrong: The three months AFTER: that looks into the future.
Q5
What does this print? (Two rows share d = 1.)
sql = """SELECT d, x, SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)
         FROM (SELECT 1 AS d, 10 AS x UNION ALL SELECT 1, 20
               UNION ALL SELECT 2, 5)
         ORDER BY d, x"""
print([row[2] for row in conn.execute(sql)])
[30, 30, 35]
Why: The default frame (RANGE ... CURRENT ROW) includes every row that ties with the current one in the window's order, so both d = 1 rows see 10 + 20. With ORDER BY d, x ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW the answer would be [10, 30, 35].
Q6
A SQL column is AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). A colleague computes df["revenue"].rolling(4).mean(). Where do they disagree?
A) On every row: SQL counts rows, pandas counts days
B) Nowhere: the two are identical
C) Only on the last row, because SQL has no following rows
D) On the first three rows: SQL averages the rows that exist, pandas gives NaN until four rows exist
Why: SQL uses whatever part of the frame exists. pandas rolling(4) needs a full window unless you add min_periods=1, which reproduces the SQL column.
A is wrong: Both count rows here (ROWS in SQL, an integer window in pandas).
B is wrong: They agree from the fourth row on, not before.
C is wrong: The frame looks backward; the last row has a full frame in both.

5.3 · Predict, then run

P1
Output and reasoning
show(MONTHLY + """
    , lagged AS (
        SELECT month, LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS year_before
        FROM monthly
    )
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS months, COUNT(year_before) AS with_a_year_before
    FROM lagged
""")
Answer: 
 months  with_a_year_before
     24                  12
LAG(revenue, 12) looks twelve rows back; only the twelve months of 2025 have one. (COUNT of a value skips the NULLs.)
P2
Output and reasoning
show("""
    SELECT NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS bucket, v
    FROM (SELECT 1 AS v UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4
          UNION ALL SELECT 5 UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7)
""")
Answer: 
 bucket  v
      1  1
      1  2
      1  3
      2  4
      2  5
      3  6
      3  7
Seven rows into three buckets: 3, 2, 2. NTILE gives the extra rows to the first buckets.
P3
Output and reasoning
show(MONTHLY + """
    SELECT month, revenue,
           LAST_VALUE(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS last_value
    FROM monthly
    ORDER BY month
    LIMIT 2
""")
Answer: 
  month   revenue  last_value
2024-01 106287.63   106287.63
2024-02 104687.91   104687.91
The default frame ends at the current row, so the "last" value of the frame is the row itself. Extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or sort the other way and use FIRST_VALUE.

5.3 · The lesson page's own quiz

  1. Question 1: B. 20,302, one per order: a window function keeps every row.
  2. Question 2: A. (30, 4, 3): RANK skips after the tie (10, 20, 20, 30 gives 1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 2, 2, 3).
  3. Question 3: C. Compute ROW_NUMBER() per customer in a CTE (newest first, with a tiebreaker) and keep rn = 1 outside it.
  4. Question 4: C. They match from the third row on; SQL averages the rows that exist, pandas gives NaN until the window is full.
  5. Question 5: A. Each store's first month gets the previous store's last month instead of NULL: the partition is missing.

5.4 · Query Optimization: self-check

Q7
Which plan line means the engine answered from the index alone and never opened the table?
A) SCAN orders
B) SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_store_date (store=?)
C) SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX idx_orders_store_date_total (store=? AND order_date>? AND order_date<?)
D) USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
Why: COVERING means the index holds every column the query needs, so the table is not touched.
A is wrong: A SCAN reads every row of the table.
B is wrong: A plain index search finds the rows in the index, then fetches each one from the table.
D is wrong: That is a sorting step, not a way of finding rows.
Q8
orders has an index on (store, order_date) and no other. Which filter can NOT seek in it?
A) WHERE order_date = '2025-07-04'
B) WHERE store = 'Bend'
C) WHERE store = 'Bend' AND order_date = '2025-07-04'
D) WHERE store = 'Bend' AND order_date >= '2025-07-01'
Why: The leftmost-prefix rule: dates are sorted only within each store, so there is no single place to jump to for a date alone (before ANALYZE, the plan is a SCAN of the index).
B is wrong: The first column of a composite index works on its own.
C is wrong: Both columns, equality on each: the best case.
D is wrong: Equality on the first column and a range on the second: exactly what the index was built for.
Q9
After DROP INDEX, you run the same EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN text again on the same connection and it still names the dropped index. What is going on?
A) The DROP did not happen until you commit
B) SQLite keeps dropped indexes until VACUUM
C) Python's sqlite3 reused its cached prepared statement, planned while the index existed; connect with cached_statements=0 or open a new connection
D) EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN always shows the plan from the first time a query ran
Why: The connection caches prepared statements by their text. Lesson 5.4 opens its connection with cached_statements=0 so that every plan is made afresh, which matters only in a lesson about plans.
A is wrong: DROP INDEX takes effect on your connection at once; committing makes it permanent for others.
B is wrong: VACUUM reclaims space; the index is gone from the schema as soon as it is dropped.
D is wrong: EXPLAIN plans the statement it is given; the stale answer comes from the cache in Python, not from SQLite.
Q10
What does this print?
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b TEXT)")
conn.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_t_a ON t (a)")
sql = "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM t WHERE a + 0 = 5"
print(conn.execute(sql).fetchone()[3])
SCAN t
Why: The index is sorted by a, not by a + 0. Arithmetic or a function around the column hides it from the index; WHERE a = 5 would give SEARCH t USING INDEX idx_t_a (a=?). The same happens with strftime('%Y', order_date) = '2025': write a range on the bare column.
Q11
A table receives thousands of inserts a minute and has nine indexes, most added "to be safe". What does each extra index cost?
A) Nothing: indexes only affect reads
B) Wrong query results when two indexes cover the same column
C) A full table scan on every SELECT
D) Slower inserts and a larger file, because every index is a sorted copy that must be kept up to date
Why: The lesson measured it: the same 45,490-row load got slower and the file larger with every index added. Index for the queries that are slow and matter; drop the rest.
A is wrong: Every insert, update and delete must update every index.
B is wrong: Results stay correct; only speed and size change.
C is wrong: Indexes never force a scan; the planner may simply not use them.
Q12
Before adding an index a query took 12 ms; after, 4 ms, each measured once. What should you do before reporting "3 times faster"?
A) Nothing: the numbers speak for themselves
B) Run ANALYZE and report the plan instead of times
C) Repeat each measurement several times, take the best, and check the plan changed from SCAN to SEARCH
D) Measure on a different computer
Why: Single timings vary, and the first run is often slowest because later runs find pages already in memory. Best-of-N timings plus a changed plan are evidence; one pair of numbers is not.
A is wrong: One before and one after can show nothing but the cache warming up.
B is wrong: ANALYZE gives the planner statistics; it does not replace measuring.
D is wrong: Another machine gives different absolute numbers and the same noise problem.

5.4 · Predict, then run

P1
Output and reasoning
plan("SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE sku = ?", ("TNT-1001",))
Answer: 
    SCAN order_items
No index on sku, so a SCAN. The Tuning Report adds idx_order_items_sku for exactly this lookup.
P2
Output and reasoning
plan("SELECT sku FROM products WHERE name LIKE ?", ("%Tent%",))
Answer: 
    SCAN products
A pattern starting with % can match anywhere, so sorted order is no help: a SCAN whatever indexes exist.
P3
Output and reasoning
plan("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY order_date", (12673,))
Answer: 
    SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_customer_id (customer_id=?)
    USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
A SEARCH on the customer index, then a TEMP B-TREE to sort that customer's handful of orders: cheap, because only a few rows are sorted.

5.4 · Worked example and lab reference notes

Worked example (product lookup). The plan changes; the time barely does, because products has 242 rows. The point is the judgment: an index that changes the plan is not automatically worth keeping. Learners who say "SEARCH, so keep it" have skipped the measurement and the cost.

same answer: True | 488 customers in Boise, ID

state and city, newest first, with (state, city, signup_date):
    SEARCH customers USING COVERING INDEX idx_customers_state_city_signup (state=? AND city=?)

after DROP INDEX:
    SCAN customers
indexes named idx_... left in the copy: 0

Points to draw out: city-only is SCAN customers USING COVERING INDEX after the composite index, which is still a scan (leftmost prefix); the speedup for state and city is modest because about one customer in ten matches; the third column removes the TEMP B-TREE because, within a state and city, the index is already in sign-up order. Common wrong answers: calling the covering-index scan a SEARCH; putting city first "because it is more selective" (then a state-only filter cannot seek); re-planning after DROP INDEX on a connection without cached_statements=0 and reporting that the drop failed.

Gold customers in the list: 300

plan of the per-customer query:

       orders   spent
count   300.0   300.0
mean     10.6  2335.2

The loop was the slow part, not SQL: 300 scans of 20,302 orders. Either fix works; together
they are best. On a server database each loop query also pays a network round trip, which no
index can remove, so the one-query version is the habit to keep.

The IN list is built from one ? per id and the ids are passed as parameters, so the Lesson 5.1 rule holds. Common wrong answers: pasting the ids into the SQL with str(tuple(ids)) (works on integers, and is exactly the habit that breaks on text); forgetting to sort before comparing the two results (row order is not guaranteed); concluding "the index makes the loop fine": it does on a local file, not where each query is a network round trip.

5.4 · The lesson page's own quiz

  1. Question 1: C. The engine read every row of the table to find the three.
  2. Question 2: A. A range on the bare column can seek in the index; a function or a leading wildcard cannot.
  3. Question 3: B. Inserts are slower and the database is larger than it needs to be.
  4. Question 4: B. Almost every row matches, so there is almost nothing to skip.
  5. Question 5: A. SCAN inventory: location is the second column of the primary-key index, so there is no place to jump to (leftmost-prefix rule).

Warm-up and Exit Ticket

Warm-up: retrieval from Session 14
  1. In one sentence each: what does WHERE filter, and what does HAVING filter? Answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. (Today adds a third stage: window functions run after both, in the SELECT step.)
  2. orders has 20,302 rows and 739 have no customer row. How many rows from JOIN customers, and from LEFT JOIN customers? Answer: 19,563 and 20,302.
  3. Total revenue came out as $10.3 million instead of $3.7 million after joining order_items. What happened, and what is the rule? Answer: Fan-out: each order's total was repeated once per line, then summed. Sum a column at the level where it lives; aggregate first (a CTE), then join.
  4. Why does WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees) return 0 rows? Answer: The list contains a NULL (the CEO's manager_id), and a comparison with NULL is unknown, so NOT IN is never true. Use NOT EXISTS or filter the NULLs out of the list.
  5. A value travels into SQL through a placeholder. What can a placeholder NOT stand for, and what do you do then? Answer: A table name, a column name or a keyword. Check the name against a fixed list of allowed names in Python, and only then put it in the query text.
Exit ticket
  1. orders has 20,302 rows and 5 stores. How many rows from SELECT store, AVG(order_total) FROM orders GROUP BY store, and from SELECT store, AVG(order_total) OVER (PARTITION BY store) FROM orders? Answer: 5 and 20,302. GROUP BY collapses the rows; a window function keeps every row and attaches the group value to it.
  2. Give the three steps of "top N per group". Answer: Number the rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY measure DESC, tiebreaker); put that in a CTE; filter the CTE with WHERE rn <= N. (WHERE cannot see a window function in the same SELECT.)
  3. You have just created an index. Name two things you check before saying it helped. Answer: Any two of: the plan for the query it was meant for now says SEARCH ... USING INDEX (or COVERING INDEX) instead of SCAN; best-of-several timings before and after; the query returns exactly the same rows; what it costs in file size and write speed.
Common wrong answers and what they reveal
  • "5 rows" for the window query (exit 1, Q1). The learner still reads OVER as a kind of GROUP BY. Show the two results side by side and count.
  • Filtering in the same SELECT (Q3, exit 2). The running order from Session 14 has not absorbed the window step. Add it to the board: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, windows, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
  • [10, 30, 35] for the tie item (Q5). The answer for an explicit ROWS frame, which means the learner has not met the default frame's RANGE behavior. That is the bug they will ship in a running total.
  • "The index makes it faster" with no plan (exit 3, Q12). Belief without evidence. Ask for the plan line and a best-of-N time every time.
  • SEARCH for the arithmetic item (Q10). The learner thinks an index is about a column name, not about sorted values. Ask: "Is the index sorted by a, or by a + 0?"

5.5 · NoSQL with MongoDB: Self-check

Q1
In the sessions collection, utm is absent from direct visits and never set to null. Which query counts exactly the sessions where the field is not there, and would still be right if some documents held utm: null?
A) {"utm": None}
B) {"utm": {"$exists": False}}
C) {"utm": ""}
D) {"utm": {"$size": 0}}
Why: $exists tests whether the field is present at all, which is the precise question.
A is wrong: None matches documents where the field is null and documents where it is missing, so it stops being exact the day a null appears.
C is wrong: That matches only documents whose utm is the empty string. No session has that.
D is wrong: $size is for lists (arrays); utm is an object, and a missing field has no size.
Q2
What does this print?
c = mongomock.MongoClient()["demo"]["notes"]
c.insert_many([{"n": 1, "tags": ["a", "b"]},
               {"n": 2, "tags": ["b"]},
               {"n": 3}])
print(c.count_documents({"tags": "b"}), c.count_documents({"tags": None}))
A) 3 0
B) 2 0
C) 1 1
D) 2 1
Why: A query on a list field matches when any element equals the value, so "b" matches documents 1 and 2. None matches a missing field, so {"tags": None} finds document 3.
A is wrong: Document 3 has no tags at all, so it cannot contain "b".
B is wrong: None in a query also matches documents where the field is missing: that is document 3.
C is wrong: Document 1 counts too: "b" is one of its two tags.
Q3
What does this print?
c = mongomock.MongoClient()["demo"]["sales"]
c.insert_many([{"store": "Bend", "units": 2},
               {"store": "Boise", "units": 5},
               {"store": "Bend", "units": 4}])
rows = c.aggregate([{"$group": {"_id": "$store", "units": {"$sum": "$units"}}},
                    {"$sort": {"units": -1}}])
print([(r["_id"], r["units"]) for r in rows])
[('Bend', 6), ('Boise', 5)]
Why: $group makes one output document per _id value ("$store" means: the value of the field store). {"$sum": "$units"} adds the units: Bend 2 + 4 = 6, Boise 5. $sort with -1 puts the larger total first.
Q4
Which pipeline stage turns every element of a list into its own document, the way explode does in pandas?
A) $unwind
B) $group
C) $project
D) $match
Why: {"$unwind": "$pages"} turned 2,400 sessions into 9,348 page-view documents, each still carrying its session's other fields.
B is wrong: $group goes the other way: many documents in, one per key out.
C is wrong: $project chooses or computes fields; the number of documents stays the same.
D is wrong: $match filters documents; it never splits one.
Q5
What does this print?
c = mongomock.MongoClient()["demo"]["visits"]
c.insert_many([
    {"id": 1, "pages": [{"path": "/cart", "seconds": 10},
                        {"path": "/sale", "seconds": 200}]},
    {"id": 2, "pages": [{"path": "/cart", "seconds": 150}]},
])
loose = {"pages.path": "/cart", "pages.seconds": {"$gte": 100}}
strict = {"pages": {"$elemMatch": {"path": "/cart", "seconds": {"$gte": 100}}}}
print(c.count_documents(loose), c.count_documents(strict))
A) 1 1
B) 2 2
C) 2 1
D) 1 2
Why: Without $elemMatch each condition may be met by a different element: visit 1 has a /cart page and (another) page of 200 seconds, so it matches the loose query. Only visit 2 spent 100 seconds or more on /cart itself.
A is wrong: The loose query also matches visit 1: its two conditions are satisfied by two different pages.
B is wrong: The strict query needs one page that is /cart and at least 100 seconds. Visit 1's /cart page lasted 10.
D is wrong: The counts are the other way round: $elemMatch is the stricter question, so it can never match more.
Q6
What does this print? (The collection holds the three sales documents from Q3.)
rows = list(c.aggregate([{"$group": {"_id": "store", "n": {"$sum": 1}}}]))
print(rows)
A) [{'n': 2, '_id': 'Bend'}, {'n': 1, '_id': 'Boise'}]
B) [{'n': 3, '_id': 'store'}]
C) []
D) A KeyError: there is no field called store
Why: Without the leading $, "store" is just a piece of text, the same for every document, so all three land in one group whose key is the word store.
A is wrong: That is what "_id": "$store" returns. The dollar sign is what says "the value of this field".
C is wrong: Nothing was filtered out; every document went into the single group.
D is wrong: MongoDB raises no error here. A wrong pipeline gives a wrong answer quietly.

6.1 · HTTP with Requests: Self-check

Q7
A script runs r = requests.get(url, timeout=10) and the server answers with status 404. What happens on that line?
A) requests raises HTTPError
B) r is None
C) The call is retried until it succeeds or 10 seconds pass
D) A normal response comes back; r.ok is False and nothing is raised
Why: To requests a 404 is a complete conversation. You get a response whose body is an error page. It only becomes an exception when you call r.raise_for_status().
A is wrong: That happens only when you call raise_for_status().
B is wrong: requests.get returns a Response or raises; it never returns None. (Our own fetch() helper does.)
C is wrong: requests never retries on its own, and timeout is not a retry budget.
Q8
What does this print?
star = "★".encode("utf-8")
print(len("★"), len(star), star.decode("cp1252") == "★")
1 3 False
Why: One character, three bytes in UTF-8. Decoding those three bytes with the wrong table (cp1252) gives three junk characters, not the star, so the comparison is False. That junk is called mojibake.
Q9
You print r.text from a category page and every rating shows â˜… 4.5. What is the first thing to check?
A) r.encoding and the Content-Type header
B) Whether the page needs JavaScript
C) r.status_code, because this means the page is a 404
D) Your timeout value
Why: Three junk characters in place of one symbol means UTF-8 bytes decoded with a Western European table, usually because the server did not name a charset. Set r.encoding = "utf-8" or parse r.content.
B is wrong: JavaScript changes which elements exist, not how a character decodes.
C is wrong: The page arrived; a 404 would give you a different page, not garbled stars.
D is wrong: A timeout raises an exception. It cannot change the characters.
Q10
What does this print? (prepare() only builds the request; nothing is sent.)
params = {"status": "returned", "since": "2025-12-01"}
prepared = requests.Request("GET", "http://127.0.0.1:8000/orders",
                            params=params).prepare()
print(prepared.url)
http://127.0.0.1:8000/orders?status=returned&since=2025-12-01
Why: params becomes the query string: a ?, then name=value pairs joined by &, in the order of the dictionary. Nothing here needs encoding, so the values appear as written.
Q11
A site's robots.txt says Disallow: /staff/ and Crawl-delay: 1. The staff page has no login. What should your collection script do?
A) Fetch the staff page, but only once
B) Fetch it with a browser's User-Agent so the site cannot tell
C) Skip the staff page, and wait at least one second between its other requests
D) Skip robots.txt: it has no legal force
Why: robots.txt is the owner's request to programs. Nothing technical enforces it, which is exactly why honoring both lines is your job.
A is wrong: Once is still going where you were asked not to go.
B is wrong: Disguising your script to get around a site's wishes breaks two ground rules at once.
D is wrong: Whatever its legal weight where you live, ignoring it is the fastest way to get blocked, and it is not how professionals work.
Q12
What does this print?
resp = requests.Response()
resp.status_code = 503
print(resp.ok)
try:
    resp.raise_for_status()
    print("fine")
except requests.exceptions.HTTPError:
    print("caught")
A) True then fine
B) False then caught
C) False then fine
D) True then caught
Why: ok is True only below 400, and raise_for_status() raises HTTPError for every 4xx and 5xx status. 503 is a server-side error, and it is still an error.
A is wrong: 503 is not a success code.
C is wrong: raise_for_status() does not let 5xx through; only 2xx and 3xx pass quietly.
D is wrong: ok and raise_for_status() always agree: both treat 400 and above as failure.

Predict, Then Run: Answers

5.5

1.

1653
1653
737

None matches null and missing, so the first two lines agree: 916 sessions with no utm plus 737 with a utm that has no campaign = 1,653. The third line asks for the 737 alone. Common wrong answer: 916 for line 1 (forgetting the sessions that have utm but no campaign).

2.

15 0

A cursor can be read once. The first list uses it up; the second gets nothing. Common wrong answer: 15 15. Fix: docs = list(cursor) and reuse docs.

3.

200
2400
1857

$size tests an exact length: 200 one-page sessions. "pages.0" is "element 0 exists", true for all 2,400. The third line counts carts whose item list has length 0: the 1,857 sessions with an empty cart (2,400 − 543 with items).

6.1

1.

200 True 2
404 False 0

Page 13 exists and holds the last 2 products. Page 14 is a 404: ok is False, and its body (the site's error page) contains no product cards. The dangerous part is that the second line raises nothing. Common wrong answer: "the second line is an error".

2.

http://127.0.0.1:8000/products?category=Tents&per_page=5&page=2

The pairs appear in dictionary order, joined by & after a ?. Common wrong answers: a path (/products/Tents/5/2), or the parameters in alphabetical order.

3.

text/html; charset=UTF-8
JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)

The content type says HTML, so .json() fails with JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0): the first character was the < of a page. Common wrong answer: "it returns an empty dictionary".

  • TODO 1 {"pages.path": "/sale"}: a condition on a list field is true when any element matches.
  • TODO 2 {**saw_sale, "converted": True} and {**saw_sale, "device.type": "mobile", "cart.value": {"$gte": 200}}. Pairs in one dictionary are joined by AND.
  • TODO 3 {"pages": {"$elemMatch": {"path": "/sale", "seconds": {"$gte": 60}}}}. 81, not 218: in 137 sessions the minute was spent on some other page.
  • TODO 4 {**saw_sale, "utm": {"$exists": False}}. Here {"utm": None} would give the same 92, because no document stores a null utm; $exists is still the query that says what you mean.
  • TODO 5 coll.find(saw_sale, {"_id": 0, "session_id": 1, "device.type": 1, "cart.value": 1}).sort("cart.value", -1).limit(3). The projection keeps the nesting: device is still an object with one key.
  • The sentence for line 6. 37 of 290 (12.8%) against 230 of 2,400 (9.6%). It is a difference between groups, not proof of cause: sessions with more page views are more likely both to include /sale and to end in an order. A full-credit answer names that.

Common wrong answers and what they reveal. 0 for TODO 1: the path was written sale or /Sale (values are exact and case-sensitive). 218 for the strict count: $elemMatch was not used. 2,400 or an error for TODO 4: "$exists" was written without quotes or placed outside the inner dictionary.

Lab 5.5-B · landing_pages_solution.py

File: labs/module-16/l5_5-nosql-mongodb/landing_pages_solution.py. Output of a real run:

1. landing pages with at least 80 sessions:
          landing  sessions  orders  order_pct
                /      1301     125        9.6
         /account        96       6        6.2
            /sale        87       5        5.7
/category/apparel        85      10       11.8
    /help/returns        83       7        8.4
          /stores        80       8       10.0
2. top five SKUs by units in carts:
     sku  units  carts
SNW-1016     16      8
KIT-1027     13      9
PCK-1008     12      7
SNW-1022     12      8
ACC-1024     11      6
3. one row per cart line: (734, 4) ['sku', 'qty', 'unit_price', 'session_id']
   pandas says the top SKU is SNW-1016 with 16 units
   total units in all carts: 1106 | lines: 734 | sessions with a cart: 543
  • Pipeline 1 is $addFields (the landing page is element 0 of the list of paths) → $group on "$landing" with {"$sum": 1} and a $cond count → $match on the group size (HAVING) → $sort. The percentage is computed in pandas because mongomock has no $round.
  • Pipeline 2 is $unwind on "$cart.items" → $group on "$cart.items.sku" → $sort → $limit. The second sort key ("_id": 1) makes the order repeatable when units tie (PCK-1008 and SNW-1022 both have 12).
  • The check flattens with record_path=["cart", "items"] and meta=["session_id"]. 543 sessions with a cart is the same 543 as the lesson's funnel.
  • Reading the result honestly. /category/apparel has the highest rate, from 10 orders in 85 sessions. That is a small sample; a learner who writes "apparel landing pages convert best" without the counts has over-read it.

Common wrong answers. One group of 2,400 in pipeline 1: "_id": "landing" without the dollar sign. An empty result in pipeline 2: {"$unwind": "cart.items"} without the dollar sign, or $limit before $sort.

Lesson Quiz Answers

Lesson 5.5: NoSQL with MongoDB

The five-question quiz at the end of sql_nosql_mongodb.html (three options each).

ItemAnswerReason
Question 1BSupport tickets are self-contained, nested and irregular, and are read whole: what a document holds well.
Question 2A916. In a query None matches null and missing; $exists tells them apart.
Question 3C$elemMatch makes one list element satisfy both conditions (path and seconds).
Question 4AAfter $group, $match filters groups: the role HAVING plays in SQL.
Question 5Cpd.DataFrame leaves nested objects as dictionaries in the cells; json_normalize flattens them.
Lesson 6.1: HTTP with Requests

The five-question quiz at the end of webscraping_requests.html (three options each).

ItemAnswerReason
Question 1BA 404 is a complete conversation: a normal response with .ok False; nothing is raised until raise_for_status().
Question 2Aparams builds ?category=Camp+Kitchen&page=2: the space is encoded as +.
Question 3Ctimeout bounds the wait to connect and the wait between bytes, not the whole download, and it retries nothing.
Question 4AMojibake: UTF-8 bytes decoded with the wrong table. Set r.encoding = "utf-8" or parse r.content.
Question 5Crobots.txt is the owner's request to programs; honoring it is the script's job.

Warm-up and Exit Ticket Answers

Warm-up (retrieval from Session 15)
  1. How does a window function differ from GROUP BY? Answer: A window function computes over a set of related rows and keeps every row; GROUP BY collapses each group to one row.
  2. Three orders tie for first place. What do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK give the fourth row? Answer: ROW_NUMBER 4, RANK 4, DENSE_RANK 2. They differ only in how they treat ties.
  3. You want the top 3 products per category. Why does WHERE rn <= 3 fail in the same query, and what is the fix? Answer: WHERE runs before window functions are computed. Number the rows in a CTE, then filter in the outer query.
  4. In EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, what is the difference between SCAN and SEARCH? Answer: SCAN reads the whole table; SEARCH jumps to the rows it needs through a primary key or an index.
  5. Name one situation in which an index does not help. Answer: Any one of: the column is wrapped in a function, the LIKE pattern starts with a wildcard, most rows match, the table is small.
Exit ticket
  1. In a pymongo query, what does {"utm": None} match, and which operator asks the precise question? Answer: Documents where utm is null and documents where it is missing. $exists tells the two apart.
  2. requests.get() comes back with status 404. What has happened in your program, and which one line makes the failure loud? Answer: Nothing was raised; you hold a normal response whose body is an error page. r.raise_for_status().
  3. Name any two of the six ground rules. Answer: Any two of: obey robots.txt; read the terms; prefer an API; go slowly and identify yourself; never go around a login or block; no personal data.

What wrong answers reveal. Question 1 answered "only null": the learner is carrying SQL's IS NULL over unchanged; show the first predict item. Question 2 answered "it raises an error": they have not yet separated "the conversation failed" from "the server said no"; rerun demo steps 6 and 7. Question 3 left blank: the ground rules were heard, not read; start Session 17 with them on paper.

6.2 · Parsing HTML with Beautiful Soup: Self-check

Q1
Which call gives you None (not an empty list, not an exception) when nothing on the page matches?
A) soup.select("p.sale-price")
B) soup.find_all("p", class_="sale-price")
C) soup.select_one("p.sale-price")
D) card["data-sale-price"] on a card without that attribute
Why: select_one() and find() return one element or None. Calling a method on that None is what produces AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ....
A is wrong: select() always returns a list; with no match it is an empty list.
B is wrong: find_all() also returns a list, empty when nothing matches.
D is wrong: Square brackets on a missing attribute raise KeyError. Use .get() to receive None instead.
Q2
What does this print?
soup = BeautifulSoup('<ul><li class="card" data-sku="A1"><b>Tent</b></li>'
                     '<li class="card"><b>Stove</b></li></ul>', "html.parser")
print([li.get("data-sku") for li in soup.select("li.card")])
['A1', None]
Why: Both items match li.card. The first has a data-sku; the second has none, and .get() returns None instead of raising KeyError, the safe way to read an optional attribute.
Q3
Your loop follows nav.pagination a.next from page to page. How does it know it has reached the last page?
A) On the last page "Next" is a plain span, so select_one("nav.pagination a.next") returns None
B) The server answers the last page with a 404
C) The last page has no product cards
D) The loop counts to 13, the number of pages
Why: The site marks the end itself: the last page has span.next.disabled instead of a link. The loop needs no page count, and max_pages stays as a seat belt.
B is wrong: Every catalog page answers 200. Probing for a 404 sends one useless request and treats an error as normal.
C is wrong: The last page has 2 cards. Stopping on an empty page would need one extra request past the end.
D is wrong: A typed count is exactly what breaks when the shop adds products. Let the site say where the end is.
Q4
What does this print?
soup = BeautifulSoup('<p class="stock low-stock">Low stock</p>', "html.parser")
print(soup.p["class"], soup.p["class"][1].replace("-", "_"))
A) ['stock low-stock'] low-stock
B) stock low_stock
C) ['stock', 'low-stock'] low-stock
D) ['stock', 'low-stock'] low_stock
Why: Beautiful Soup splits class into a list because an element can carry several classes. Element 1 is low-stock, and .replace("-", "_") turns it into low_stock.
A is wrong: class is never one string with a space in it: it is a list of class names.
B is wrong: The first value printed is the whole list, not its first element.
C is wrong: The replace call changed the hyphen into an underscore.
Q5
Lesson 6.2 fetches price-list.html with requests and passes io.BytesIO(resp.content) to pd.read_html(), instead of giving read_html the URL. Why?
A) read_html cannot read a URL
B) So that your User-Agent, your timeout and raise_for_status() apply, and pandas reads the exact bytes you checked
C) Bytes make read_html return numbers instead of text
D) BytesIO removes the second table
Why: Fetching yourself keeps the polite habits of Session 16 (identify yourself, time out, check the status) and lets you save or reuse the bytes.
A is wrong: It can, but then you have no say over the User-Agent, the timeout or what happens on an error.
C is wrong: read_html reads what a person sees either way: Price still arrives as text such as $299.95.
D is wrong: Both tables come back; you choose one with attrs={"id": ...}.
Q6
What does this print?
html = ('<table id="t"><tr><th>City</th><th>Price</th></tr>'
        '<tr><td>Bend</td><td>$1,299.00</td></tr></table>')
t = pd.read_html(io.StringIO(html), attrs={"id": "t"})[0]
print(t["Price"].dtype, t["Price"].str.replace("[$,]", "", regex=True).astype(float)[0])
str 1299.0
Why: read_html reads the visible text, so $1,299.00 arrives as a string. Removing $ and , with a regular-expression replace and converting with astype(float) gives 1299.0.

6.3 · Dynamic Pages with Selenium: Self-check

Q7
requests gets the Search page and finds 0 results in #search-results, while the browser shows 24. What should you try first?
A) Drive a headless browser with time.sleep(5) after get()
B) Find the data file the page loads (Network tab, or read its script) and, if you may, request it directly
C) Send a browser's User-Agent so the server sends the full page
D) Use pd.read_html on the page instead
Why: The page's own script fills the list from a data file (products.json). One request for the file is faster, lighter for the server and sturdier than any browser automation.
A is wrong: A browser is the last resort, and a fixed sleep is always too short or too long.
C is wrong: The server sent the same HTML it sends everyone; the list is empty until JavaScript runs. Disguising your script also breaks the ground rules.
D is wrong: There is no table in the HTML that requests received, and the results are not a table anyway.
Q8
What does this print?
print(urlencode({"q": "", "category": "Snow", "max_price": "", "in_stock": 1}))
q=&category=Snow&max_price=&in_stock=1
Why: urlencode writes every pair, empty ones included, in dictionary order, joined by &. This is the exact query string the shop's search form sends when the text boxes are left empty.
Q9
Which line waits correctly for the deals status line to exist?
A) time.sleep(3)
B) WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(EC.presence_of_element_located(By.ID, "deal-status"))
C) WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(EC.presence_of_element_located((By.ID, "deal-status")))
D) driver.find_element(By.ID, "deal-status")
Why: An explicit wait with the locator as ONE tuple: (By.ID, "deal-status"). It continues the moment the element exists and raises TimeoutException after 10 seconds if it never does.
A is wrong: A fixed sleep is too short on a slow day and wasted time on a fast one.
B is wrong: The inner parentheses are missing: the condition receives two arguments instead of one locator tuple, and fails with a TypeError.
D is wrong: That looks once, immediately, and raises NoSuchElementException if the script has not finished.
Q10
After clicking Submit on the GET search form, the demo waits twice: first EC.url_contains("category=Packs"), then for #search-results[data-loaded="true"]. Why not only the second wait?
A) The second condition is slower
B) url_contains is the only wait that raises on failure
C) The form submits twice
D) The OLD page's results are already marked loaded, so the second wait alone could pass instantly, before the new page arrives
Why: Submitting loads a new page. Until it arrives, the old page still satisfies the results condition. Waiting for the address first guarantees you are looking at the new page.
A is wrong: Speed is not the issue; correctness is.
B is wrong: Every wait.until raises TimeoutException when its limit passes.
C is wrong: One click, one new page.
Q11
You stored status = driver.find_element(By.ID, "deal-status"), called driver.refresh(), and now status.text raises StaleElementReferenceException. What happened?
A) The handle pointed at an element in the page that was replaced; find the element again after anything changes the page
B) The browser crashed and must be restarted
C) The element's text was empty
D) The wait limit was too short
Why: A WebElement is a handle on one element in one loaded page. Store the data you read, not the element.
B is wrong: The browser is fine; only the old handle is dead.
C is wrong: An empty text is just "", not an exception.
D is wrong: No wait is involved: the element you hold no longer exists.
Q12
What is in driver.page_source after the deals have loaded and Load more was clicked twice?
A) The HTML exactly as the server sent it, with an empty deal list
B) Only the 24 deal elements, without the rest of the page
C) The JSON from deals.json
D) The page's HTML as it is now, after its scripts ran: all 24 deals are in it
Why: page_source is the current document, which is why Beautiful Soup finds the deals in it while the soup from requests found none.
A is wrong: That is what requests receives.
B is wrong: It is the whole document: head, banner, navigation and all.
C is wrong: The page fetched that file, but page_source is HTML, not the data file.

None
None

Two elements carry the class price; one carries sale. The sale paragraph has no data-price, so .get() gives None, and select_one with no match gives None too. Common wrong answer: [] for the last line (that is what select returns).

https://example.com/shop/page-4.html
https://example.com/robots.txt
https://example.com/shop/products/A-1.html

urljoin resolves like a browser: a bare name replaces the last part of the path, ../ goes up one folder, and a path starting with / starts again at the site root. Common wrong answer: https://example.com/shop/robots.txt for the second line.

'★ 4.2 (31 reviews)'
'★ 4.2 | (31 reviews)'
31

With no arguments get_text() keeps the inner spacing as it is; a separator plus strip=True gives tidy pieces. The regular expression \d+ takes the first run of digits from (31 reviews).

Zero: get() returned before the page's script had added the deals. This is the race that explicit waits solve.

Warm-up and Exit Ticket Answers

Warm-up (retrieval from Session 16)
  1. In a pymongo query, what does {"utm": None} match? Answer: Documents where utm is null and documents where it is missing. $exists tells the two apart.
  2. Which aggregation stage does what pandas explode does? Answer: $unwind: one document per element of a list.
  3. requests.get() comes back with status 404. Has an exception been raised? Answer: No. You hold a normal response with .ok False; r.raise_for_status() makes it loud.
  4. Why does every request in this course carry timeout=? Answer: Without it requests waits forever for a server that has gone quiet.
  5. You see â˜… where a star should be. What happened, and what is one fix? Answer: UTF-8 bytes were decoded with the wrong table (no charset sent). Set r.encoding = "utf-8", or hand r.content to a parser that reads the page's <meta charset>.
Exit ticket
  1. Which Beautiful Soup method returns None when nothing matches, and which returns an empty list? Answer: select_one() (and find()) return None; select() (and find_all()) return a list, empty if nothing matches.
  2. Why is WebDriverWait(...).until(...) better than time.sleep(5)? Answer: It continues the moment the condition is true and raises a clear TimeoutException if it never is. A sleep is always too short or too long.
  3. Before you start a browser for a page that JavaScript fills in, what do you look for first? Answer: The data file or API the page loads (Network tab, or the page's script). If you may request it, do that instead.

What wrong answers reveal. "select returns None": mixing the two families; redo predict item 1. "Sleep is fine if it is long enough": the cost has not landed; ask what a thousand pages times five seconds is. "Use Selenium" for question 3: the order of the routes needs another pass at the start of Session 18.

6.4 · API Authentication: Self-check

Q1
The orders endpoint wants a key in the X-API-Key header. What do you get with no key at all, and with a misspelled key?
A) 401 for no key, 403 for the misspelled one
B) 403 for both
C) 401 for both
D) 404 for no key, 401 for the misspelled one
Why: 401 means "I cannot tell who you are" (no credential). 403 means "I understood, and the answer is no" (a credential that is rejected). The practice API answers missing_api_key and invalid_api_key.
B is wrong: With no key there is nothing to refuse: the server cannot tell who you are, which is 401.
C is wrong: A wrong key was understood and rejected: 403. Sending it again will never help.
D is wrong: 404 is for an address that does not exist; /orders exists.
Q2
What does this print? (ApiError is the class from the demo.)
err = ApiError(401, "token_expired", "Log in again.")
print(err)
print(err.code == "token_expired", isinstance(err, Exception))
401 token_expired: Log in again. then True True
Why: super().__init__(f"{status} {code}: {message}") sets the text that print(err) shows. The code is stored as an attribute, so a program can branch on err.code, and ApiError inherits from Exception.
Q3
What does this print?
pages = {"/o?page=1": {"items": ["a", "b"], "next": "/o?page=2"},
         "/o?page=2": {"items": ["c"], "next": "/o?page=3"},
         "/o?page=3": {"items": [], "next": None}}
items, url, calls = [], "/o?page=1", 0
while url:
    page = pages[url]
    calls += 1
    items.extend(page["items"])
    url = page["next"]
print(items, calls)
A) ['a', 'b'] 1
B) ['a', 'b', 'c'] 2
C) ['a', 'b', 'c'] 3
D) ['a', 'b', 'c', None] 3
Why: The loop reads a page, then follows next until it is None. Page 3 exists and is empty, so three pages are fetched and the items are a, b, c.
A is wrong: The loop does not stop after the first page: page 1 has a next.
B is wrong: Page 2 also points onward, so a third request is made (it returns no items).
D is wrong: next is not an item; extend adds only the items list.
Q4
In get_all() the first request sends the filters in params, then the loop sets params = None. Why?
A) To save memory
B) The next address already carries the filters; sending them again would attach every filter twice
C) The server rejects a second page that has parameters
D) To force the server to start again at page 1
Why: next looks like /orders?page=2&per_page=10&since=2025-12-15&status=returned: the filters are already in it.
A is wrong: A small dictionary costs nothing.
C is wrong: The server accepts parameters on every page; the problem is duplicates you did not mean to send.
D is wrong: Page numbers come from next; dropping params does not reset anything.
Q5
Which header sends a bearer token correctly?
A) X-API-Key: <token>
B) Authorization: <token>
C) The token as ?token= in the URL
D) Authorization: Bearer <token>
Why: The value is the scheme, a space, then the token. Without the word Bearer the practice API reports missing_token.
A is wrong: That header is for the API key, a different credential.
B is wrong: This is mistake 1 in the lesson: the server does not recognize a token at all.
C is wrong: URLs are written to logs and histories: never put a credential there.
Q6
You will share this notebook. Which line may stay in it?
A) print(API_KEY)
B) print("key loaded:", API_KEY[:4] + "...")
C) API_KEY = "pinecrest-demo-key"
D) url = f"{API}/orders?api_key={API_KEY}"
Why: A hint confirms the secret loaded without revealing it. The key itself comes from os.environ at run time.
A is wrong: Output cells are saved with the notebook: the whole key would be shared.
C is wrong: A secret typed into code travels with every copy of the file.
D is wrong: The key would end up in logs, histories and error messages.

6.5 · Rate Limiting and Retries: Self-check

Q7
A response carries X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and X-RateLimit-Reset: 3. What should your next request do?
A) Go at once: the request itself is valid
B) Switch to a second API key
C) Wait about 3 seconds, until the window starts over
D) Stop the job: the limit is used up for the day
Why: You have used this window's allowance, and the window resets in 3 seconds. Waiting is the polite move and the fastest route to a 200.
A is wrong: It will be refused with 429 and count as wasted traffic.
B is wrong: Getting around a limit with extra keys breaks the ground rules.
D is wrong: Reset is in seconds for this API, not a daily quota.
Q8
What does this print? (CaseInsensitiveDict is the type of resp.headers.)
print(int(requests.utils.CaseInsensitiveDict({"retry-after": "3"}).get("Retry-After", 1)))
3
Why: Header names ignore case, so Retry-After finds retry-after. The default 1 is not needed here, but it protects you when a 429 arrives without the header.
Q9
What does this print?
print([min(2.0, 0.2 * 2 ** n) for n in range(5)])
[0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6, 2.0]
Why: Each wait doubles (exponential backoff) and min caps it at 2.0 seconds.
Q10
The demo's Retry policy has allowed_methods=["GET", "HEAD"]. Why not retry POST too?
A) Repeating a POST can repeat its effect, such as placing an order twice
B) urllib3 cannot retry POST
C) POST requests never fail with 503
D) A POST is always faster
Why: GET and HEAD only read, so sending them twice is harmless. A POST changes something on the server.
B is wrong: It can when told to; the policy deliberately does not.
C is wrong: Any request can meet a busy server.
D is wrong: Speed has nothing to do with whether a repeat is safe.
Q11
A cache function writes resp.text to disk and only then calls check(resp). One request gets a 429. What happens on every later run?
A) Nothing: the cache refreshes itself
B) The next run raises FileNotFoundError
C) The 429 is retried automatically
D) The saved error body is served from the cache, as if it were data
Why: A cache that stores a failure serves it faithfully forever. Check first, write second.
A is wrong: This cache has no expiry: a file that exists is always used.
B is wrong: The file exists; that is the problem.
C is wrong: A cache hit never touches the network, so nothing is retried.
Q12
A job is slow because the API allows 10 requests per 5 seconds per client. A colleague suggests running three copies of the script at once. What happens?
A) It finishes three times faster
B) The limit applies to you, so the copies hit 429 three times as often and the job is no faster
C) Each copy gets its own 10 per 5 seconds
D) The server queues the extra requests politely
Why: The limit counts the client (the key, or the address). Parallel copies share it; on a public service this looks like abuse.
A is wrong: The allowance does not grow with the number of copies.
C is wrong: The copies send the same key from the same machine: one client.
D is wrong: Over the limit, the answer is 429, not a queue.

400 False | 401 False | 404 False | 429 True | 500 True | 503 True |

Only temporary failures are retried: 429, 500, 503. 400, 401 and 404 describe the request. (An expired token is the one 401 worth handling, by renewing once, which is a different mechanism.)

The schedule is min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt) with base 0.25 and cap 3; jitter draws random.uniform(0, ceiling). The policy's is_retry shows the design: GET 503 and 429 yes; 404, 401 and any POST no. The cache writes only after check(), so the 404 is raised and not saved.

Model answer

File: labs/module-18/checkpoint-2/checkpoint2_solution.py. The three parts:

conn = sqlite3.connect((DATA / "pinecrest.db").as_uri() + "?mode=ro", uri=True)
from_db = pd.read_sql(
    """
    SELECT order_id, order_date, order_total
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = ? AND order_date >= ?
    ORDER BY order_id
    """,
    conn, params=(STATUS, SINCE))
conn.close()

api_key = os.environ.get("PINECREST_API_KEY")
items, pages = [], 0
url, params = f"{API}/orders", {"status": STATUS, "since": SINCE, "per_page": 50}
while url:
    r = http.get(url, headers={"X-API-Key": api_key}, params=params, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()
    items.extend(data["items"])
    pages += 1
    url = f"{API}{data['next']}" if data["next"] else None
    params = None
from_api = pd.DataFrame(items)

Output of a real run (offline; the online run against the practice API printed the same lines):

A. database: 118 returned orders since 2025-11-01, total $25,191.92
B. key loaded: pine...
   API: 3 pages, 118 rows (the API promised 118), total $25,191.92
   unique ids: True | first date: 2025-11-02
C. same order ids: True | same total value: True
   ids only in the API: 0 | ids only in the database: 0
ANSWER: Yes. Both sources hold the same 118 returned orders placed since 2025-11-01, worth $25,191.92 in total; no order is in one source and missing from the other.

A typical partial answer: Part A correct; Part B reads only the first page (50 rows, $9,877.33) and concludes "No, they disagree". That is rubric row 3 at 0 and row 5 at 1: the sentence was honest about the numbers it had, but the pull was incomplete. Point at next in the first response.

Warm-up and Exit Ticket Answers

Warm-up (retrieval from Session 17)
  1. Which Beautiful Soup method returns None when nothing matches? Answer: select_one() (and find()). select() and find_all() return a list, empty when nothing matches.
  2. Why does get_soup() pass resp.content, not resp.text? Answer: From bytes, Beautiful Soup reads the page's own <meta charset>, so the text decodes correctly whatever the server said.
  3. How does a pagination loop know it has reached the last page of the catalog? Answer: There is no a.next link on the last page, so select_one("nav.pagination a.next") returns None.
  4. requests sees an empty list where the browser shows deals. What do you try before Selenium? Answer: Find the data file the page loads (Network tab or the script) and request it directly, if allowed.
  5. Why WebDriverWait(...).until(...) instead of time.sleep(), and where does driver.quit() go? Answer: The wait continues as soon as the condition is true and raises clearly if it never is. quit() goes in a finally block.
Exit ticket
  1. What is the difference between a 401 and a 403, and what does your program do with each? Answer: 401: no valid credential (missing, malformed, expired): fix how you send it, or renew an expired token and retry once. 403: understood and refused: stop; a person must fix the key or permission.
  2. The server answers 429 with Retry-After: 5. What does your client do? Answer: Wait at least 5 seconds, then send the request again (with a maximum number of tries). Better still: pace requests so this rarely happens.
  3. Name one failure that must NOT be retried, and say why. Answer: Any of 400, 401 (except an expired token, once), 403, 404: they describe the request, so the same request gets the same answer.

What wrong answers reveal. 401 and 403 swapped: redo predict item 1 at the start of Session 19's warm-up. "Retry immediately" for a 429: the cost to the server has not landed. "Retry everything": the difference between the request and the server's mood needs one more example.

7.1 · Statistical Graphics with Seaborn: self-check

Q1
Which of these is a figure-level seaborn function?
A) sns.histplot
B) sns.boxplot
C) sns.displot
D) sns.heatmap
Why: displot creates its own figure, can facet with col= and row=, and returns a FacetGrid. The other two figure-level functions are relplot and catplot.
A is wrong: histplot is axes-level: it takes ax= and returns an Axes. It is what displot calls for you.
B is wrong: boxplot is axes-level; its figure-level front door is catplot(kind="box").
D is wrong: heatmap draws on one Axes and accepts ax=.
Q2
What does this print?
ax = sns.histplot(data=sales, x="revenue")
print(type(ax).__name__)
A) Axes
B) FacetGrid
C) Figure
D) Histogram
Why: An axes-level function returns the Matplotlib Axes it drew on, so every Module 3 method (set_title, set_xlabel, ...) works on the result.
B is wrong: A FacetGrid comes back from the figure-level functions (displot, relplot, catplot).
C is wrong: The Figure is one level up: ax.figure.
D is wrong: There is no such class; seaborn draws with ordinary Matplotlib artists.
Q3
What does this print?
g = sns.relplot(data=sales, x="visitors", y="revenue",
                col="store", col_wrap=2, height=2)
print(g.axes.shape)
(4,)
Why: Four stores make four panels. With col_wrap the FacetGrid keeps its Axes in a flat array, so the shape is (4,), not (2, 2). Loop over it with g.axes.flat.
Q4
sales has about 60 rows for each store and month. What does sns.lineplot(data=sales, x="month", y="revenue", hue="store", errorbar=None) draw?
A) A zigzag through every daily row, in file order
B) One line per store through the monthly means, with no band
C) One line per store through the monthly totals
D) Nothing: it raises an error because x has repeated values
Why: lineplot aggregates rows that share an x value. The default estimator is the mean, and errorbar=None only removes the shaded band.
A is wrong: That is what estimator=None would do.
C is wrong: The default estimator is the mean. For totals, pass estimator="sum", or better, sum with groupby first and plot that table.
D is wrong: Repeated x values are exactly the case lineplot is built for.
Q5
A chart shows the mean staff rating (1 to 5) for four stores, about 200 answers each. Every bar runs from roughly 3.2 to 5.0. What do the bars most likely show?
A) A 95% confidence interval for each mean
B) One standard error either side of each mean
C) The lowest and highest rating given
D) One standard deviation either side of each mean
Why: Individual ratings vary by about one point, so mean plus or minus one standard deviation spans almost two points. That is spread of the data.
A is wrong: With 200 answers the interval for a mean is only about 0.1 to 0.15 either side: far shorter.
B is wrong: A standard error here is about 0.06: the bar would be barely visible.
C is wrong: Ratings run from 1 to 5, so a min-to-max bar would start at 1.
Q6
What does this print? (Two lists.)
t = pd.DataFrame({"size": ["M", "S", "L", "S"], "n": [3, 1, 2, 5]})
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(data=t, x="size", y="n", errorbar=None, ax=ax)
print([lab.get_text() for lab in ax.get_xticklabels()],
      [float(b.get_height()) for b in ax.patches])
['M', 'S', 'L'] [3.0, 3.0, 2.0]
Why: Two lessons in one line. Categories are drawn in the order they first appear (M, S, L), not sorted: pass order= when order matters. And barplot aggregates: the two S rows (1 and 5) become one bar at their mean, 3.0.

P1
Prints:

print(type(g).__name__, g.axes.shape)
FacetGrid (1, 2)

store                   
Asheville  2064.0   77.0

7.1 · The lesson page's own quiz

  1. B. scatterplot is axes-level: it accepts ax= and draws on the Axes you give it. relplot would ignore ax with a warning.
  2. C. lineplot aggregates rows that share an x: the line is the mean and the band a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval for it.

7.2 · Interactive Charts with Plotly: self-check

Q7
You run fig = px.line(monthly, x="month_start", y="revenue", color="store") in a script and nothing appears. Why?
A) The call only builds a Figure object; it is displayed when you call fig.show() (or write it to a file)
B) px.line needs kind="line" before it draws
C) Plotly needs an account before it can display a chart
D) monthly has more than one row per month, so Plotly refuses to draw
Why: Python builds a description (traces plus layout). Drawing happens in a browser, when you show the figure or open the HTML file you wrote.
B is wrong: kind= belongs to seaborn's figure-level functions.
C is wrong: The plotly library is open source and runs entirely on your machine.
D is wrong: Four stores with 24 months each is what color="store" handles: four traces.
Q8
sales has four stores and promo_day is 0 or 1. What does this print?
fig = px.scatter(sales, x="visitors", y="revenue",
                 color="store", facet_col="promo_day")
print(len(fig.data))
8
Why: Express makes one trace per combination of color and facet: 4 stores times 2 panels. Knowing how many traces to expect is the quickest check that a figure is what you meant.
Q9
Which hover_data entry shows revenue as $27,677 in the hover label?
A) "revenue": True
B) "revenue": "$%d"
C) "revenue": ":$,.0f"
D) "revenue": ":.2%"
Why: A string that starts with a colon is a d3 number format: $ adds the dollar sign, , the thousands separator, .0f no decimals.
A is wrong: True adds the column with its raw value: 27677.1.
B is wrong: That is Python's old percent formatting; Plotly uses d3-format after a colon.
D is wrong: .2% multiplies by 100 and adds a percent sign: right for a rate, wrong for dollars.
Q10
What does fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified") change on a line chart with four stores?
A) Zooming one panel now zooms every panel
B) One hover box appears for the x position under the mouse, listing all four stores
C) The four lines are merged into one trace
D) The x axes of all facets are forced to the same range
Why: Unified hover reads a time series the way people compare it: one date, every series. It is a layout setting, so it applies to the whole figure.
A is wrong: Shared zoom comes from facets sharing axes, not from the hover mode.
C is wrong: The traces are untouched: the legend still switches each store on and off.
D is wrong: Axis ranges are set with update_xaxes; the hover mode only changes the label.
Q11
What does this print?
totals = sales.groupby("store", as_index=False)["revenue"].sum()
fig = px.bar(totals, x="store", y="revenue")
print(fig.data[0].type, len(fig.data[0].x))
bar 4
Why: Four rows in, four bars out: px.bar draws one bar segment per row and never aggregates. Hand it sales itself and the same print says bar 2903.
Q12
You will email one chart to a manager who is online. Your table has one row per customer, including an email column the chart does not use. What is the right way to prepare the file?
A) fig.write_html("chart.html") from the full table: unused columns are left out automatically
B) fig.write_image("chart.html"), so that no data is included
C) Put email in hover_data so the manager can check individual customers
D) Aggregate to what you mean to publish, pass only the columns the chart needs, then fig.write_html("chart.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")
Why: The HTML file contains the data you passed to the figure as readable text. Decide what the reader may see before you build the figure; "cdn" keeps the file to a few kilobytes because the reader's browser fetches plotly.js.
A is wrong: Columns you did not map are indeed left out, but one point per customer still ships every customer's x, y and hover values; and the default embeds a multi-megabyte library.
B is wrong: write_image makes a PNG, SVG or PDF chosen by the extension; .html is not an image format.
C is wrong: That writes every email address into a file you are about to send.

P1
Prints:
fig = px.line(monthly, x="month_start", y="revenue", facet_col="store")
print(len(fig.data), len(fig.layout.annotations), fig.layout.annotations[0].text)
4 4 store=Asheville
Why: One trace per panel, and one annotation per panel: facet titles are layout annotations whose text is store=Asheville. That is why fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=")[-1])) cleans them up.

Why: px.histogram lets Plotly do the averaging, but it does it in the browser: the figure still carries all 2,903 rows. The chart shows four bars; the file holds every store-day. Aggregating with pandas first sends four numbers.

7.2 · The lesson page's own quiz

  1. C. The default include_plotlyjs=True embeds the whole library, so the file works offline. "cdn" needs the internet; False will not display by itself.
  2. A. color="store" makes 4 traces, and px.bar draws one segment per row: 2,903 in total. It never aggregates.
  3. B. Every column named in hover_data is stored in the file as readable text: the emails travel with the chart.
  4. B. Two trace types on two y axes needs make_subplots with secondary_y and graph objects. Lines by color and facets are single Express calls.
  5. A. Small multiples put every month on screen at once; an animation makes the reader compare from memory.

Lab Reference Solutions

Lab 7.1-A · labs/module-19/l7_1-seaborn/tier_order_sizes_solution.py

Merge check: 18,762 completed orders, 18,079 with a customer row, 683 dropped (closed accounts). 3,738 customers. Median order total: Basic $110.66, Silver $146.98, Gold $162.28. Mean completed orders per customer: Basic 2.05, Silver 5.12, Gold 10.81. Gold against Basic: order size ×1.47, orders per customer ×5.26.

How the solution works. The merge uses validate="many_to_one", so pandas itself would complain if a customer id repeated in customers. The left panel is sns.ecdfplot(..., hue="loyalty_tier", hue_order=tiers, log_scale=True, ax=axes[0]): an ECDF, because three overlapping histograms of a skewed quantity are hard to read. The right panel needs one row per customer first (groupby(["customer_id", "loyalty_tier"]).agg(orders=("order_id", "count"))), then sns.pointplot(..., errorbar=("ci", 95), seed=42). Finishing is Matplotlib: set_title(..., loc="left"), axis labels that name the unit and the bars, sns.move_legend.

What to accept. Any pair of titles that states the finding (order size differs modestly, order count differs a lot). A box plot or bar plot on the right is fine if the label says what is drawn. Common wrong turn: running pointplot on table with y="order_total": that answers the first question twice. A caution worth saying: tiers are defined by completed spend, so "Gold customers order more" is partly true by construction; the chart describes how they got there, it does not explain why.

Lab 7.1-B · labs/module-19/l7_1-seaborn/website_by_age_solution.py

1,800 responses, 472 with no website rating. Means by age group: 3.69, 3.67, 3.67, 3.66, 3.72 and 65+ 3.04 (n = 291, 95% CI 2.94 to 3.15); everyone else 3.68, a gap of 0.64 points. The gap is the same for online shoppers (65+ 3.06) and store shoppers (65+ 3.02). catplot returns a FacetGrid with axes shape (1, 2). No website rating: 3% of online shoppers, 46% of store shoppers.

How the solution works. Step 1 draws the same pointplot twice with errorbar=("ci", 95) and errorbar="sd". Step 2 is the hand check: agg(n="count", mean="mean", sd="std", se="sem"), then mean ∓ 1.96 × se. The left panel's bars match ci_low to ci_high (to within bootstrap wiggle); the right panel's match mean ± sd. Step 3 is sns.catplot(kind="point", col="shopper", ...), which returns a FacetGrid: titles with g.set_titles("{col_name} shoppers"), saving with g.savefig(...).

What it reveals. A learner who writes g.set_title(...) or passes ax= to catplot has not yet separated the two kinds of function. A learner who reports the 65+ gap without Step 4's caveat has the chart and not the analysis: 46% of store shoppers gave no website rating, so the store panel is the store shoppers who use the website.

Lab 7.2-A · labs/module-19/l7_2-plotly/product_map_solution.py

242 products, 8 with no rating, 234 rows in the chart. Figure with 9 traces of type scatter. Spearman correlation of price and rating: −0.01. Lowest rated: Juniper Vane Trailhead Down Jacket, $372.95, rating 2.8, 4 reviews. product_map.html is about 31 KB with the CDN link; a product name is inside the file (True) and the cost column is not (False).

How the solution works. The table is cut to five columns before the figure exists. px.scatter(..., color="category", size="review_count", log_x=True, hover_name="name", hover_data={"category": True, "price": ":$,.2f", "rating": ":.1f", "review_count": ":,"}) gives nine traces (one per category) of type scatter (234 points is under the WebGL threshold of a thousand). The hover template that comes back is <b>%{hovertext}</b><br><br>Category=%{customdata[0]}<br>List price=%{x:$,.2f}<br>Rating=%{y:.1f}<br>Reviews=%{customdata[1]:,}<extra></extra>. On a log axis an annotation's x is math.log10(price).

What to accept. Any title that states the near-zero relationship. Common wrong answers: the correlation printed as Pearson (−0.03 is not the number asked for, though the conclusion is the same); "price": "$,.2f" without the leading colon (Plotly then shows the raw value); the full products table passed to px.scatter, after which the last check prints False only by luck, because unmapped columns are not written. The habit being taught is to decide the columns on purpose.

Lab 7.2-B · labs/module-19/l7_2-plotly/promo_share_trend_solution.py

20,302 orders, 2,148 with a promo code. Weekly table (210, 4); median weekly share 6.6% online, 7.9% in store. 2 traces, hover mode x unified. Six sale weekends shaded, each four days (Friday to Monday). Share of orders using a code: 51.0% on sale-weekend days, 8.0% on all other days. January 2024 is 25.3% with no sale on: the data starts there and WELCOME10 marks a customer's first order in the data.

How the solution works. orders["order_date"].dt.to_period("W-SUN").dt.start_time labels each order with the Monday of its week; groupby(["week", "channel"]).agg(orders=("order_id", "count"), share=("used_code", "mean")) gives 105 weeks times 2 channels = 210 rows. custom_data=["orders"] carries the count so the hover can say 11.4% of 153 orders. The sale weekends are found from daily_sales.promo_day, grouped into runs of consecutive dates with (promo_dates.diff().dt.days != 1).cumsum(), and shaded with add_vrect.

The stretch question. January 2024 shows a high share with no sale: WELCOME10 marks a customer's first order in the data, and the data starts on 2024-01-01, so long-standing customers look like new ones for the first weeks. It is a small preview of a trap in one capstone question; do not say which.
